The definitive WW2 RTS experience. Hands down the best out there. 
I owned this game for several years before trying it, as coming from Company of Heroes I was intimidated by the micro-management aspect. I started playing a few months ago and I am hooked. It blows CoH out of the water in all aspects. Despite there being a few 'issues', I cannot recommend this enough for a WW2 immersion RTS game.

Pros:
- Incredibly immersive with very strong dev support. Several expansions that cover different theatres of the war with different factions, and more coming. I hope and expect in the fullness of time the game will cover every theatre.
- Sound design is so good. Rifles crack, shells whistle and whine, impacts are deadly. It's a horrifying experience.
- Micro-management adds another level of depth to the game. It's quite easy to learn, and looting fallen soldiers (allies and enemies), repairing tanks and using them is very satisfying.
- Combined arms warfare. You cannot just bum-rush the enemy with tanks like CoH. You need to combine your forces, support your tanks, secure your positions before pushing forward. One wrong move can be a disaster, one lucky shot can destroy your tanks or an enemy tank. It's brutal, merciless but incredibly rewarding and makes you play smarter as you progress.
- Variety of gameplay. Single player scripted mission, a dynamic conquest mode where you build an army, defend and attack positions, and research new units. I've not personally played multiplayer yet so cannot comment on that.
- Diverse gameplay style. You can macro manage squads of soldiers, or you can control them individually in 3rd person. You could send a squad of 12 men into cover to fire upon the enemy, or you could control 1 soldier in 3rd person to storm a trench, or control an individual tank and manually aim.
- Strong mod support in the Steam workshop.

Cons:
- Stiff animations. Soldiers have idle animations but when they are in cover or in 'combat mode' they are completely static. The 3rd person soldier animations are also a bit janky.
- Maps have this weird white edge to them which slightly breaks immersion. This is a personal con for me as you can't see into the distance, but usually it doesn't matter because you will be focused on the battlefield. 
- The learning curve is quite high, and the in-game tutorials are not great. You have to learn yourself through trial and error. 
- Voice acting is both very good, but also quite bad, especially in cinematics. Kind of odd considering how good the sound design is. 
- This might be a con depending on your playstyle, but missions take a LONG time. Expect to spend several hours on each missions. It is not an arcade game where you can just jump in, but Dynamic Conquest kind of is as you cannot save, slow time or re-start once you begin. 
- AI is quite hit-and-miss. Your soldiers will often stop moving if they encounter an obstacle, and the enemy AI seems much better at hitting you with weapons, especially mortars. Expect to fire 10-20 mortar rounds to hit a target, whilst AI can hit you with only a few.

Having been a fan of the original line of Best Way games going back to Soldiers: Heroes of WWII through Men of War Assault Squad 2 (look them up, they've all aged reasonably well at worst), when CTA and CTA: Gates of Hell branched off I had to try them both. Gates of Hell is the better of the two CTA games (to me), and the support, content and available workshop mods are outstanding.

It's a great rts game for the ww2 genre, but pathfinding and AI needs a lot of work. I have to spend way too much time micromanaging my units or else they'll make irrational decisions that get them killed. The AI seems to also favor enemy units over your own in initial engagements. Often time, your own units will not react to enemy units once they come within their line of sight. This gives the enemy ample time to wound or neutralize some of your forces which leads to losses in manpower and equipment. Enemy tanks and fire support will often hit your units in the first few attacks. It can be unbelievably frustrating at times. The AI seems to be set up in a way that gives their tanks and support fire the edge in initial engagements in conquest mode. Apart from that, soft unit AI is worse. Enemy infantry and engineers will not make entrenchments. There are no separate lines of defense around or near strong points. Entrenchments are typically only utilized by the player. Enemy AI does not fight defensively in a manner that a player would. They are only focused on holding and rushing strongpoints. They also do not utilize support call ins prior to counterattacks. They will often charge in waves. Most conquest matches seem to be a rinse and repeat of this. 

In a typical match, the player will attack enemy strongpoints that are defended by a combination of infantry and some support units. They are not entrenched and are often not positioned in a way to effectively defend the point. When defeated, the enemy AI will reinforce with waves of more infantry. Sometimes, their reinforcements will be accompanied by some armored and support units. They, however, do not react logically. Their units will be positioned in places that expose them to your line of fire. This makes them easy targets for allied units in a defensive line. The enemy will not withdraw when faced with superior fire. As the player, the only things to really look out for are enemy armor and support units. Direct and indirect fire support from enemy mortars, artillery, and AA guns that are shielded by the fog of war will often hit your units first in engagements. It is important to utilize reconnaissance units to establish line of sight and to neutralize these types of enemy units with support fire and/or call ins.

Call to Arms: Gates of Hell: Ost Front is an interesting combination of tactical level RTS and first-person shooter set during WW2 on the East Front, 1941-45. Graphics are quite good and the game offers a wide variety of equipment from both German & Soviet arsenals. The sim/FPS shooter aspect is an engaging high point. At times, combat can convey a real feel for the chaos of battle. However, numerous design flaws, & unnecessary micromanagement spoil what could be a potentially great game. 

GoH possesses an incredible amount of detail and control over individual units (particularly infantry); however, these detailed features end up causing unneeded over-complexity which leads to constant micromanagement. If the game had some decent AI that allows you to give general orders to groups of units it wouldn’t be a problem; but other than some basic defensive commands for individual units, you have no help with this respect. 

Additionally, there is little comprehensive feedback indicating what you’ve done once you’ve given orders. Location markers that note your troops destination only appear if you’re clicked onto a unit, and there’s nothing to affirm whether your unit is positively aiming at an enemy target. So you’re largely left trying to memorize what you’ve targeted & where you’ve sent numerous units. Pausing the game helps little, since this feature limits many of your unit’s actions. 

A lack of a decent battlefield overview is another major defect. The mini-map is a muddied cluster of symbols that gives inaccurate locations and a highly restricted camera narrows your overall map view down to a small segment of the battlefield. So it’s hard to get a comprehensive view of combat during battle. Frequently you’ll find yourself unable to locate enemy units at critical times when your troops are being annihilated.

On top of this, virtually all battles require some sort of needless preparation in order to complete objectives. This primarily amounts to manually supplying each infantryman with special weapons, reorganizing numerous infantry squads, hastily planting mines, or hectically sending your units to defensive locations around the map just before the enemy arrives. It’s quite time consuming and, frankly, annoying. At the very least, the game should have some sort of set up phase that allowed the player to equip & place his units on the map before the battle begins. 

So in the end, you find yourself spending much more time trying to organize, equip and command your troops than attending to the enemies attacks. When you do get around to engaging the enemy, you’ll find yourself hyper-focused on small areas of the enemy’s assault while all other parts of the map are completely ignored. In larger battles, ones where many dozens of units are involved, you’ll simply be overwhelmed by everything that’s happening. 

So, overall, Gates of Hell is a mixed-bag. It can be genuinely entertaining, but unfortunately far too frequently, it’s just an aggravation to play.

[h1]Great RTS, But the AI will make you uninstall[/h1]

This is probably the best RTS in its genre. The [b]attention to details[/b] is amazing, the [b]atmosphere[/b] and historical accuracy you feel like you're really there. It feels great to play, [i]up until[/i] it doesn't.

[h2]Why I'm so frustrated[/h2]

The game gets ruined by an [b]immense amount of AI spamming[/b] in some missions. It gets to the point where it's literally unplayable. Strategy doesn't matter when the enemy gets infinite units, as the game just turns into a meatgrinder where you focus on endlessly killing AI tanks and hoping yours survive.

To make things even worse, sometimes your own AI just picks a weird path and runs straight into the enemy for no reason. So you're fighting an enemy that's a perfect micromanager, while also trying to stop your own guys from getting themselves killed like idiots. It's frustrating as hell.

A lot of these missions are likely meant for co-op, but [b]you can't host your DLC missions for friends who don't own them[/b]. Since the game's missions are mostly locked behind DLCs, I was forced to play them alone. I can micromanage a few squads, but trying to defend a huge area against an overwhelming amount of AI attacking you (on a mission where you are the one supposed to attack) makes me uninstall this game.

And when the AI starts spamming, the performance starts to show some cracks. It all just becomes a huge, laggy mess.

[h1]Final verdict[/h1]

Basically a hit-and-miss game.

[b]BUY THIS FOR CO-OP[/b], if your friend has enough money to buy all the same DLCs.

[b]AVOID THIS FOR SINGLEPLAYER[/b], unless you're ready to waste hours battling an AI that's 100 times better at micromanaging crap than you are. I really liked this game, but I've got enough of AI spamming ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

This game only recently came to my attention, quite a while after its release — which is surprising, since I’ve always loved games set during World War II.

In my opinion, I’ve played almost every title that explores this theme, and this one might be among the very best. The fact that it’s a simulation and also allows you to control any unit directly in a quasi–first-person view adds tremendously to the overall experience. The landscapes, the level of detail, and all the little touches the developers paid attention to are simply fantastic. For example, the way soldiers react when they’re hit — how they fall, the realism of the animations — may seem like a small thing, but it greatly enhances immersion.

I definitely recommend it — whether for the mission mode or the practically endless research-based conquest and defense gameplay.

If I could suggest one improvement, it would be to allow players to preview units or vehicles in the research tree before unlocking them — like seeing the size of a squad or the layout of a tank. Maybe there’s a way to do that and I just haven’t figured it out yet.

Another great addition would be if soldiers could receive medals or distinctions as their XP and rank increase, or if there were a main commander character leading the troops who could earn unique decorations — that would make the experience truly next level.

In short, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys deep and strategic WWII simulations!

This game is almost perfect. I wish I had ignored the things that turned me off the first time I tried this game. There are little bugs like units getting stuck/reduced to a near-0 speed on environment or objects they could have avoided. Particularly with team weapons, they are often stopping before the ordered destination. Units have stamina limits for sprinting so maybe that's the issue and not a bug, since pushing a field gun seems like it would drain stamina.

There is as much or more micromanagement possible or even necessary at times than any other RTS I've ever played. This isn't a complaint. It really results in excellent immersion, especially when you take direct control of a unit and get down in the thick of it. One example of excellent gameplay was seeing an armored car roll up on my understrength, barely covered squad. So I took direct control of one man, looted a frag grenade off a corpse, snuck around to flanking cover, threw a grenade directly aimed inside the open turret, waited a few seconds til the crew inside were mincemeat, and drove the armored car over to pick up my squad. Later, I ditched the armored car when I discovered I could ride a freaking bicycle sitting on the side of the road, and ordered the car off to a better position while I just joyrode around France a little bit. 

There is almost a Grand Theft Auto aspect to this game, when you take direct control. And even outside of DC, the ability interact in a real way with unit equipment and supply is just an amazing level of immersive detail. Like the excellent Men of War: Assault Squad, where a shot strikes a target will determine the type of damage recieved. Aim, conditions, cover, veterancy, etc are all highly relevant. Attempting a frontal assault on an MG nest will cause you to lose most of the men you send at it, as you'd expect.

The sheer NUMBER of different units and equipment modeIs and variants etc is mind boggling, though it isn't all dumped on a new player early on - from what I've seen so far from the single player campaigns, it'll give you only a limited choice from among the troops and equipment you'd expect to have access to for the type of unit you're commanding (armor, arty, mech, etc).

I could keep going, this game is wildly detailed, and the Winter War expansion adds an absolutely wild amount of the kind of content we all wished for in Men of War: AS2 or COH3.

I will be playing this one an unhealthy amount for a long time.

Recipe for Potato Dumplings (Varenyky)
Ingredients:
For the dough:
Wheat flour – 500 g
Water – 200 ml
Egg – 1
Salt – 1 tsp
For the filling:
Potatoes – 1 kg
Onions – 2
Lard or butter – 50 g
Salt – to taste
Ground black pepper – to taste
Preparation steps:
Making the dough:
Sifting the flour: Sift the flour into a large bowl.
Making the dough: Add salt and the egg to the flour. Gradually pour in the water, constantly stirring. Knead the dough until it becomes smooth and elastic.
Resting the dough: Wrap the dough in plastic wrap or cover it with a towel and let it rest for 30 minutes.
Preparing the filling:
Boiling the potatoes: Peel the potatoes, cut them into large pieces, and boil until tender in salted water.
Preparing the onions: While the potatoes are boiling, finely chop the onions. Sauté the onions in lard or butter until golden brown.
Making the potato puree: Drain the potatoes and mash them. Add the sautéed onions, salt, and pepper to taste, and mix well.
Forming the dumplings:
Rolling out the dough: Roll out the dough into a thin sheet about 2-3 mm thick. Use a glass or cutter to cut out circles approximately 7-8 cm in diameter.
Forming the dumplings: Place a spoonful of potato filling on each circle of dough. Fold the dough in half and pinch the edges tightly to seal the dumplings.
Cooking the dumplings:
Boiling water: Bring a large pot of water to a boil, add salt.
Cooking the dumplings: Gently drop the dumplings into the boiling water, stirring carefully to prevent sticking. Cook until done (approximately 5-7 minutes after they float to the surface).
Serving:
Removing the dumplings: Remove the dumplings with a slotted spoon and place them on a plate.
Serving: Serve the dumplings hot, optionally drizzling with melted butter, sour cream, or sautéed onions.
Enjoy your meal!

10/10 - The Definitive WW2 RTS Experience

For anyone seeking a World War II real-time strategy game that captures the harrowing intensity of the Eastern Front, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell - Ostfront stands unparalleled. I discovered it after growing weary of less ambitious titles in the genre, and it quickly became an obsession—a refined evolution of classics like Men of War, elevated with contemporary precision. It immerses you in the unforgiving theater of war, where every command carries the weight of historical authenticity and tactical brilliance.

The audio design is nothing short of extraordinary. Gunfire rings out with sharp, visceral clarity that heightens every engagement, while the low growl of tank engines reverberates through the speakers, conveying the sheer power of machinery in motion. The Katyusha rocket launches deliver a thunderous crescendo that echoes the terror of the battlefield, maintaining an atmosphere of unrelenting tension. These elements transform routine maneuvers into pulse-quickening events; even subtle cues, like the crunch of boots on frost-covered ground, draw you deeper into the simulation.

The visuals complement this immersion with meticulous attention to detail. Troops emerge muddied and battle-worn, their movements realistically hindered by the terrain, while vehicles leave authentic tracks and debris in their wake. Shell impacts produce sparks and structural failures that feel tangible, and idle moments reveal squads methodically repairing or resupplying amid the chaos—details that ensure no two sessions play out identically.
At its core, the gameplay delivers unparalleled depth. With an expansive array of historically accurate units, from rudimentary early-war equipment to formidable late-game assets, you can customize forces with granular control over loadouts and formations. Campaigns present evolving challenges that demand adaptive strategies, the AI responds with intelligent aggression yet allows for masterful counterplays, and co-op multiplayer fosters coordinated operations of remarkable scale.
One highlight is commanding the Tiger tank, a behemoth that instills an overwhelming sense of dominance. As it rumbles across the battlefield to seize a contested zone, its guttural engine roar shakes your teeth, underscoring its unstoppable presence. Disposing of enemy armor with a single, precise shot to the hull feels profoundly satisfying—nothing else on the field seems capable of challenging it, turning advances into exhilarating displays of superiority.

Equally captivating is unlocking the artillery barrage, a spectacle that elevates the strategic layer to cinematic heights. The anticipation builds as you call in a strike on a stubborn enemy position, eyes fixed on the sky, willing that perfect shell to land true. When it does, the devastation unfolds in breathtaking fashion: troops ragdoll violently from direct hits or convulse from the concussive force of nearby blasts, scattering debris and morale in equal measure.

If there's a minor drawback, it's that Gates of Hell has redefined expectations for WW2 RTS titles to such an extent that returning to others feels diminished by comparison—their shallower mechanics pale against this benchmark of excellence. Yet this speaks volumes about its quality.

This is essential for enthusiasts of tactical depth and immersive warfare. Acquire it without hesitation; it is, without question, the gold standard for the genre.

As someone who’s been around since the Soldiers: Heroes of WWII days and sunk countless hours into Faces of War, Men of War 1 & 2, and the Assault Squad series, I can confidently say Call to Arms – Gates of Hell feels like the true evolution of the franchise I grew up with. It’s the perfect blend of the old-school tactical chaos we loved and a more polished, modern experience that finally does justice to the series’ potential.

What immediately stands out is the authenticity and weight of the combat. Tanks feel heavy and lethal, infantry positioning actually matters, and every bullet and explosion has that gritty, grounded feel that Men of War always aimed for but didn’t quite perfect. The new ballistics, damage modeling, and vehicle mechanics are phenomenal. The infantry animations, though not on par with Company of Heroes, are improved and smoothed out quite a bit. 

The battlefield feels more alive, from the crack of distant gunfire to the way smoke and debris linger after a shell hits. It’s still got that distinctive, slightly janky charm that defines the series, but this time it feels intentional.

For a casual player like me who just enjoys skirmishes and campaigns, Gates of Hell hits the sweet spot. You can play seriously, micro-managing every soldier like a real-time tactics veteran, or you can just dive in, experiment, use the enemy's weapons against them, and enjoy the spectacle. 

The stealth missions actually make sense. Some of the previous titles drove me up the wall on how unpredictable stealth gameplay was.  This time around you, it's a bit of a throwback to Faces of War's stealth missions where you actually have decent silenced pistols.   

What I love most is how it respects its roots while feeling like a true modern successor. The DNA of Soldiers and Men of War is still here - the direct control system, the destructible environments, the single grenade inadvertently blows up a whole base when the fire reaches the fuel tanks. 

If you’ve ever loved this series but wished for a more refined, serious take on it, this is it. it’s the definitive version of this formula.

Massive content library — campaigns, factions, and scenarios galore

A true sandbox for WWII enthusiasts

Cons:

Steep learning curve — not beginner-friendly

Framerate dips (40–50 FPS is common) and long load times

Pathfinding can be clunky, especially in urban maps

Mods disable achievements (a shame for first-person fans)

Wishlist:

North Africa, Italy, and Pacific theaters would be incredible additions

A polished first-person mode baked into the base game

Infantry gameplay that feels closer to Hell Let Loose

Stealth and sniping mechanics with the tension of Sniper Elite 5

Air combat — even limited — would elevate the battlefield scale

Despite its rough edges, Gates of Hell is the closest thing we have to a playable WWII documentary. It’s not just a game — it’s a passion project, and it shows. June 6, 1944. My Airborne Pathfinders have just landed. Our mission is to place signal beacons to help guide the rest of the airborne drops. 

We have just come to a field we need to cross, however, there is an AA placement that will shred my troops if caught in the open. I order a private to prep a smoke grenade, and throw it over the hedgerow we are using as cover.

But... Something goes wrong.

My private fumbles the smoke grenade, or he can't quite see in the dark. He throws the smoke grenade, only to have it clip the top of the hedgerow and bounce back to the ground at his feet. There are a few moments, mere heartbeats, of silence among the AA fire and the aircraft overhead. 

Then the silence is broken. The grenade goes off. It's willie pete, WP, white phosphorous. All hell breaks loose. It immediately catches the hedgerow, shrubs, bushes, and trees on fire. It also sets the private on fire, alongside the rest of the squad huddled with him. My squad, now all on fire, scatter into the open field. Paratroopers run in the open, screaming as they burn the death. The AA gun and defending squad notice the commotion. They shift their focus from the aircraft to the 5 or so human flames running free in the field. They put them out of their misery, gunning down my squad in the open. 

The beacons are never placed. The airborne drops are a failure, and as a result the beach landings fail. One smoke grenade has ruined any chances of Third Reich being brought the heel.

This game is genuinely so beginner friendly, and although specs might be quite a turnoff since the game is very performance heavy - If your PC can handle it, I would honestly get it if this is your type of game. Easy to get into, there's 5 dedicated tutorial missions that the game basically tosses you into. Veeery easy to familiarize yourself with how the game functions, i.e., how to move your troops, tanks, and other strategies needed to win battles.

The campaigns vary in difficulty but generally are quite easy, I'd say especially the German campaign. You are better off doing the standard German campaign, and then do the Russian campaign. 'Back to Square One' & 'Absolute Zero' are my personal favorites to replay. Do keep in mind, stealth missions ARE difficult. Hence why I suggest you do the German campaign first if you are new.

Things begin to get hard in the Western Front campaigns though remain doable, & I'd say DO NOT go into the Scorched Earth & generally the Finnish campaigns unless you are VERY FAMILIAR with the game & are skilled. These are, to me, the hardest campaigns - doesn't matter which difficulty. Don't play these if you are a noob like me.

Anyways, enough talk of beginner friendliness. Gameplay-wise, it's very engaging. AI skirmishes is my personal way to play the game. The AI is rough around the edges, but it's not enough to bother me since it still is advanced at times. It just needs a few more tweaks honestly, especially when it comes to actual strategic planning. Though, that is probably asking for too much, AI will typically rush into a battle without thinking of consequences. So that's probably the main downside of the AI, the idea of there being a consequence isn't present. 

Back to Gameplay, tanks firstly feel very fluid & heavy. Trucks, cars etc drive nicely & speed varies through terrain which is a good detail. Troops do require micromanaging which is a huge point in this game. You need to be micromanaging your soldiers on the battlefield. But it's not super bad, just a bit tedious at times.

Anyways. I'd recommend. Just make sure your PC can handle it, it'll run on something lower-end but just not very good. Solid pick if you like sandbox or just typical RTS war games. Good modding community too, it's quite active.

TLDR, good pick for beginners getting into ww2 RTS

First of all, in russian those games were called "В тылу Врага" which could be translated as "behind the enemy lines". Not Men of War ([i]МУЖИКИ ВА-АЙ-НЫ[/i] *голосом Гуфовского*), and not Call to Arms (yes, the company who made this siries is ukranian, but the games were fully in russian, like STALKER series too, for example). Additionally, both infantry and vehicles were not terminators either. They were fairly easy to kill and had normal shoot RANGES. Just as for example, ranges in AS2 - most popular game in the series (for its MP features):

small arms - 50-60 meters, expect for sniper rifles that could shoot up to 110 m.
AA-guns or small AT-guns - 110-120 meters
medium and some heavy ATs - 130-140 meters
and the best, most powerful guns - 150 meters

And because of that, the game doesn't become a f-king Wargame. U don't get overwhelmed with redicilous distances and u always more or less focused on the action and the map it self, which with TTK in those games - pleasing to play both tanks and soldiers, either its close combat or some sneaky-peaky small operations behind the lines.

And, yeah, to be very fair, there were not only stealthy missons too in those games. Best campaigns in the series: The Road To Victory (Братья по Оружию), Fox Hunt and Blazing Lands (Лис Пустыни) are filled with those huge battles: Sevastopol, Moscow, Seelow Hights, Tobruk etc. And these missions had big maps too, but they were not as big as those f-king default maps in GoH. Enemy units mostly staying still and absolutly not moving. There's also no friendly ally AI, who could've just fight along with u just here and there to make the battle actually feel like a battle. No, every single unit on a map - ur unit. And those dialogues... Holy cringe... If want a really good campaign - play mods or original Men of War, that i talked a little before. The variety of missions and scenarios keeps the game fresh, from tense infantry skirmishes to massive armored clashes. Each encounter feels unique, and the AI puts up a good fight. Vehicles and weapons are modeled with care, and using them effectively requires real tactical thought, just like in a true battlefield setting.

Another highlight is the community and mod support. The developers have built a solid foundation, and players are constantly adding content that makes the game even better. It feels like a living, evolving project rather than just a one-off release.

Overall, Gates of Hell – Ostfront is a must-play for fans of strategy and WWII history. It strikes a perfect balance between realism and fun. If you enjoy games like Men of War or Company of Heroes but want something even more detailed and immersive, this is the game to get.

Their update blog published today is a spectacular example of how they continue to develop their product.

Critics will point at the expensive and sometimes theoretically unnecessary (i.e. could have been in the base game) DLC, but with the state of the gaming market, supporting a good developer's progress is an essential way for the community to tell them to keep up the good work. If it gets too expensive to justify, just don't buy the DLC's--Barbedwire Studios is small enough (and receptive enough) to notice that lost revenue and community disapproval pretty fast.

I'm not really a game reviewer, but here is a small list of opinions I personally possess (C2A vs MOWAS 2) as a casual RTS player.

- Generally improved gameplay appearance/polish
- Improved variety of units
- Conquest is my new favorite RTS mode, especially with upcoming map persistence
Nitpicks:
- When in direct control mode, the camera remains at a fixed height, making control on elevated surfaces feel kind of janky. It's doable, but it feels distinctly unfinished, because you have to zoom out to remain at the same distance of the unit you're controlling, if that makes any sense. If you don't, the terrain (and vehicle) rises to meet the camera. This issue is the same as in MOWAS 2, so perhaps it's a game engine limitation? In any case, it's a disappointing flaw.
- Sometimes there are issues selecting units/squads by clicking on their squad icon/tag. For example, in my current german conquest playthrough, if I combine a 10-man rifle squad and 2-man medic squad at the beginning of the match, I lose the ability to click their squad icon/tag to select the squad, and I have to manually click and drag a selection area around them. It is often annoying and occasionally damaging to tense combat scenarios.

Suggestions/requests
- Give us improved direct control behavior for tanks. The game already has reticle behavior similar to World of Tanks (to simulate the gunner's confidence in accuracy), so maybe that could be a goal to strive for in terms of how polished direct control could feel. I'm not sure how this could be implemented, but it would be spectacular to have a proper tank game inside of an already spectacular RTS game.

“Good, [strike] bad[/strike] and ugly"

As someone who enjoys playing the Men of War series, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell – Ostfront immediately felt familiar. It’s a real-time tactics game set on the Eastern Front of World War II – gritty, grounded, and utterly relentless. You command squads of infantry, tanks, artillery, and everything in between in brutal and historically grounded battles.

What makes this game shine for me is its authenticity and attention to detail. The visuals, the sound design, the pacing – it all comes together to recreate the look and feel of warfare in a way that’s hard to match. The units behave like real soldiers, the armor feels weighty and vulnerable at the same time, and each engagement feels personal and intense. The penetration and damage model are spot on.

As a self-declared historical nerd, I adore the sheer variety of equipment. Whether I’m fielding early-war Panzer Is or later beasts like the Tiger I and II, the game constantly feeds my need for historically accurate gear. The same goes for the Soviets – T-26s, KV-1s, and the mighty IS-series make appearances in all their brutal, riveted glory.

One of my favorite aspects is the dynamic campaign mode. It's not just battle after battle – there's an economy to manage, a tech tree to develop, and meaningful strategic decisions to make between missions. It adds depth and consequence to every victory (or defeat), and scratches that long-term strategy itch without getting in the way of the core combat.

I still remember one battle where my defenses were holding just fine – until a Soviet KV-1 rumbled onto the field. My 50mm PaK AT gun couldn’t even scratch it. It was like watching history unfold – just like in real life, the KV heavy tank series was a shock for the Germans early in the war, a machine that could shrug off nearly all early AT weapons. I was forced to scramble, reallocate units, call artillery, bait it into a minefield – whatever I could do. It was a desperate, cinematic moment that ended in victory, and I swear I had a wide grin on my face afterwards. Moments like that are why I play these games.

Now… let’s talk about the ugly. Because yes – the UI. It's bad. No – ugly. The interface feels like a relic. It’s like someone dropped a toolbox on the screen and said “good luck.” It takes time to get used to, and even after that, it feels like a major missed opportunity. A cleaner, more streamlined UI would be most welcome.

Still, despite the interface struggles, Gates of Hell – Ostfront delivers one of the most immersive, satisfying, and historically rich RTS experiences I’ve had in years. If you’re into WW2 tactics and love games that reward positioning, timing, and authenticity – this one's for you.

A game similar to the Men of War series. A top-down masterpiece.

After a considerable amount of game time, this game is much more in-depth than many others. Only the Men of War series can hold a candle to how in-depth this game goes.

Tanks, the thing the majority of the players see at first glance, are a bit different than what most games do. They have multiple weapons, and multiple ammo types for their main guns! You can de-crew them, allow infantry to catch a ride, and even take their inventory of repair kits, top-mounted machine guns, demo charges, and other ammo, and give them to other troops/vehicles that need it!

Infantry, the bread and butter of the game, are as complex as they are simple. Long gone are the groups of infantry with clunky mechanics, low control, and irritating AI. Here, you can separate your squads of engineers to plant fields of mines, dig tank ditches, and put up barbed wire and sandbags. Your scouts can go their separate ways and either spy on the enemy, or watch for possible attacks in the fog of war. The infantry in the game is versatile, having snipers, scouts, commanders, at-units, and more, all with tradeable items and inventory!

Artillery, finally getting some action, is not only an off-map resource, but you can tow your cannons behind your trucks and halftracks! From the piddly little 37 and 40mm cannons, to the 200mm howitzers, they all have an on-map use!

Supplies, they are a necessity. Units will run out of ammunition, and vehicles will run dry of fuel, that's where the supply trucks and ammo boxes come into play. Keep them safe, or you might not have enough ammunition for your troops!

Campaign missions are played either by yourself, or with a multitude of friends! Up to 8 players can play on certain campaign maps, and duke it out with the enemy AI, or take it to your friends in up to 4v4 multiplayer!

All in all, it's a great, yet complicated, game to play. See you boys and girls on the battlefield!

Never thought I'd like this game. The top-down view for me was for Age of Empires style managing resources, building stuff and for overall strategy. But when I got back from a military exercise a few years back, I found this game. And I love it. Especially on hardcore. I spent hours advancing little by little, strategically blocking enemy from areas with pioneers and their buildings and indirect artillery. But the enemy was brutal. It used the good old Russian strategy of driving tons of tanks and other vehicles on to the battlefield and getting them destroyed to give infantry some cover. Conquest is pretty quite ♥♥♥♥ and underdeveloped, but it has so much potential.

It’s the best WWII RTS ever made. Literally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ever.

That said, there are two major flaws. And even though I do recommend the game, I am putting a thumbs down in hopes that more people see this outlying post.

First: Vanilla Conquest is so barebones that an aborted fetus has more qualifications for being alive. You get two mission types, attack two zones or defend two zones. That’s it. There’s no dynamic feeling whatsoever. We could’ve had so much more: defend-from-air-attack missions, bombing runs, protect-the-supply-truck missions, build-a-thingy-while-being-shot-at missions, storm-the-fortified-point missions, or deliver-supplies-across-a-river-while-dodging-aircraft missions. I get that’s a lot of work, but Conquest has literally never been updated in anyway regarding the mission objectives.

And don’t even get me started on the AI. I’d genuinely rather play against my 8-year-old nephew than whatever the hell vanilla AI is doing. There’s no coherent strategy, no “tanks first, infantry follows.” It’s just pure chaos. The AI is the embodiment of: “RANDOM ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, GO!”

Second: Modding. Oh. My. God. I have never raged at a game before, I’m a chill dude, but the modding in this game is so unbearably frustrating it might actually be my 13th reason why. The in-game “mod manager” randomly switches your load order, and when you exit, it sometimes deactivates mods for absolutely no reason. Every single tiny patch nukes 99% of the Workshop mods. The worst part is that some of these mods fix things that shouldn’t even have to be mods, like “make AI not vehemently mental.”

I love the devs, genuinely. They made an amazing game. But this stuff feels like it should be have been done by now, and I can’t for the life of me understand why they don’t make it even slightly more mod-friendly.

I got the base game deeply discounted on a sale, played for about 10 hours through some of the single-player campaigns, then bought all of the DLC full price to support the creators. This is easily one of the most fun WWII strategy games I've ever played, the attention to detail is really what makes it stand out to me - it's like being 12 years old again playing with tank and infantry models in the sand box except it's all animated with exquisite detail and sound design. 

There are multiple different game-types to explore, I've personally enjoyed the carefully crafted campaign missions for various factions (the US Airborne is my favorite so far) and Conquest campaigns where you slowly (or quickly) build your own army up through continuous missions. Conquest campaigns can range from small to infinite, so there is a lot of content to explore there. 

Additionally there is a decent selection of mods for the game if you're into that. 

I have to mention the ability to enter 3rd and 1st person views for troops and vehicles as that is one of the primary aspects that differentiates this game from others in the genre. I personally don't switch views too frequently and like to play with an overhead view like a classic RTS but there's definitely a lot of fun and shennanigans to be had with this concept. Plus, you've never felt more bad-ass in an RTS game then rushing a trench in 3rd person view with your Winchester pump-action shotgun. 

While there's definitely a learning curve regarding controls and management of troops, it's not too steep and RTS veterans will probably pick it up quicker than I did.

One of the Most Cinematic and Authentic WWII RTS Games Ever Made

Gates of Hell: Ostfront is easily my favorite in the Men of War / Call to Arms series. It’s brutally realistic, deeply immersive, and incredibly rewarding for those who want a true WWII experience. The historical accuracy here is top-tier—campaign missions reference real-world events, from the American liberation of France (with missions based on actual war footage) to the Airborne DLC’s Band of Brothers-style operations. Each faction (U.S., Germany, USSR, Finland) features unique intro cinematics and HUD overlays, adding immersion and flavor that’s rarely seen in RTS games.

Visually, it’s stunning. Units and vehicles are modeled in extreme detail, and with the UI off, it often looks like you’re staring at a war documentary. The sound design is visceral, the effects hit hard, and every battle feels tense and cinematic. It’s a massive game with tons of content—and it keeps growing.

Gameplay-wise, it’s a huge step forward in realism over Assault Squad 2. Units aren’t bullet sponges. You have to move carefully, think tactically, and truly earn every inch of ground. It’s not for the faint of heart—but that’s what makes it special.

That said, micromanagement can be intense. AI sometimes struggles with pathfinding, taking cover, or reacting smartly under fire. Missions can feel like grinds when you’re solo against waves of elite enemy units, and maps can sometimes lack the handcrafted feel of older titles like Red Tide. I generally prefer maneuvering smaller squads than controlling the entire map. Still, the potential is enormous—and many of these issues can be ironed out with future updates.

If you’re into challenging, authentic WWII strategy games and want something that captures the brutality and scale of the war in a way few games do, Gates of Hell is a must-own. I’ve supported this series for years, and this is the most ambitious and promising it’s ever been.

Call to Arms – Gates of Hell: Ostfront – A Deep, Gritty RTS with Tactical Brilliance and Technical Baggage

Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)

Few real-time strategy games manage to capture the chaos, brutality, and nuance of World War II combat like Call to Arms – Gates of Hell: Ostfront. Developed by Barbedwire Studios and published by Digitalmindsoft, this title builds upon the legacy of the Men of War series while carving out its own niche in the hardcore tactical RTS genre. At its best, it delivers incredibly detailed battlefield control, immersing players in the thick of war like few other titles can. However, it is not without flaws—technical and performance issues still persist, and the aging engine is starting to show its limits.

A New Standard for Tactical Control
What immediately sets Gates of Hell: Ostfront apart is its remarkably granular unit control. Players can issue traditional RTS commands to entire squads, but the game also allows direct control of individual units—either in third-person or even first-person view. This is more than a gimmick; it's a fully integrated mechanic that adds a layer of immersion and micro-level tactics rarely seen in the genre. Sniping enemy soldiers from cover, manually driving tanks, or taking out an enemy MG nest from the perspective of a lone rifleman adds a cinematic intensity that feels visceral and engaging.

The ability to take command of vehicles—especially tanks—is a standout feature. You can aim the gun, maneuver around cover, and even manage crew members. This level of control blurs the line between RTS and tactical shooter, offering a hybrid experience that is both exhilarating and rewarding for players who take the time to master it.

Incredible Cover and Line-of-Sight Systems
The cover system is among the most realistic in any strategy game to date. Nearly every piece of the environment can be used for protection—walls, trenches, rubble, wrecked vehicles—and soldiers will intelligently use available cover when not under direct player command. The line-of-sight mechanics are equally impressive: spotting enemies depends on elevation, foliage, and lighting, making flanking, reconnaissance, and positioning crucial. You can’t just send units into the fray and hope for the best; every movement has to be calculated, every angle considered.

Environmental destruction also plays a pivotal role. Buildings collapse under sustained fire, trees are shredded by artillery, and terrain changes dynamically. The battlefield evolves throughout the course of a match, and adapting to these changes is essential to victory.

Historical Authenticity and Scale
The game’s devotion to historical accuracy is evident in everything from unit design to battle scenarios. It covers the Eastern Front in brutal detail, with campaigns that immerse players in the often-overlooked Soviet-German conflict. From rural villages to bombed-out cities, the maps are meticulously designed to reflect the grim atmosphere of WWII combat.

The scale is equally impressive. Battles can include dozens of units, with infantry, armor, artillery, and aircraft all playing essential roles. Unlike many RTS games where units feel like disposable game pieces, here they are valuable assets. Losing a squad due to poor planning or a poorly executed flank can turn the tide of a battle.

But Then Comes the Engine…
Unfortunately, all this ambition comes at a cost. Gates of Hell suffers from noticeable performance issues, especially in larger battles. Even on relatively powerful systems, frame drops, stuttering, and long loading times are common. The game’s engine—while clearly pushed to its limits to accommodate the complex systems—is showing its age.

Pathfinding can occasionally be frustrating, with vehicles getting stuck or taking bizarre routes. The AI, while competent in many respects, sometimes behaves unpredictably, especially when under direct control. There’s a sense that the foundation, while serviceable, isn’t quite sturdy enough to support the game’s full potential.

Mod support is a bright spot, but even that is hindered at times by the technical limitations of the engine. It’s clear that the developers have done a commendable job with what they have, but the game would benefit enormously from a modern, more stable engine in future installments.

Community and Multiplayer
Multiplayer is robust and continues to grow thanks to an active and passionate community. PvP and co-op modes allow for intense tactical engagements, and the Steam Workshop adds value with a growing list of mods, maps, and unit packs. However, matchmaking can sometimes be spotty, and desyncs or crashes aren’t unheard of.

The developers have shown continued commitment to updating and improving the game, which gives hope for further optimization and content expansion. Community feedback has shaped much of the post-launch development, and that transparency is appreciated.

Verdict
Call to Arms – Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a brilliant but flawed gem. Its deep tactical gameplay, unparalleled unit control, and stunningly realistic combat scenarios make it a must-play for fans of military strategy and WWII history. However, its technical shortcomings and underpowered engine prevent it from reaching the true heights it otherwise deserves.

If you can overlook some rough edges and are willing to invest the time to learn its systems, you’ll find one of the most rewarding and immersive strategy games on the market today. It’s not for everyone—but for those who appreciate tactical depth and historical authenticity, it’s an unforgettable experience.

Call to Arms Gates of Hell: Ostfront is one of the most authentic and satisfying WWII real-time tactics games I’ve played. The base game already offers really good Eastern Front combat detailed armor and ballistics and the rare ability to jump from classic RTS controls straight into direct third-person action with any unit. Combined with its dynamic campaign system, every battle feels personal and consequential.

What really elevates the game though is how much the DLCs expand its world. Talvisota takes you to the harsh Winter War with Finland adding unique units, snowy battlefields and a very different style of combat Scorched Earth deepens the Eastern Front with new missions, factions and late-war equipment, while Liberation shifts the focus to the Western Allies, introducing U.S. forces and new great maps for MP and SP. Airborne builds on that by giving the American airborne divisions their own campaign covering everything from Normandy to the Bulge.

And then there’s Finest Hour, the biggest expansion yet. It brings in the full Commonwealth—British, Canadian, Polish and more—together with huge new campaigns, dozens of Western Front maps, and an enormous lineup of vehicles and weapons. It feels less like a DLC and more like whole new game.

Altogether, Gates of Hell and its DLCs form a deep, historically rich WWII experience with incredible replay value. If you’re into realism and tactical warfare, this game plus its expansions is absolutely worth diving into.

Edit: 9 Feb 2026
It's clear by my hours played there is something special here, and in my opinion it gives one of the most comprehensive 'toy box' experiences you can find on Steam. It's not a sandbox experience like Arma but there is A LOT here for WW2 enthusiasts to dig into.

But there is a substantial amount of problems with the game that a lot of other reviews cover so I shan't touch on them, with the exception of the UI scaling. It annoys me even more than it did then. There's a lot of detail on the models (especially the vehicles) and it sure would be swell to appreciate them in more resolution. 

I will offer my opinion on a common complaint I see mentioned in the reviews; the enemy AI in the dynamic conquest mode. Yes it is not good, and the route the devs have taken to offer a challenge to players is to dramatically increase the number of forces you face against, outnumbering you at least 10:1. It is not ideal but it is the only way the player can reasonably be challenged without the inclusion of a genuine 'smart' AI opponent, but I personally don't believe this is doable. 

You can see similar problems with the Combat Mission games, where only missions created by the devs or the modding community with curated AI plans offer genuine intelligent (or the illusion of intelligence) opposition. But the quick battle mode in CM titles don't offer this, and I believe the same is true for this game's conquest mode. So for me I come to this game to play around with a lot of cool stuff from WW2, and if that's all your after there is a decent amount of fun to be had here.

Its feels like a first person shooter pushing the PS1 to its limits, and I love the devs for this.   Its brings me down memory lane when I go 1st person on some of my units with these graphics and the wonky yet simple control.

I haven't touched co-op so I cannot tell you anything about that, other that it is there. Both campaign and it seems dynamic also has it, but I do not know how that works.  

Which brings me to the graphics.  They ain't to fancy, they ain't cheap.  Its just right.   Some computers can go max, others may not.  I love it, and its wildly attractive. The firefights are pretty wicked, but man when you ammo rack a tank, it feels like the devs hired Micheal Bay for that.  

Then the Dynamic campaign is quite the drug.  You can play it short for a few missions, or long for about 30 or so.  Or infinite, but I dunno how that will work.   You get to choose how your army develops, resupply after each mission, and improve your reinforcements. The research tree is very extensive.  Each turn you get , you have missions to choose one of.  Low risk or high risk, as indicated by the stars. Then the enemy gets to counter attack, rinse and repeat until game is finished. You earn supply and research points each mission. The enemy is affected by the difficulty level you chose for it.  So beware.

Downsides of this game.  The tutorial is basic as expected.  It needs a layer of advanced tutorial.    I had to learn a few things the hard way from some key bindings, to how to auto supply and auto medic.  The AI can be frustrating,  Its a double edged sword affecting both you and them.  Mods disable achievements, so if you want some sort of cushion like infinite supply crate for the harder campaign missions.  You pretty much S.O.L.  Same with Sound mods, they disable achievements too. 

I will recommend this game.  I have been ejoying it alot.

Call to Arms – Gates of Hell: Ostfront isn’t your typical World War II strategy game—it’s a gritty, hardcore RTS that pulls you into the mud and blood of the Eastern Front with brutal authenticity and a steep learning curve that rewards patience and precision.

Built on the Men of War engine, Gates of Hell combines large-scale strategic control with direct-unit management, giving you the ability to zoom out and command entire armies—or dive in and manually control a single soldier or tank. This hybrid approach is where the game shines, offering a dynamic battlefield experience few other titles can match.

The attention to historical detail is impressive: from realistic armor penetration and ballistics to accurate uniforms and terrain, the game feels like it respects its source material without falling into cinematic clichés. Every skirmish feels earned, every loss stings, and victories are often narrow and hard-fought.

The single-player campaigns are intense, focusing heavily on Soviet and German perspectives during the harshest years of WWII. Missions often feel more like tactical puzzles than traditional RTS fare, with limited resources forcing you to think creatively and use the terrain to your advantage.

However, Gates of Hell is not without its rough edges. The interface can be clunky, especially for newcomers, and AI behavior (both enemy and allied) occasionally breaks immersion. It’s a demanding game that assumes its players are already familiar with the Men of War/Call to Arms formula.

That said, for fans of tactical realism and historical warfare, Call to Arms – Gates of Hell: Ostfront delivers an uncompromising and deeply rewarding experience. It’s not trying to be cinematic—it’s trying to be authentic. And on that front, it absolutely succeeds.

Rating: 8/10

Atmosphere, asset quality, environment is perfect. So are the sounds and cries of infantry. The amount of vehicles and their detail is also very solid, except that I would expect much more planes in WW2.

The tough part is controlling everything, first thing you notice is that the groups are dynamic, and if you don't set control group on every infantry squad you get, they quickly mix together randomly, so their combat capability changes along with that (mg gunners with ammo bearers, AT clumped together in other spot). This leaves less room for control groups for vehicles, which are much more important in most scenarios. Another issue is having multiple vehicles selected (or in the same control group), when you issue move order, they all clump together in one spot instead of creating some regular line / square formation. I had to forfeit multiple missions because my units (even whole combat groups) blew themselves up after getting to their destination.
Last thing about control are Shift-commands, you need to have specific pacing for clicking so you won't deselect the whole group, I frequently lose control of the group when spamming frags/smokes/rockets/foxholes with the whole group (there are multiple solutions for this, one of them is called mouse rapidfire).

Combination of those issues make many points in the battle needlessly frustrating, especially when there is fast paced combat. Cherry on top for this is that you can't issue commands in pause, which isn't huge issue for me, but I imagine it makes learning the intricate control mechanics much harder.

Oh yeah... I forgot to mention, for some reason there is no reverse command, so for getting your tank column out of the harms way, you need to select each of them individually, and individually set a path of Shift+move commands, in correct distances, otherwise the vehicle will likely turn at one of the points. Tanks generally die very quickly when they expose themselves like that, and it breaks the immersion every single time.

As for suggestions, please do add the reverse button, air and ships (even if it was just destroyers at lower quality, it would still be even more one of a kind RTS game in last decade)

Call To Arms - Gates Of Hell: Ostfront is a sublimely well crafted second world war game! Being just as much a strategy title as a sandbox experience, the enjoyment I've had with this game has primarily come from the amount of control your allowed to have over your units. Gates Of Hell's gameplay excels at tactical small scale engagements where you're in command of a platoon sized force, and rewards you for effectively controlling sight lines with fire superiority and using map terrain for cover and concealment. Thankfully this process feels very intuitive, because you have full control over individual infantrymen and their individual equipment and positioning, meaning that you'll generally perform better the more time you spend micromanaging your forces. That being said, gameplay starts to become very stressful if your given too many units to control and you can't give each squad or vehicle enough attention to allow it to effectively contribute to the battle.       Overall, I had lots of fun spending my first 150 hours of playtime playing Gates Of Hell's singleplayer missions and the dynamic campaign while occasionally playing multiplayer with my friends. However, my favorite place to spend time in this game is within the map editor, where I can create my own battles and observe the fighting rather than directly commanding any units. The map editor is a wonderful creative resource and allows you to recreate any battle you saw from a movie or history documentary and allows you to give units scripting so they fight each other. I'm not kidding when I say I've spent at least four hours straight watching the AI kill each other. This is aided by how easily modifiable this game is. For instance, if you have 7-zip installed you can literally create your own steam workshop mods by rewriting some of the game files. Personally, I made a mod that changed the soundtrack of the main menu and also added my own German infantry breeds with modified uniforms, and when it comes to this level of detail your able to fully customize each soldier's inventory, health, veterancy, weapon loadout, their helmet, the magazine pouches they carry, their shirt sleeves, and even the rank insignia on their shoulder. I highly recommend you attempt modding this game, even though it may be very frustrating at times, it will reward you with confidence. Better yet, with all the DLCs installed this game has a nearly comprehensive library of vehicles and equipment from the major nations of the European Theater of World War 2. The map editor combined with my own mods has made this one of my favorite games ever!

Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a mess when it comes to performance. Even on high-end rigs with RTX 4090s and top-tier CPUs, the game barely utilizes GPU resources — hovering around 30–50% usage during battles, while FPS tanks below 60 or even 30. The absurd part? When you pause the game (press Esc), GPU usage jumps to 80–90%, which perfectly highlights how poorly optimized the engine is. It runs on the outdated GEM engine that lacks proper multithreading support, making the CPU a major bottleneck while the GPU just idles. Large maps like Liberation are a slideshow, and tweaking graphic settings does next to nothing. Some players tried DXVK or other hacks, but the results are marginal at best. This game has huge potential, but in its current state, it's borderline unplayable unless you're willing to overlook the fact that your $3000 setup is sweating harder in the pause menu than in actual combat.

This is one of my favorite games of all time, and is for me the pinnacle of WWII RTS games. In one sentence, I would describe it as being like the last battle scene in Saving Private Ryan. Scrambling for weapons and ammo, improvising defenses, a single rifleman beating all odds to get within range to hurl a Molotov cocktail at an approaching tank—or, maybe, get obliterated at close range by a high explosive shell.

If you’ve played any game in the Men of War/Call to Arms series, Gates of Hell will feel familiar, but while the engine is very old, the developers have really made GoH feel like a big step forward, with phenomenal visuals for explosions and fire, and much needed quality of life features, like disabling ammo type switching so your antitank guns won’t keep loading HE every time they see an infantryman, and medics healing their comrades without having to be told. 

The detail is very satisfying if you’re a WWII nerd. If your rifle squad lacks a machine gun, you can scavenge the MG-34 from the roof of a knocked out tank. Medic too vulnerable with only a revolver? Pick up a submachine gun from a dead enemy. You can lay mines, both AT and AP. You can dig trenches and foxholes. You can set up sandbags and lay barbed wire. You can blow a hole in the side of a building or burn it down with a Molotov cocktail or a white phosphorus round. My favorite moments in Gates of Hell have all been when I’m about to be overrun, and one random artilleryman who happened to survive his howitzer getting getting mortared becomes John Rambo and scavenges a machine gun and and antitank rifle and singlehandedly holds off the assault.

The direct control feature has long been present in the series, but is incredibly helpful when you just can’t quite get your soldier to go where you want, or keeps missing that weak spot on the tank. If you haven’t played the series, you can press a button and take third person control of a soldier or vehicle/gun, and use WASD and mouse to directly control them. But it also doesn’t feel cheaty—you can get blown away just as easily when direct controlling your units. It just saves a lot of frustration.

The AI is also pretty good on both sides. Don’t expect any advanced infantry tactics, but your soldiers will automatically flee from an enemy grenade, and will automatically switch weapons as appropriate, e.g. switching to a bazooka when encountering a tank, and enemies will use grenades and take cover as you would expect. 

It’s not perfect of course. There is no morale or suppression, so some weapons like machine guns and artillery may not have the effect you might expect, and you can’t take an enemy out unless you kill him—no surrendering like in Steel Division. While damage on vehicles and emplaced weapons are very good for an RTS of this scope, infantry just have a health bar. No fancy injury mechanics, just aim for the head. There is a great cover system, but you can’t count on concealment unless there’s a a wall or a hill between you and the enemy, so ambushes are harder. With no morale mechanic, rear echelon troops like border militia or convict recruits simply have less health than elite troops, but it still comes out feeling balanced.

I don’t really play multiplayer so I can’t speak to the balance of that aspect, but you can play multiplayer game modes against AI, and the different doctrines to a decent job of letting you switch up your strategy without going the full Eugen deck-building route. 

The DLCs deserve their own reviews but they are generally very worthwhile additions to the game. Talvisota adds some great missions, and the Finnish feel very distinct from the Soviets and Germans with their more outdated equipment and defensive focus. They have WWI-vintage Renault FT tanks and an interesting variety of captured and loaned equipment. Liberation is an even bigger addition with tons of new vehicles and equipment, and a welcome change of pace from the mostly winter maps of the base game and Talvisota. Scorched Earth is smaller and includes less content, but it’s cheaper and with the price. I haven’t yet played Airborne, but there is also a British DLC on the way, and plans for more after that. My biggest disappointment when the game first released was the exclusively eastern front setting, but the DLCs have fixed that and continue to give the game new life for me.

You ever want to feel like a powerless general with the reflexes of a sloth and the patience of a Buddhist monk? Play Gates of Hell. It's like the developers asked, "What if we made war as unfun as possible?" and then just ran with it.

First, the AI. I’m not sure if I’m commanding soldiers or babysitting a kindergarten field trip. I tell a squad to take cover, and they run past the sandbags, stand up, and do jumping jacks in a mortar zone. My tank crew? Decided it was a great time to hop out for a stroll. In the middle of a gunfight. I watched one guy reload a gun, drop it, and then get vaporized by a plane. Felt symbolic, honestly.

The interface? Oh you sweet summer child. It's like wrestling a 2006 Russian-made spreadsheet simulator. You want to rotate the camera smoothly? Tough luck. Want to select multiple units without accidentally selecting nothing? Too bad, comrade. Every click is a gamble. Every command is a prayer.

Now let’s talk difficulty. “Realistic,” they say. I’d call it “psychologically abusive.” The enemy sees through trees, walls, your soul—meanwhile my troops act like they’re in a LARP session. If the devs wanted realism, why not just ship the game with a brick and have it fall on my foot every time I lose?

And oh joy, the campaign missions. Nothing like spending 40 minutes carefully positioning troops just to get instantly wiped by an off-screen artillery barrage you couldn’t possibly predict. Retry? Sure—after 5 minutes of reloading and repositioning everything because there's no checkpoint system. I’ve seen IKEA instructions with better user experience.

Want to feel like the world’s worst commander while getting gaslit by your own units and losing to AI psychic ninjas? Gates of Hell is the hell you’ve been looking for.

This is the best WWII RTS game to date, and there is no comparison. Company Of Heroes's developer may have more money and the competitive twitch crowd on their side however not in the gameplay department. Call To Arms original launch was a mess since they went modern with it, but now that Gates Of Hell : Ostfront and it's DLC's are out it's back in the right wheelhouse. There is a ton of nations to play as, and an awesome variety of different types of units. You have all the infantry and small arms you can imagine, as well as everything from light to medium and heavy armored tanks. And there is also a large amount of other unit types such as mortars and artillery and large anti-tank and machine guns!. The AI isn't the best but it can be challenging, and there is a lot of content with all the campaigns and also dynamic campaign mode and conquest etc. The gameplay is awesome, every unit has detailed information about it and it's own inventory and rank etc. Each soldier even has his own name!, it's really cool!. Your vehicles and soldiers can run out of ammo, get their helmets shot or blown off and even interact with soldiers and items and vehicles around them!. Meaning you can repair and steal an enemy vehicle, pick up ammo off a dead ally when you run out, or even pick up that MG42 from that machine gun foxhole you just took out and use it against them!. And once again in comparison to Company Of Heroes 3 the gameplay and it's dynamic factors are not all RNG bullcrap, and your strategy and planning and execution is key. Ontop of the usual RTS tactics this game also gives you another incredibly powerful option to control your selected unit. Direct control. Direct control allows you to literally play your unit as if it was a third person game. You can move with WASD and aim and reload and cook and throw grenades etc. Using direct control when in an engagement can result in your squad being victorious, as compared to the other player if they are just letting the AI do their thing. You will often see online matches involve intense direct control battles, with players using their armor and artillery and mortars to get the most cheeky kills. Vehicles are realistically modelled with historically accurate weapons and armor, all of which has fully simulated ballistics and armor penetration values and models. In COH 3 you will see tanks fight and health bars go up and down. In CTA: GOH you will see bounces, crews being shocked, impacts and penetrations causing the nearby crew to be killed. You will see tanks get tracked, turretted and their engines taken out. And they can also cook off and explode!. But the crew can also repair and salvage them sometimes!. And once again unlike COH 3 if your crews tank gets disabled and cannot be repaired and is destroyed you can still save the crew if you have them exit the tank before it's destroyed!. That crew retains their experience and can be used to man a new tank!. There is so much going on during a battle that you have to micro-manage and macro-manage it's insane. The only bad thing is that there isn't a replay system like in their Men Of War games. Also unlike Company Of Heroes 3 there is FULL terrain destruction, so you will see shells create craters, and even buildings get chunks blown off of them and get leveled if they are shelled enough!. The grass and foliage will burn due to fire as well, and you will see awesome and epic particle effects where rounds impact no matter what surface!. If they hit dirt you will see grass and dirt flying up, if it's a wall you'll see concrete smoke, if it's wood you'll see wood particles etc it's all very detailed!. You will even see small arms and artillery and mortars eject their casings/shells on the ground where they are fired!. The more you zoom in and look at what's going on the more fine and amazing details you see!. The only downside aside from the lack of a replay system is the fact there is such a small player base. You can still find and join online games with ease, but there is not a ton of lobby's to choose from, and mods narrow that further. If you are a WWII RTS fan, this game and it's DLC's are a no-brainer. And I highly recommend checking out the Steam Workshop for mods, I personally use these ones. 1 : Everything Stays , 2: Blood Mod , 3 : Wounded Animation. These addons make it so that there is realistic blood and gore and that all the debris and remains from each engagement stays and does not despawn. Also there will be animations for wounded soldiers for some additional immersion. 10/10 Highly recommended!.

Ok a more detailed review 

The AI in this game can be incredibly dumb. Soldiers will stand out in the open, tanks won't face their armor correctly, you give them a SHIFT command with lots of dots in-between, but the tank decides to go 180 exposing the engine, though you gave a shift command for every meter, and gun crews will just sit there while a threat walks right up to them. This forces you to micromanage everything, all the time. You can't just give an order and trust it'll be done; you have to constantly check on every unit. It's less like being a general and more like being a stressed-out kindergarten teacher who has to make sure nobody eats glue.

For all its detailed realism, the game can feel like it's falling apart at the seams. Units get stuck on terrain, vehicles bug out, pathfinding (again even with SHIFT)sends your troops on bizarre suicide runs, and sometimes things just don't work the way they should. It's built on an old engine, and it shows. Losing a critical unit because it got stuck on a fence post is infuriating.

Forget the gameplay itself; the multiplayer is fundamentally broken on a technical level. In 2025, it's unacceptable that the game runs on a peer-to-peer (P2P) connection system. This means every match is a lottery based on a random host's internet stability/performance(or another player).
You will constantly deal with stuttering, laggy units, and input delay that isn't your fault.

TLDR 
Your biggest enemy isn't the player across the map, it's the terrible netcode, even worse AI and the high probability that the host will crash or rage quit.

While the genre has no shortage of titles vying for attention, this game stands out as the definitive WWII RTS experience, surpassing its rivals in both depth and realism. With a blend of tactical complexity, historical accuracy, and unparalleled immersion, it delivers a wargaming experience that few others can match.

[h1]Unmatched Realism and Attention to Detail[/h1]

One of the most striking features of Call to Arms: Gates of Hell is its obsessive commitment to realism. Every vehicle, weapon, and soldier is meticulously modeled based on real-life counterparts. Unlike its competitors, such as Company of Heroes or Men of War, this game takes realism to a whole new level with advanced ballistics, armor penetration systems, and realistic damage modeling.

Infantry dynamics feel authentic, with soldiers reacting to suppression, environmental cover, and morale conditions. Tanks are not mere damage sponges but lethal war machines where armor angles, shell types, and weak spots all play a crucial role. This granular approach to combat makes every encounter feel meaningful and every tactical decision critical.

[h1]Tactical Freedom and Deep Gameplay[/h1]

Where many WWII RTS titles focus on arcade-style action, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell prioritizes tactical depth. Players have the freedom to command on a macro level or dive into the action with the Direct Control mode, which allows you to personally maneuver and fire vehicles or soldiers. This dual-layer of gameplay is far more nuanced than other games in the genre, offering both large-scale strategy and individual precision.

The game's extensive arsenal—ranging from early-war bolt-action rifles to late-war heavy tanks—ensures that battles evolve over time, reflecting the technological progression of WWII. Additionally, the detailed terrain destruction system means that no cover is permanent, forcing players to adapt their strategies as the battlefield changes dynamically.

[h1]Robust Multiplayer and Modding Community[/h1]

While many RTS games offer limited multiplayer experiences, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell excels with its robust online modes. Whether engaging in competitive PvP, cooperative campaigns, or custom scenarios, the game offers a wealth of content to keep players invested.

Moreover, the game boasts a thriving modding community. Fans continuously create and share new maps, factions, and scenarios, extending the game’s lifespan far beyond what its competitors offer. This community-driven approach ensures the game remains fresh and continues to evolve with player feedback.

[h1]Historical Accuracy Meets Cinematic Intensity[/h1]

From the Eastern Front to the streets of Berlin, the game covers a broad array of historically significant battles. The developers’ dedication to historical authenticity is evident in the meticulously recreated battlefields, period-accurate uniforms, and authentic sound design. Explosions, gunfire, and the mechanical grind of tank treads create a soundscape that immerses players in the ferocity of World War II combat.

Yet, despite this dedication to realism, the game never sacrifices the cinematic spectacle. Battles are intense and visually stunning, with dynamic weather systems, realistic physics, and destructible environments combining to create moments that feel straight out of a war film.

[h1]Why It Stands Above the Competition[/h1]

While competitors like Company of Heroes offer a streamlined, accessible experience, and Men of War provides tactical flexibility, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell seamlessly blends both approaches while pushing the envelope on realism. The Direct Control feature adds a unique layer of immersion that most other WWII RTS games lack. Additionally, the ongoing support from developers and the active modding community ensure the game remains a living, breathing experience that evolves over time.

For fans of tactical wargaming and World War II enthusiasts, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell represents the pinnacle of the genre. Its attention to detail, deep strategic options, and immersive combat make it a must-play title that not only surpasses its rivals but sets a new standard for WWII RTS experiences. This is not just a game—it is a battlefield brought to life with staggering authenticity and strategic depth.
