I am in love with this game's Conquest mode.

What it boils down to is that you start with choosing what faction you want to play as and what faction you want to play against, in the base game your choices are the Ussr/Soviet union and Germany.
As of writing this review there is a DLC that adds U.S. and Finland.
Then you choose the difficulty and length of your Conquest, I play on the hardest difficulty, least amount of resources and unlimited amount of missions.
In my current campaign I play as the U.S. vs Germany,
When I get in the game I will start with limited research points and resources, just enough to unlock the most basic tank and enough to buy 2 cheap M3 Stuarts early versions and one basic rifleman squad, I divide them in two deployment phases.
Then I have to choose what goal (type of recourse I want to focus on ammo, credits, support points or research points) and difficulty I want in the upcoming match, then I have to do an assault mission where I have to defeat a digged in enemy with AT guns, MG's and infantry and capture 2 to 3 objectives to win. Meanwhile the enemy will send reinforcements to stop you, usually vehicles, tanks, artillery and waves of soldiers.
You can have up to 5 deploy Phases, each Phase has a maximum amount of points allocated to it, as you fill up the Phase with units, you will need to spent that same amount of points to call upon the Phase in battle, these points are earned gradually as you play in a match but it can be a fun balance to make a strong Phase but also try to keep it cheap at the same time.
After you have completed the objective and taken out the enemy you have to choose to head back to the menu or to go over the battlefield to scavenge enemy gear, weapons and vehicles to use in the upcoming battles.
When you get back to the menu, you resupply your units, research and buy new units.
Now it's time to do a defense mission, you have about 5-6 mins to set up your defenses before the enemy will show up, your goal is to fill up the score bar by killing and holding to the capture objectives.
Then once again you scavenge anything you want or head back to the menu.
You keep doing this back and forward.
As you are unlocking better units, the enemy will also field more advanced units.

Now for mechanics the game works similar to Men of War, your soldiers and vehicles have limited ammo, you can scavenge more corpses, resupply in between matches or use supply trucks.
Soldiers are squishy but at the same time a soldier with an AT grenade can screw up your tank in seconds.
Tanks are modular, parts can be damaged and be broken to disable the vehicle (tracks, engine, turret, gun), the crew can be killed by penetrating through the armor, after de-crewing the tank you can steal it for yourself.
A tank can also be instantly destroyed by setting the engine on fire or hitting the ammo rack.
Because you keep your forces between battles it's important to keep at least one member of your tank or squad alive, as long as one member is alive you can fully recover it in the menu.
And to give you one more unique way of playing compared to other strategy games, you have the option to play in direct control mode, where you play as the individual unit, in or top down view or third person mode.

The AI can be very tricky to play against, especially with some workshop mods or if you don't research your army fast enough and let the enemy outpace you with their better tanks.

As a huge fan of RTS games like *Company of Heroes*, *WARNO*, and others, this game instantly grabbed my attention with its blend of tactical strategy and direct unit control. If you love commanding squads from a top-down perspective but also enjoy getting hands-on with individual units, this is definitely worth checking out.  

The core RTS mechanics feel familiar, with positioning, cover, and combined-arms tactics playing a crucial role—much like *CoH*. However, the ability to directly control units like tanks, machine gunners, and infantry is what truly sets it apart. While the third-person control isn't as in-depth as a full-fledged shooter, it's serviceable enough to be a fun change of pace. That said, I find myself mostly playing in RTS mode while also using direct control from the top-down perspective—essentially like *Foxhole*.  

There are technically three ways to control units: standard RTS mode, top-down direct control (similar to once again *Foxhole*), and full third-person shooter. The ability to switch between these modes adds a unique layer of flexibility to gameplay. While third-person control is fun, it’s not as tactically useful as the traditional top-down view, but jumping into a unit and landing crucial kills feels amazing.  

If you're looking for a strategy game that mixes classic RTS mechanics with immersive direct control, this one is a great pick. A must-play for RTS fans who want a little more control over the battlefield!  

⭐ **9/10 - Would command my troops again.**

Nice and complex RTS where good plan matters more than the number of clicks per second. The third person shooter part is rather clumsy by shooter standards, but serves an important purpose of dealing with edge cases (like lacking that extra meter of range). Even the AI is half-decent, "lazy" solutions (like charging your heaviest tank into the fog of war or passive shelling with poorly defended artillery) will go horribly wrong.

The game has several modes, including scripted campaign, dynamic campaign ("conquest"), single- and multiplayer skirmishes. Scripted campaign provides a diverse set of battles where you will master different aspects of the game, from stealth to defensive preparations to tank warfare. 

As for the dynamic campaign, it consists of skirmishes, alterating between defence and offence (which require very different approaches), and has tech tree and other "global" resources. Notably, there's no saves during battle in this mode, and the enemy army strength scales with your strength (which is usually an annoying game design but here you would otherwise get total dominance or impossible battles afrer, like, third mission). Many say conquest mode is too repetititve but I kind of disagree: it took me maybe 20 very bad failures and 10 successful missions to develop an approach for winning reliably and with reasonable losses, and winning with zero risk seems to be impossible. This process of "solving" the game is far from repetitive, and even after that you will encounter different enemy army compositions (I believe enemy does "research" too) that will require some thinking. 

Advice for new players to avoid some frustration: put your infantry in "don't shoot" mode unless you know what you're doing. Shooting makes them immediately visible to the enemy (with some exceptions), and you won't be able to react before they die, which is way more problematic than toggling fire when they are discovered otherwise. Also, don't neglect digging foxholes. Oh, and Russian for anti-tank gun is "Protivotankovoje orudije", you'll need that one.

The predecessor Men of War: Assault Squad 2 (MoW) with RobZ 1.28.6 (specifically this version) is a lot better, in pretty much every single way, but there are some improvements in this game

IN DETAIL

POSITIVES
Gates of Hell (GoH) does offer some compelling features:

General Overview
- The single-player campaign missions are exceptional, potentially the best in the Men of War series
- The graphics are a bit odd here, some things look better, some things look worse, there seems to be some sort of saturation filter that goes over your whole game and it makes everything look so weird, you can tweak your settings but it still is off-putting to the eyes
- Refined mechanics, such as trench-digging, are more intuitive and visually appealing
- There are some innovative features like first-person tank and infantry control, even being able to sprint while direct controlling infantry units
- There's a couple of cool things you can do in GoH like putting a Kar98K on a machinegun tripod, just adds to the "That's useless but cool I guess"
-The layout of objectives actually makes sense, if an objective is a factory building, the actual capture point is that entire building, not just a circle within it like it is in MoW
-The game is much more stable than MoW, MoW has the tendency to crash mid-matches and specific maps don't run well at all
-All of the maps are functional and playable
-The AI are much more functional than they are in MoW, but still aren't really improved much, really the only difference is the AI continue to spawn things in instead of giving up halfway through the match
-The planes in this game are implemented a lot better than in MoW, they actually fly on the map and drop a bomb or strafe with their guns (Although it's a little awkward because bombs have no momentum so they just fall straight down), and vehicles meant as anti air actually shoot at the planes

NEGATIVES
The game suffers from several significant design issues that dramatically make for a worse experience:

Performance & Graphics
-Somehow the game both runs worse and and looks worse at the same time, I've done so much tweaking but nothing seems to make the game look good, it just looks alright, as listed before the game does look better in some aspects but overall I think it looks worse compared to MoW

Resource Management
-The rate at which you gain money to buy things is different from MoW, and overall you'll be able to afford less than you would be able to in MoW, meaning shorter games with less things on the map in general, makes the matches feel empty and boring
-Restrictive Command Points (CP) system, which basically is how much you can have on the map at once, allows only a few units on the map at one time for each player
-Officers don't increase your CP like it does in MoW, so you're limited even more than you would be in MoW
-Matches typically feature only 1-2 large tanks, which are locked behind the doctrines special points system, compared to MoW where if you manage your money well, you could get a handful per player

Lack of Unit Variety and Design
-Infantry squads are very limited in their variety, you get access to generally a few squads with similar purposes, this is also affected by which doctrine you choose
-Squad sizes are unnaturally small, whilst in MoW the squad sizes depend on the quality of unit, the faction you're playing, the equipment they have, and the price of the unit
-Instead of location-specific damage, units now have generic health bars, bullets simply reduce a uniform health pool rather than simulating realistic wound mechanics
-The ranges of tanks and vehicles in general are pretty low, no such thing as a long range tank engagement, tanks feel like they "facetank" each other instead of having a tank duel
-The map variety is mostly just "field in Russia" copy and pasted, even the Stalingrad frontlines map is mostly an empty field with a few buildings, with the USA faction being added in now we have "field in Normandy" maps, there are a few good maps though
-A lot of the interesting vehicles like the Thor can't be used in multiplayer, they aren't even overpowered, in MoW they are expensive and usually get 1 shot off on a bad target (Because their range is pretty bad) then get countered in 5 seconds

General Game Design Issues
-You are forced to use the "doctrines" mode in this game, which is not a horrible idea, but vehicles that were just normal purchases in MoW are now locked behind special points, things like the tiger tank or even a flame tank are now locked behind this doctrine special point system
-One of the reasons MoW RobZ 1.28.6 felt so good was the unresponsiveness of the tanks, makes it feel much more realistic and tense when things are hitting the fan, but in GoH everything drives around like a modern MBT
-In general, in MoW you can win by doing a lot of different strategies (Even meme strategies like spamming conscripts or suicide chargers), but in GoH it feels like you have to buy specific tanks and units to win effectively

Presentation Issues
-Tanks exploding and explosions in general aren't as spectacular and happen much less often compared to MoW
-When you're selecting your infantry it's very difficult to see them and to mentally keep track of what's going on, and when you select them they start glowing

Factions
-Besides the base game USSR and Germany, each faction is locked behind an expensive PAID DLC

Overall, while Gates of Hell has some positive improvements, it falls short of the depth and quality of Men of War: Assault Squad 2 with RobZ 1.28.6 in quite a few ways

I've bought many copies of this game and DLCs as gifts for friends, hoping that with time it will become the new great GEM game like MoW:AS2 was for example. But even though I personally continue to play it, objectively I just can't recommend this game when after 3 years we have:

- occasional synchronization issues in multiplayer/coop, when one player sees different things to another
- tanks sometimes teleporting/instarotating in multiplayer/coop
- very minor things like fences or some trees eating tank shells completely
- visibility/battlefield readability issues ignored even though I came up with multiple mockups
- random hard to diagnose performance degradations (especially at game start)
- a feeling that networking is even worse than in MoW:AS2
- pathfinding being stupid, causing stuff like people getting out of trenches for no reason at all when ordered to go to another part of the trench and getting killed
- a lot of other small but annoying issues, like inventory contents occasionally vanishing, bugging out, soldier AI being stupid, shells flying in whatever direction etc.


That isn't even mentioning things like Soviet SPGs not having the switchable indirect fire mode that was apparently promised ages ago, and missing armor mechanics that make certain matchups biased, like Panther upper glacis being able to tank endless amount of early IS-2 shots at distance and not giving a damn, even though the armor would've cracked IRL already (and the devs also won't do anything about it). Sometimes, it feels like GoH's engine has more broken things than fixed things compared to the iteration of engine in MoW:AS2, which makes playing a frustrating experience, if you're not a hardcore historism fan.

I was reporting many of the things above that make the experience frustrating, but I feel like my feedback is mostly neglected, so I stopped doing that mostly.

I really want to love this game because I like the idea of a more realistic MoW:AS2, but currently it feels like basic playability is neglected. You can't make up basic playability issues with accuracy to details and a lot of contents. I honestly regret my decision to spend so much money on copies of this game when this is the experience I get after all this time.

I only recommend to buy the base game at discounts and see for yourself if you enjoy or get frustrated. To the credit of devs, the DLCs are not mandatory to have fun and the base game is also updated for free.

Sound effects, details, gameplay is overall very enjoyable.
As for negatives, having played for 238 hours at the time of writing this, I can certifiably say the AI atrocious at times and uninspired at others. I routinely lose men when they run in front of an enemy machine gun or my tank prioritizes infantry over the much more preeminent threat of another tank 20 meters in front of it. It does pain me to say that given how much I enjoy the game, but I'd be lying if I said I hadn't restarted battles in frustration because of it. Also armor ratings are all sorts of whack. I had a recent example of a PAK40 and several other guns/tanks, all at close range, pummeling a KV-1 tank and doing practically nothing to it except dazing the crew and detracking it.

If you're like me, someone who has been a long-time player of MOWAS 2, you would naturally be excited by this kind of game. MOWAS 2 but newer, and improved? What could go wrong!

One thing, AI.

AI has been a pain point for the men of war series, but gates of hell takes it a step further. How it is possible that after over 5 years from MOWAS 2 to now, and with assumed improvements/learnings since then, AI could be worse?!

*AT rocket and tank gun infantry fails to engage tanks as their role suggest. In one game, I had AT infantry on both wings of my front line, and my enemy repeatedly attempted to drive armoured cars through the defenses. Every time, despite me furiously clicking to attack the armour, the AT did nothing. The only way I could solve this was through direct control, or if the enemy stood completely still. This happened repeatedly.  in MOWAS 2, AT would take out armoured units that came within range independently. 
*Cover and concealment is terrible. Hard cover is not hard cover, eg. fences. Concealment is rarely advantageous as it is in real life, and was in MOWAS 2. Plus, for some reason the actual cover points on the map (where the silhouettes show up) are few and far between. I regularly have trouble finding somewhere where my troops can anchor to. This was not a problem in MOWAS 2. Also, there seems to be no positioning advantages in this game. For anyone that has played the Company of Heroes series, this game feels very familiar. The graphics are pretty good, map design is impressive, sound effects are some of the best making you feel like you are part of the battlefield. Gameplay wise, it is packed with tense action, strategic choices, logistic planning of your forces (they need to be resupplied and refueled) and has an interesting party trick: at any time you feel the need, you can jump into a 3rd person view of ANY soldier or equipment you field. It can be from a simple conscript rifleman to a Tiger tank, or from a supply truck to a mortar. This ability not only gives a totally different perspective of the battlefield, but also enables you to survey the terrain from a ground level, pin point the positioning of your forces, and also be the hero of the hour by manning anything that needs to be manned in the time of need.

The title offers a scripted campaign for each faction, a procedurely generated dynamic conquest where you build your armies, conquer land and defend it from the enemy, and stand alone battles called Skirmishes. Of course, you can also play online so there's enough content to keep you busy for a while.

However, there are plenty of stuff that are extremely annoying. First and foremost, pathfinding is -I believe- the worst I've seen in any game. Your units seem to take the most weird choices for their navigation. To make things worse, vehicles often tend to run over other units of yours (and utterly destroy them) if they cross some in their path. Or, trucks that haul artillery pieces sometimes detach their cargo if the latter collides with an obstacle, only to reach their intented destination without their cargo which was left somewhere along the way. Also, your units ignore the fact that some times friendlies are in their line of fire, so for example a Flak cannon positioned 10m behind a Howitzer will fire its gun killing all of the Howitzer's crew. All of the above require a LOT of micromanaging to avoid so it often makes your gaming experience frustrating and cumbersome. Finally, it seems like some maps or units from the DLCs are poorly optimized causing huge performance drops in some situations.

Overall this could be a brilliant game because of the immersion, ability to switch from RTS to 3rd person, and content variety of the game, but with all those bugs I can only give it a 7/10 at best.

A beautifully well-made game. Gates of Hell is everything I was looking for in an RTS game and more. Before playing this game, I spent a long time on the Men of War series of games, and I feel like this game just does everything Men of War did but way better, adding a ton of its own touches and changing most of the gameplay for it to feel way more grounded and grittier (and more fun). Not to forget how immersive everything feels, from the well-made maps, weather to the detail of the units and, best of all, tanks. The tanks are so historically accurate. They all have so many different parts, like the engine or the tracks, where if broken, they each disable the tank. So, if you don't want to fully destroy an enemy tank for some reason, shoot it in its turret neck, or gun, making it unable to shoot anymore. I also love how each side of the armor plates on them actually have different armor values. So, for example, if you are having difficulties penetrating a KV-1 frontally, you should aim for its lower frontal armor, which isn't angled and thus, easier to punch through it with weaker guns. This all makes me immersed into the game most of the time, and I love it. I feel so bad when I lose even one single rifleman. 

Yes, it does have its flaws, like the AI pathfinding and my units being dumb sometimes, but that is just a small thing that doesn't really push it down. Whenever that happens, I just take manual control of them and tell them what to do. You are the one controlling your army after all, like a general, telling them everything they need to do.

There’re so many missions in the game as well. Sure, to actually access them, you need the DLCs. But I find them to be at a reasonable price for what they give. You start with the German and Russian missions on the eastern front (the reason it's called Ostfront). But the DLCs open the game so much more, giving you the Americans and Finnish in new and completely different maps than the ones you are used to. Fighting in France made me realize how annoying hedgerows can be. It made me immediately miss the flatter maps of the Ostfront. The Americans have also a different play style, preferring their medium tanks over any heavy tank. Or their heavy artillery. And the Finnish? They are the hardest to play, in my opinion, due to how much more different you have to play them. Because they don't have nearly as many resources as anyone else, you have to be way sneakier. Instead of destroying the enemy tanks, you should only break their hulls so you can repair them and use them against the enemy. And best of all? None of the missions felt like they were repeating, even if there's so many defense missions. They all had their own twists and doctrines to them. You can be given so many good units, making it easier, or you can be given so much less and are expected to stop the red tide on your own. That's when you become creative, using well placed mines, AT guns and infantry to gain the upper hand. And in all of these missions, even if you get many units, the game can punish you greatly if you make even a small mistake. Moved that squad in front of an AT cannon? Say goodbye to them. Shown the side of your tank to the enemy which can't pen its frontal armor? Say goodbye to the tank. I love it, it makes you think twice or even thrice before deciding something.

But enough of speaking about the premade campaign, I want to talk about my favorite part of the game. Or well, favorite parts of the game. First is the modularity of it and how many mods there are. They can range from just light sounds replacements to whole game conversions. Sure, there aren't nearly as many mods as in Men of War, but there's enough of them to where you can extend the playtime of the game way further. And the second favorite part is the conquest mode, or better said, custom campaign. This is where the game becomes very interesting. Basically, it's as it sounds. You make your own campaign. You choose your own faction and the faction you want to play against and then battle it out. It amazing to see you going from very, very early war tanks, such as the Panzer 38 or Panzer II to late war units. It's immersive. There’re two game modes for conquest that always rotate with each game played. You either defend or attack the enemy. And even if that's it, the AI being smart and always bringing different type of units with each match makes it interesting enough to where I can't stop playing it. There’re so many units to research in the tech tree that it takes at least 10 or so hours of gameplay to unlock all of them. Now, what happens when you combine conquest with mods? You guessed it, even more replayability! If you get bored of the units you have, you can always add mods to get more units. I recommend MACE due to it adding SO MANY more units. Most of them are concept tanks that were never used in war, so you get to see what it would've been like if they saw battle. I love just marching 2 Maus tanks and 4 E-100 tanks right into the enemy and seeing all of their attempts at killing them be useless. 

All of that makes the game one of my favorites. Rant over, thank you for listening!

I have ~100 hours and I think I got this two weeks ago. 
I have 450 in Company of Heroes 2 since that game came out and I'm a huge CoH fan.

This and Company of Heroes are NOTHING alike except that they're about WWII and share some units. This has FAR more units and variations on the units where CoH will be like: Early infantry, Medium infantry, Heavy infantry. This has different branches of infantry and inventories for each one that you can target depending on strat. What's more, you can pick up your enemy's materiel and deck out ANY of your soldiers however you want. 
If you liked Codename Panzers, this will more than scratch the itch that that old game gives you. This is Codename Panzers with direct unit control, custom inventories, even more vehicles, WAY more infantry. 

Want to solo a capture point with a tank crew driver that started with a pistol? You can. Grab a dead guy's rocket launcher and take out the tank. Smoke the MG to work around behind it and toss a grenade at its crew. Go into Direct Control TPS/FPS mode and blast the rest of the defenders. 

On that note: Direct Control is janky but it's so damn fun. You can control any of your selectable units and go into third person or scoped mode. Be aware that units 'see through' bushes and stuff and the line of sight in DC isn't as far as your AI might have.

Vehicles have soft and hard spots and it appears that an armored vehicle's angle on the armor affects your shots. So your bullets and even your tank shots will deflect off of armor depending on where you hit it.

MGs, especially those with a high rate of fire like the MG42, mow down infantry if you try to swarm it. Better to force you to use tactics or tanks. Just using tanks alone though won't work most of the time because enemy infantry will wreck it with Panzerfaust or AT grenades.

Some bad: The unit control is not NEARLY as good as in CoH. Facing your vehicles is especially bad. It has directional facing like CoH but it doesn't seem to work or only works 10% of the time. Enemy AI; tanks, TDs, and AT guns can hit you from far away so you really want the strongest part of your armor facing where you think they're coming from. 

Doing combined arms (tanks/APCs and infantry) movement is garbage. You can hardly tell what's selected and they don't move how you expect them to. Half the time (even without a vehicle selected) infantry gets 'stuck' on some obstacle. 

You can't select very large groups. The game allows you to control each infantry unit (each man) individually which is really cool but it's a huge pain in the ass if, for example: You smoke a control point and want to rush it with a bunch of squads. You have to iterate over all your squads (as each numbered group appears to only be able to hold 15 guys) and tanks and hope that they actually move on the point. It is good that they attack on their way but a lot of times you just want them to run in there (so you can nade or fodder) and they don't do that.

This review comes from someone who had genuinely been fed up with Digitalmindsoft and the Men of War series as a whole after I had been burned by the last Call to Arms title.  Add to that, the awful release of whatever MoW: CW was and I was certain I'd never buy a game from these devs again.

Up until GoH, and with the exception of AS2, the entire MoW series had felt like a copy-paste of the same game, over and over.  Now, with the release of GoH, the whole thing has had a facelift with much needed optimization of the code and physics taking front stage.  Sure, the textures look pretty, but now when a tank explodes, it doesn't freeze up the entire game as it processes particle effects and area of effect destruction.  Not to mention the new animations and sound design that make close combat much more convincing and not like the models are playing pretend at kindergarten.

The most negative thing that I have to say about the game is that the single-player campaign is mostly forgettable.  There are a few stand-out missions, like the defense ones that let you play with some interesting equipment, but even those are just simple wave-defense.  Even the DLCs that include missions suffer in the SP experience.  

I won't knock anyone that enjoys the campaign, but the real meat of the game is in the Skirmish and Dynamic Campaign modes.  Skirmish is as its always been, but this time players need to choose a division type to play before match start.  This mostly limits the type of vehicles that you can deploy, but also unlocks some unique ones and a range of other special units.  Overall, while it doesn't drastically change the depth of matches, it does improve the variety of units that you see people using and kinda lets them hone in on a role.

The Dynamic Campaign, however, is where I think GoH shines!  First introduced in the prior CtA title, this is the game mode that I tend to play every time.  Without getting too lost into the mechanics, its basically a semi-turn-based mode where one side attacks and the other defends.  The maps are mostly random, but there is some control over where you choose to fight and the rewards for each battle are resources to further build your army.  I don't know why I like this mode so much but its my go-to every time I get an itch to play.

As a final point, the game has been out for almost 4 years now and is still getting a heavy stream of support from patches to added content.  Its clearly a labor of love and that amount of effort shows.  Top it off with Steam Workshop support and nearly limitless playability.  Do I play it all the time? No, but I always come back to it because its a genuinely good title in a series I used to love so much.

First of all: I like it a lot. I already put over 400 hours into it and bought all dlcs. 

As a ww2 and tank nerd this game is a must. The details of the tanks and other equipment are very well done.
The whole concept of an rts in which you can play every single unit from 1st ord 3rd person perspective is a lot of fun and bring way more complexity into the gameplay. To be fair this concept is not new but its new to me, i never played for example MoW

But as much as i like it, it has a few big and a few minor issues. I am writing mainly in hope, that the devs hear more voices from the community and will fix the issues. (btw i am talking about the vanila game without mods)

What i really dont like are the menus in conquest. the layout of the pre-game menu is not structured at all. for example why is there no option to filter or sort units in the recruitment / reserve box? there is one tab for air support but why is there not one tab for infantry, one for tanks etc. it doesnt seem to be very difficult to implement and would be a huge improvement. the conquest map could also be much more interessting. its nice that it is random but a real map with the battleground at their real locations on a map would be much more interesting. it would be nice if this would at least be an option. and it would be great if you could make the conquest campaign bigger, that it takes longer to beat the enemy hq. the unlimited option is nice but there is a lack of a long term goal.

there are a few bugs but most of them are not really a big issue except for the unit pathfinding (sometimes they just get stuck) and the occurence of friendly fire. you might argue that friendly fire can be realistic but not in this way, very often the artillery/at guns just shoot each other in the back because one of them were in the way of the other. that can be very annoying and lead to quite a few match restarts. 

the game could be more optimised especially on dlc maps. to be fair i dont have the strongest gaming pc and i upgraded my ram especially for this game. dont get me wrong. the graphics are not bad and i guess an engine has to provide a lot in a game that has typical rts birds-eye perspective and 1st/3rd person on the ground but still, it should run smoother.

But the main issue is enemy ai in conquest. I mainly play conquest on hardcore and it is still too easy. In an attack match, when the ai has to defend, the ai just tries to rush you with its units and the player simply has to shoot down the incoming waves until the ai is out of reinforcements. after that the ai defenses are just too weak and its is often not necessary to employ any interessting tactics. In defense matches the ai does the same, but of course, this makes much more sense when the ai is attacking. the issue is that the player simply has to set up a good defense line and then watch the ai throw wave after wave on your defenses. i just watch the match unfold and dont have to do much. at least these matches usually dont take too long. 

These are mainly conquest issues, the missions can be very hard on the higher difficulties. The missions are very mixed. There are quite a lot i havent played but the missions in which you have to attack can be quite fun. i didnt really like the missions in which you have to defend. in defense there is just no room for interesting tactics. and developing new tactics and using combined arms is where the game shines. 

The strength of the game really lies in the necessity to use combined arms and the environment to execute a succesessful attack. you cant just drive to the enemys base with a powerfull tank and shoot everthing (sadly thats exactly what the ai does). you are seen by infantry in cover and the AT units/guns will take you out especially in close combat areas like towns where you need infantry. on the other hand infantry is very vulnerable on open fields.
and this is the main draw for me. the "realism". it just feels real that you have to use very different units and tactics depending on the environment.  this is why it doesnt get boring and you often have to think of new ways to attack, making it more complex and adding to the feeling of realism. and you have to use the enviroment because line of sight matters a lot. for example it is much easier to take a valley than to take a hill. most rts feel really 2d and flat, this game doesnt and i love it. all of this makes it feel so much closer reality. the tactics you have to use in the game feel so much more real and close to what a real company / battalion commander would have to use, than in most other (ww2) rts games. 

of course there are a lot of things that are not really realistic like distances. but these are compromises that are useful to make it a fun game. you cant really use the same scale in a rts game in which you can direct control artillery and infantry. it just wouldnt work. 

there is so much more that i could go into that is great or could be improved but i will keep it there. 
all in all it is a great game and can be lots of fun but really has to improve on some big issues, to really unfold its full potential.

Gates of Hell stands out because it doesn’t just throw you into chaotic battles it demands strategy, precision, and adaptability. Every encounter feels like a puzzle, and success requires more than quick reflexes; you need to out think your enemies.

The level design is phenomenal, with environments that aren’t just visually stunning but also strategically rich. Each area feels like it has a story to tell, and the dynamic AI keeps you on your toes. No two fights feel the same, which makes every victory feel earned.

I especially appreciated how the game rewards careful planning. Rushing in is rarely an option; instead, you’re pushed to use the terrain, your resources, and your brain to survive. It’s challenging but never unfair, and that balance is rare in today’s games.

If you’re someone who loves strategy and thrives on the thrill of overcoming steep challenges, Gates of Hell is your battlefield.

If you're into strategy games with a focus on gritty realism and intense combat, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell - Ostfront is worth your time. This game takes World War II strategy to a whole new level, combining real-time tactics with a heavy dose of detail that makes every battle feel alive.

What stands out right away is the level of realism. From the environments to the units, everything feels authentic. You’re not just moving generic tanks and soldiers; you're commanding historically accurate vehicles, weapons, and troops that behave as you’d expect on the battlefield. Tanks feel like massive, destructive beasts, but they’re vulnerable if you expose their weak spots. Infantry units aren't just cannon fodder—they're versatile and critical to holding ground or taking objectives.

The graphics and sound design really add to the immersion. Watching explosions tear through cover or hearing the crack of rifle fire gives the game a visceral edge. It’s not just eye candy either; the destructible environments mean you have to think on your feet. If a building gets leveled, you lose cover, and that changes the flow of the battle instantly.

The gameplay strikes a balance between micromanagement and broader tactical planning. You can control individual units directly if you want, which is perfect for lining up that crucial tank shot or sneaking infantry into a better position. At the same time, you’re managing resources, reinforcements, and objectives across the map. It’s satisfying to see a well-thought-out plan come together, but it’s just as intense to adapt when things go sideways (and trust me, they will).

Multiplayer is where the game really shines, though. Going head-to-head with other players who know how to use the game’s mechanics is both challenging and rewarding. The community, while not massive, is passionate and filled with players who take the game seriously. This can make for some truly epic battles where every move matters.

The game isn’t perfect, though. The learning curve is steep, especially if you're new to this type of strategy game. The tutorials help, but there’s a lot to take in, and it can feel overwhelming at first. Also, while the graphics are solid, some of the animations can feel a bit clunky at times. None of this breaks the experience, but it’s something to keep in mind if you’re looking for polish on every detail.

Overall, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell - Ostfront is a must-play for strategy fans who crave depth and authenticity. The mix of tactical gameplay, historical detail, and intense battles makes it stand out from other games in the genre. It’s not the most beginner-friendly experience, but if you’re willing to put in the time, it’s incredibly rewarding. Whether you’re into single-player campaigns or multiplayer showdowns, this game delivers.

Gates of Hell: Ostfront - the ideological successor of Men of War

Gates of Hell: Ostfront (GoH) is a realistic and, in some ways, historical RTS game without building your own base in the usual sense. GoH focuses on the events of WWII and, in particular, on the Eastern Front with an emphasis on realism and previously unseen in large-scale games, but no less important battles: the Battle of the Dnieper, the Defense of the village of Matryonino near Moscow by the Panfilov Division, partisan sorties in the rear of the Wehrmacht and much more.

The gameplay in single missions depends on the task, but often when attacking you will need to capture the specified strategic positions and when defending, protect these same specified strategic positions.  At this point, a very important clarification is needed: unlike Men of War: Assault Squad 2, which is one of the most popular Men of War thanks to one YouTuber, attack missions do not look like alternating capture of points with a ton of infantry and equipment - no! In GoH, each mission is scripted and has its own, albeit short, "plot" in the form of a script. So, for example, when playing for the Germans at the beginning of the war, a detachment of T-34-85 will not move against you, because they simply did not exist then. 

The same is with defensive missions - each line you defend is strategically, and I will repeat this again - strategically important! In the very first mission for the Russians - Absolute Zero, you defend almost the last line of defense of Moscow. Also, in the campaign for the Soviets, you will need to defend a column leaving Crimea from German attacks as a result of the mass retreat of 1941.  Thus, in terms of the "plot" and mission structure, GoH is more reminiscent of the very first Men of War and its father, Faces of War.

The gameplay in PvP matches is painfully reminiscent of that in Men of War: Assault Squad 2, but is absolutely not similar to it. We can talk about PvP matches for a long time, but I will say briefly and only what makes them different from their ancestor. From the main ones and what radically changes the gameplay: the maps have grown in scale by at least one and a half to two times; weapons shoot about the same amount further; doctrines with unique units that can be selected before the start of the game have appeared; I can’t say why, but the full control mode feels much better; due to the change of tactical points to zones, the gameplay has stopped resembling throwing grenades at each other and has become more "tactical" than "dynamic".

+ Huge scale of battle 
+ Excellent graphics
+ Immersion in the game
+ Huge development of levels and units
- Game requirements for PC
-Long duration of battles (PvE and PvP)
-Perceptible, but not significant imbalance in PvP battles

Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a challenging and rewarding real-time strategy game that accurately depicts the brutal Eastern Front of World War II. While not perfect, it offers a unique and immersive experience for players willing to invest the time to master its complexities.

[b]Strengths:[/b]

1. [b]Brutal Realism:[/b] The game doesn’t shy away from the grim realities of the Eastern Front. The sheer scale of the battles, the high casualty rates, and the unforgiving nature of the environment contribute to a sense of historical weight rarely seen in other RTS games.
2. [b]Tactical Depth:[/b] Unit composition, terrain exploitation, and flanking maneuvers are all crucial to success. The game rewards strategic thinking and careful planning, demanding more than just mindless clicking. The variety of units, each with strengths and weaknesses, adds to the tactical possibilities.
3. [b]Atmospheric Presentation:[/b] The sound design and graphics, while not cutting-edge, effectively convey the bleak and brutal atmosphere of the Eastern Front. The sounds of gunfire, explosions, and the cries of soldiers contribute to the immersive experience.
4. [b]Modding Community:[/b] A strong modding community extends the lifespan of the game significantly, adding new units, maps, and scenarios.

[b]Weaknesses:[/b]

1. [b]Steep Learning Curve:[/b] The game’s complexity can be overwhelming for newcomers to the genre or to the intricacies of WWII Eastern Front tactics. The tutorial could benefit from improvements.
2. [b]Technical Issues:[/b] While improved over its initial release, the game still suffers from occasional bugs and performance issues, particularly on larger maps or with large numbers of units.
3. [b]UI/UX:[/b] The user interface can be somewhat clunky and unintuitive at times, hindering efficient management of resources and units.
4. [b]Repetitive Gameplay (for some):[/b] The core gameplay loop, while tactically rich, might feel repetitive to players who prefer more variety in mission objectives or campaign structure.

[b]Overall:[/b]

Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a solid RTS title that stands out with its realistic portrayal of the Eastern Front. While its steep learning curve and occasional technical issues might deter some players, those willing to persevere will find a deeply engaging and strategically rich experience. It’s recommended for players seeking a challenging and historically-grounded RTS with a focus on tactical combat and the brutal realities of WWII. However, players expecting a polished, user-friendly experience might want to temper their expectations.

This game is absolutely fantastic. I was searching for something to satisfy my craving after Company of Heroes 2, and when I saw that Company of Heroes 3 was a total disappointment, I stumbled upon this. It's easily 30 times better than Company of Heroes and the best RTS of all time. The ability to switch to first-person mode is amazing—not so much when playing as a regular foot soldier, but especially when you're mowing down enemies with a mounted machine gun or firing off artillery rounds blowing up tanks.

First-person mode is so immersive that you can lose track of time, sometimes forgetting that your allies are getting absolutely obliterated back at Base B. The game features tons of maps and has incredible replayability. I enjoy playing as both the Nazis and the Americans, though I don't care much for the Russians or the fins.

Skirmish mode is the standout feature for me—it's far better than the campaign. The campaign is cool, but it just doesn't compare to the thrill of skirmish mode. You can adjust the length of your campaigns, and as you progress through battles, you can upgrade your vehicles, tanks, and infantry units.

Don’t wait—get this game. World War II has never been this engaging!

CONS: 
The Medics most of the time (if you don't set them to "Hold Fire") will fight enemies instead of healing the wounded soldiers! Devs should PRIORITIZE HEALING to fighting, without the player having to change the Fire Mode of each Medic each time, so the Medic would FIRST HEAL the downed soldier (even if he has to go prone) and then return incoming fire! It's kinda stupid for a Medic to fire his pistol against an enemy equipped with a PPSh-41 and letting the wounded soldier die!!! With 5-6 Medics around you loose control, and soldiers...

Soldiers, in order to go from point A to B using the trenches, often climb outside the trenches, exposing themselves to enemy fire and die 90% of the time, if you let them go their own path. One should set waypoints in trenches for them to stay inside them! It's crazy really! 
The same for vehicles! Even though they are supposed to travel faster via roads (by default) than any other type or terrain, but they instead seem to run in a straight line most of the time, taking the shortest route from A to B! 
PROS:

Top tier RTS. Direct controlling units and shifting perspective so fluidly feels like a natural progression of the genre itself. You're going to get a physics simulator with obsessive and authentic details that might not always go your way. This 'feels' like either the Blitzkrieg mod from CoH1 or Spearhead from CoH2 in terms of damage tuning and unit health and engagement range is less 'arcady'. The AI is challenging enough to make comp stomps a good time and the campaigns and missions are well made and great for co-op. This is a good game.

Every one of my dynamic campaign armies has a truck that I load with either MGs or Explosives from scavenged bodies on every single map I play. The trick is that you collect the gear in combat before the map hits the maximum number of entities on the ground and the new bodies remove the old ones. You scavenge as you go for high risk and maximum reward. There's hotkeys to highlight items and corpses on the ground incase objects are difficult to see. If you look at the map from a low raking angle with the highlights on, you can identify all the dropped LMGs and irregularly shaped gear like sachels or repair kits almost instantly as you zoom in. It's like the devs knew I was going to hoard everything I could get and optimized it as a feature of the game. This is a good game.

Call to Arms: Gates of Hell - Ostfront has a lot going for it, but a few things are holding it back. First, the UI for deploying units needs improvement. Unlike Men of War: Assault Squad 2, it takes way too many clicks to switch between deploying different types of units. In a game where speed matters, this is a real problem.

Another issue is the cover system. It just doesn’t feel reliable. Sometimes it doesn’t register cover based on the objects on the map, or it does so in a messy way. Units will think they're in cover, but they’re actually exposed, which gets frustrating.

And then there's the building process for defenses. It’d be awesome if all soldiers could help speed up tasks like digging trenches or setting up sandbags by working together. Right now, it’s one soldier at a time, and there's no way to queue multiple builds. You have to wait for one to finish before starting another, which really slows things down. Adding a queue option to let them dig multiple trenches or set up sandbags without constant micromanaging would make a big difference.

If any of this already has a workaround that I missed, I’d love to know! But as it stands, these tweaks could really polish the experience and keep the action flowing.

The short version: It’s a great WW2 game with lots of content and well worth a positive review in spite of its shortcomings.
The long version: Before I go into detail, I only play single player so take it for what it’s worth. 
    
The good:
-	The game features similar gameplay as MoWAS2 and SirHinkel’s missions. There is so much you can do in this game that you can’t do in any other games. If you've played Heroes: SoWW2, FoW, MoW and MoWAS, this game is the pinnacle in the evolution of that series.
-	There’s a ton of content, especially if you buy the WW2 bundle. If you get it on sale, the price is very reasonable. 
-	The game has great attention to detail and historical accuracy as well as lots of different types of units and lots of things to do with them.
-	The graphics, voice acting and weapon sounds are greatly improved in comparison to its predecessors. This game is far more polished in its presentation.
-	The interface is simple and visually pleasing, very unobtrusive, yet it has everything you need.
-	The game is better optimized than MoWAS and MoW. It uses the computer's resources more effciently. I do recommend having it installed on an SSD to cut the long loading times in half.
-	The devs are very active.
-	Modding is easy and there are a ton of mods available in the workshop.
-	The missions are unlocked and you can skip the ones you don’t like.

The bad:
-	The game doesn’t feature all of the factions, nor all of the theaters from the previous game. It is being expanded through DLCs which you have to buy separately. When on sale, the price is not bad at all, but because of the dev team limited size and resources it may take quite a while until we get all of the major factions – Britain and Japan are missing at the time of this review.
-	There is a lot of micro around certain types of units and certain types of actions and things can get clumsy and frustrating, medics for example.
-	The player AI is nerfed in comparison to the enemy AI. This is particularly noticeable with the accuracy of artillery.
-	The pathfinding can be annoying though it’s honestly nothing we’re not already used to.
-	The visibility of units was much better in MoWAS. The units blend a bit too well with the environment. The trees are also too big and obscure the view unnecessarily. I would like to be able to see the little dudes doing their thing.
-	Some of the campaign missions have poor design and they are heavily scripted. I don’t like stealth missions at all. I prefer the skirmish format. 
-	The learning curve for complete beginners is probably steep I imagine. The game is not easy. In my experience it’s a bit more difficult than MoWAS2. There is a very nice tutorial now though.

This game killed Company of Heroes for me.

The attention to detail, tactical flexibility, and and the ability to manually control / aim with units makes for intense, god-tier tactics gameplay.

Something of a spiritual successor to the Men of War series (uses the same game engine, in fact), GoH is mostly successful in polishing that series' weak points to almost AAA standard.

Some criticisms I have are the occasional pathfinding issues where units will take the most threatening routes to their destination ("No, 101st airborne paratrooper, please don't run into the field of fire of that MG42 that you KNOW is there"). It would also be nice if units prioritised following trenches instead of preferring the straight "as the crow flies" path that has the unit wandering in and out of them.

The voice acting also varies wildly in quality, though it is never "The aim is in the reach zone!" bad.

The gameplay can be very micro-intensive as each soldier has limited ammo and an actual inventory to manage. When a soldier runs out of ammo far away from an ammo crate, you can pick up weapons off the ground and search the inventories of the dead for ammo for each individual soldier. I only play single player, so I mitigate the micro required by slowing the game down (Backspace key) enough until I can "catch up". However, you can't do this in skirmish / conquest / multiplayer, so if you're new, definitely start off with the single-player campaigns.

Pick up the base game to see if it is your cup of tea, then pick up DLC in accordance with the front/missions  you are interested in playing on.

Highly recommend.

The game is interesting and well-made, but there's just too much micro-management to be enjoyable. It has impressively realistic mechanics when it comes to armored vehicle combat, taking into account different types of armor piercing rounds and their efficacy at range and even versus sloped and non-sloped armoring. The ability to individually take third-person control of soldiers during combat is also great, letting you speed up drawn out combat or execute precision stealth maneuvers while the rest of your units are in open combat with enemy troops.

But the inventory system... Following the realism of other aspects of the game, each soldier has its own inventory with limited ammunition, ammo, repair items, healing items, grenades, ect. In theory this sounds like a cool concept, as it adds to the realism by requiring you to outfit your troops individually with the types of ammunition and weapons they'll require to create customized squads and individual soldiers. In practice, this means that you are constantly managing your soldiers' inventories when a supply truck isn't available. Managing one soldier's inventory is fun and unique. Managing ten or more soldiers' inventories at the same time is frankly exhausting. Nothing breaks pacing worse scrounging around  a battlefield to restock ten soldiers and making sure their equipment is well-distributed. What should be a unique and fun mechanic quickly becomes a complete and sudden stop to any fun you're having actually engaging in combat. And keep in mind that, true to realism, different armies use different weapons and ammunition types, so you're not just gathering generic ammo types, you're also making sure that the ammunition you just picked up works with your gun or that you have enough room to steal your enemy's weapons 

A similar problem exists with controlling individual soldiers. Joining your soldiers in combat as a third-person shooter is an amazing and fun concept, but keep in mind that this is also a real-time strategy game so while you're controlling one soldier, you're not controlling the rest of your army. I believe there are some controls for directing units while in third-person mode, but it's likely related to only that unit's squad and I'm not sure how much control you really have. The third-person mode problem is less problematic than the inventory system, since you have limited control over other units and gameplay doesn't halt while you're shooting up the place.

If it weren't for the inventory system, I would totally recommend this game, and others might thoroughly enjoy the micromanaging required, but to me it just feels like it drags the game to a grinding halt. It's sad, because this game has some amazing ideas and fun gameplay, but I want to be actually playing and not micromanaging the inventories of 10+ units at the same time. It's clear a lot of work went into this game in terms of realism and just general good quality development, but it falls into the same trap as most games with hyper-realistic mechanics. The mechanics get in the way of actually playing and enjoying the game. Maybe if the game had simplified the inventory system or just gotten rid of it entirely in favor of either a kit system or a general supply system to keep the realism of still keeping your units supplied without requiring you to sift through 10 or more inventories at the same time.

If you enjoy hyper-realistic war games and don't mind the general slog caused by maintaining said realism, I can quite easily see how you'd enjoy this game. It's well-made. Very well-made. I just can't say I personally recommend it. It's painful, because I really WANT to like it... but I also want to play the game, and it really doesn't feel like I am when I'm micromanaging inventories. It's just not for me.

Great game, every hour well spent shy a few for trial and error with mods. The game modes available for both MP and SP are enough to keep you entertained for long periods of time on their own.

   The game has a large modding community that is both dedicated and active, brings even more to the game than the devs could hope to in a reasonable time frame. Not to bash them, but modders are just built different.

   Conquest mode, found under the SP tab, is the thick of this game, at least for me that is. It allows you to select a nation to play as and fight against in a short/medium/long/Infinite battle. The mode allows you to earn money, resources, research, and stars, for unlocking and up keeping your units. You can also earn unit XP between battles (offense/defense) and keep that XP even after the battle is over. You can capture enemy vehicles and equipment at the end of every engagement, allowing you to either sell it for extra income or use against them, adding a fun looting element to the gameplay as well. Absolute blast and fairly customizable with plenty of mods also supporting it, so try it out if and when you decide to pick the game up.

   The DLC's are mostly good to ok, Talvisota has very nice maps for the most part, but the Finn's are fairly lacking compared to the 3 other nations available to the player through DLC.

   Liberation is pretty good, with fun and appropriate map design and a large roster of US units and divisions to choose from, the US really bring a lot to the table in terms of longevity and entertainment.

   Scorched Earth is a fun one, with one of the largest explosive weapons in any CTA/MoW title I know of that the player can operate personally. It comes with larger than life weapons and experimentals for both USSR and Germany.

   Game does have it's frame issues, especially on higher settings combined with large entity pools. So be warned, take an SSD or external drive and a decent graphics card with your purchase here. Also has memory crash issues but this only happens to me during Conquest, but may affect other areas of the game as well, including MP.

   MP is also a bit clunky for conquest, but for the most part works just like base CTA or MoWAS titles before it.

   DLC's are good overall, but get them on sale. Base game however is well worth the money on its own. You like WW2 RTS? Buy it. Now.

It also means you can accurately shoot tanks/infantry/vehicles through a thick forest, for example, as long as there's not anything in the path of your ordnance and somebody can see that enemy. The conquest mode is a very interesting gamemode, starting with a small amount of low quality soldiers, working your way to a whole elite army. I haven't purchased liberation because i refuse to buy an A$36 DLC for a DLC. I've also played liberation before, in COH and MOWAS2 for the last 10 years.

Conquest is the only thing that keeps me coming back to this game, but it can quickly get boring playing the same maps with the same units, making every campaign blend into one. I wish there was more incentive to care about a particular campaign, but as it stands i just start up conquest and play it until I get bored and start up a new one, rarely seeing a campaign through to the end.

There should also be much greater customization of skirmishes/conquests allowing for pseudo-roleplay. Like configurations that would see oneself leading a group of early-war partisans focusing on unit tactics and captured supplies for example. Some mods attempt things like this but nothing does it well.

Options for players allowing which units can be fielded in skirmishes/conquests and how many research points units cost and ways to determine the scale of battles are so easy to implement but could add so much in the way of roleplay which in turn drastically increases replayability in singleplayer.

Devs could also add literal customization to units such as upgrading individual units with better weapons/features on the conquest screen in addition to visual customization. It would also be a cool feature if players could name units. These small changes could add so much investment into individual conquest campaigns

In short the game needs more content, which in my eyes due to the paywall required to play the game in the first place should be free. The game is also severly lacking in customization which heavily affects SP replayability.

I wanted a WWII game where you can control small units with a handful of support units and armor, while being able to "level up" your soldiers through survival and gaining experience.  A perk would be able to level them up individually, promote them and give awards.  I really enjoyed Theatre of War 2 (which did all of this).  I'm looking for something that plays similar to that.  This game was almost it, but fell flat after a few hours of play.  

[h3]The Good[/h3]
[list]
    [*]I really enjoy the high graphics quality and I very much appreciate the historical accuracy of units and their presentation.  
    [*]Engagement with the enemy feels realistic in regards to sound, looks, engagement distances and damage received/inflicted.  
    [*]I like how broken down vehicles can be repaired.  
    [*]I like how units get better with the more experience they get.  
    [*]I like the idea of the dynamic campaign and the huge research tree.  
    [*]I love the ability to switch from RTS to third person and being able to control individual units.  
    [*]I love being able to dig in.  
    [*]I love the idea of being able to take fallen enemy soldier's weapons and ammo.  
[/list]

[h3]The Bad[/h3]
Where do I begin?
[list]
    [*]First and foremost, you can't pause the game and issue orders.  WTF.  How are you supposed to command units in the field, especially when they are "dumb" (i.e. you can't issue an order to advance the front cautiously and take cover and fire when resistance is met).  You can pause the game and do some things, but not select units and not issue orders.  I absolutely HATE that.  
    [*]Next, unit selection is absolute ♥♥♥♥.  This is such a basic thing and I'm *astounded* that it's so poor on a game that looks so good.  Did I select one guy, or the whole squad? or just part of the squad?  Here, let me drag a box over some soldiers I want to move.  Why did it not select anything?  Here I want to move an infantry squad and a heavy MG and a Scout Car to a general area.  Why did it automatically group them into one gigantic squad?  Ok, maybe I can move just one guy, so I'll click him...wait why did it now select the entire squad?  Click him again and now I have him and three other seemingly random guys.  I want to move three rifle squads across the map - seems like I should be able to quickly select them (which you can't) and then right click on the mini-map to move them (which you can't).  You have to struggle to select what you want, then scroll across the map (or right click mini-map to move camera), then try to place them (which sometimes works great, sometimes not at all).  
    [*]Unit management in general is a nightmare.  How many rifle squads do I have on the field?  I have no idea.  Can I select all my tanks...wait, how many tanks do I have here?  I select two and it looks like I have one icon now.  Incredibly confusing.  
    [*]Load times are excruciating.  Start a map.  Loading.  It gets up to 94% in a few seconds, but then sits there for 5 minutes.  (I have a high end gaming computer, so it's not my computer).  Every map, every time.  It takes FOREVER for things to load.  
    [*]The game scales up quantity far too fast and far too much.  It just keeps adding more and more soldiers to the field as your campaigns progress.  It starts out perfect for me, about 30 men each side, but that's only for the first map.  It feels like every battle you go into, the number of soldiers on each side doubles, then doubles again, then doubles again.  A couple of maps in, you have hundreds if not thousands, and it really starts to drop frame rate and my high-end gaming computer really struggles to keep up.  It's overwhelming and beyond frustrating after only a few battles.  
    [*]While I love being able to control individual units, I can't do that and control my force.  I switch to a tank and am tearing it up, having a great time, but then realize that the enemy has flanked me, and my stupid army just stands there and gets slaughtered.  They can't function unless I'm overseeing and directing every single action.  You can't play one unit and command your force at the same time - it's far too difficult continuously switching back and forth (and ESPECIALLY when you can't issue orders while the game is paused!).  So much for that aspect working.  
    [*]Unit movement is clumsy.  After you struggle to select a single squad, then you move them.  The game has a cool aspect where it can show you shadows of your soldiers where they're going to go, but that doesn't work all the time...maybe half the time I can get that feature to work.  Else, you just move them to an area in a line formation.  No option for other formations (like in ToW2).  Also, some stand, some kneel, rarely will they take cover unless directly ordered to do so soldier by soldier.  Ordering all infantry to stand, kneel or crawl seems like it should be a select then press one button to issue the order.   But no, selection is a nightmare, then you press stance button and it changes those standing to kneeling, those kneeling to crawling and those crawling to standing.  They don't all do the same thing!  They just do the next move in that order.  Ridiculous!
    [*]Unit inventory is a great idea, but again, poorly executed.  You sometimes can use the examine button, sometimes not.  Sometimes you can hover your mouse over things to examine, sometimes not.  Most of the time, you have to press one button to highlight bodies and then you can examine only while they're highlighted, but that's only for everything *except* weapons.  For weapons, you have to press and hold a different button to see and pick them up.  Far too clumsy.  In ToW2,  you walk up to an area of dead soldiers and the game would immediately and without any button pushing of  your own, show you all the things you can add to your inventory.

[b]A Superior WWII RTS Experience[/b]
[h1]Introduction[/h1]
 Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront, developed by Barbedwire Studios and Digitalmindsoft, is a standout real-time strategy (RTS) game that delivers an intense and immersive experience centered on the brutal Eastern Front of World War II. Whether you're a seasoned RTS enthusiast or a newcomer to the genre, this game offers a rich and satisfying experience that surpasses many others, including the disappointing "Men of War 2." If you're in search of a WWII RTS that blends historical accuracy with dynamic, action-packed gameplay, Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a must-play.

[h1]Gameplay and Features[/h1] 
One of the most impressive aspects of Gates of Hell: Ostfront is the sheer variety and depth of its gameplay modes. From meticulously recreated historical single-player campaigns to the dynamic campaign mode, which allows you to shape your own war experience, the game offers endless replayability and strategic variety. The dynamic campaign mode, in particular, stands out as a highlight—offering players the chance to build and lead their own army group across an ever-changing battlefield. I highly recommend this mode and hope the developers continue to expand on it in future updates.

The game features an extensive array of vehicles, with over 250 vehicles and 100 heavy weapons at your disposal. Each vehicle is meticulously modeled with accurate armor layouts, historical ammunition loadouts, and fully detailed internal components. The game's realistic armor penetration and ammunition mechanics make vehicle combat feel intense and strategic, adding a layer of depth that is rarely seen in other RTS titles.

In addition to vehicles, the game offers a wide variety of infantry and support options, allowing for diverse and dynamic combat scenarios. Whether you're coordinating an armored assault, laying down suppressive fire with infantry, or calling in air support, the game provides countless ways to approach each battle.

[h1]Realism and Immersion[/h1]
 Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront excels in its dedication to realism and historical accuracy. The sound design and visuals are top-notch, with authentic battle sounds and beautifully rendered environments that bring the Eastern Front to life. The ability to switch between different control modes—first-person, third-person, and classic RTS top-down view—further enhances the immersion, allowing players to engage in combat at both macro and micro levels.

The game's historical campaigns take place in painstakingly recreated locations, offering players a true-to-life experience of some of the most pivotal battles of WWII. The attention to detail in the game's vehicles, weapons, and environments is truly impressive, making each mission feel like a genuine WWII combat experience.

[h1]Room for Improvement[/h1]
 While Gates of Hell: Ostfront is an exceptional game, there are a few areas where it could be even better. The quest design can feel a bit repetitive at times, and while the dynamic campaign is excellent, it would benefit from further expansion with more varied objectives and mission types. This could add even more depth and replayability to an already outstanding game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
 Overall, Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a superior RTS experience that sets a new standard for WWII strategy games. It outshines its competitors, including the underwhelming Men of War 2, by offering a rich, immersive, and highly realistic portrayal of the Eastern Front. With its dynamic gameplay modes, extensive vehicle selection, and attention to historical detail, this game is a must-play for any fan of WWII strategy games. If you're looking for a game that combines intense action with deep strategy, Gates of Hell: Ostfront is the one to get.

I bought this on whim during a sale to scratch a WW2 Eastern Front itch that hasn't been scratched since Combat Mission was good. I'm not a big fan of tactical RTS games as you can only be in one place at a time while the AI is literally everywhere, so it was a punt.

I'm really enjoyng it though. The battles are more squad level than Steel Division, which is more my thing and is easier to keep on top of when the engagements are in relatively small areas. The fighting feels great with a lot of tension and moments of blind panic, and you have tons of options, both in what your units can do and the sheer variety of units in the game. 

Graphics are good, sounds are great and the overall ambience works really well. Same with the maps - they look great and feel very authentic. The music... ehhh, turn it off, you won't miss it.

The only realy criticism I've got is that  the interface isn't all that clear and it has a fairly steep learning curve, but that's this type of strategy game for you. Also, it doesn't give much information about the units - you can get the stats for them, which is good, but it doesn't really give you a sense of what the units are best suited for. Not a problem if you have a good working knowledge of Soviet and German infantry and armour, but it would be nice to see a bit of descriptive text to help differentiate the many different types of rifleman squads or Pz IVs in the game.

Overall though, it's a solid game that does a good job of balancing tactical options and control with the non-stop action of an RTS. Definitely worth a go if you're looking for something smaller scale than Steel Division or something a bit less videogamey than Company of Heroes.

Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront, often abbreviated to Gates of Hell, serves as the spiritual successor to the revered Men of War series. Where Men of War II failed to deliver an iterative product that capitalized on its excellent and intuitive concept for a real-time strategy (RTS) game, Gates of Hell innovates and improves upon that formula significantly.

One of the most significant upgrades, particularly appreciated by players like myself who have waited patiently since Men of War: Assault Squad 2, is the transition from a 32-bit engine to a 64-bit engine in Gates of Hell. This new, improved, and expanded engine provides enhanced stability, allowing for larger battles and more dynamic mayhem. This technical advancement ensures a smoother gaming experience with fewer crashes and better performance, accommodating the complex scenarios typical of large-scale RTS games.

Another notable improvement lies in the direct control feature for units. In Men of War, players were restricted to the traditional RTS camera angle, limiting the immersion and control. Gates of Hell introduces new third-person and first-person direct control modes for units. When controlling infantry, players can switch to a third-person view (and first-person when aiming down sights), which provides a more immersive experience. Similarly, when controlling tanks, players can see exactly what the gunner sees through their optics, adding a realistic layer to tactical gameplay. This innovation is a massive improvement over the older system found in the Men of War games and enhances the strategic depth and enjoyment.

The game offers a commendable selection of units from Germany, Russia, the United States, and even Finland. These units feel more responsive, accurate, and varied compared to previous games in the genre. The unit deployment icons in Gates of Hell have also been improved, making it clearer and more intuitive for players to understand what they are deploying for their first few sessions, streamlining the gameplay experience.

However, Gates of Hell is not without its flaws. The game currently faces some networking difficulties, with players encountering peculiar errors such as "Non-promiscuous NAT." While this issue is generally resolved with about a minute of waiting in the server browser or through a game restart, it can be frustrating and disrupt the gaming experience. It is hoped that these issues will be addressed and resolved in future updates.

In conclusion, Gates of Hell represents a monumental technical leap forward for the concept laid out by Men of War. The original series, despite its groundbreaking gameplay, has fallen behind technologically and is now prone to crashes and other issues. Gates of Hell proudly takes up the mantle with its vastly superior 64-bit engine, bringing with it more complex systems, improved stability, greater variety, and an incredibly polished product. The game not only revitalizes the core elements that made Men of War great but also introduces new features that set a new standard for the genre. While Gates of Hell does stumble due to its networking architecture slightly, this flaw is quickly remedied and does not prevent the game from being highly scored. The minor setbacks in online play are not significant enough to overshadow the monumental leaps this product makes in other areas. At a price point of $8 on sale, Gates of Hell is undoubtedly among the best gaming investments one could make, offering immense value and a thoroughly engaging RTS experience.
