I want to start this review by saying that I have been a fan of men of war for over 10 years, I have just about every game and ~1500 hours in MOWAS2 alone. I understand that those games too were plagued with some weird design choices and stupid AI. I would also like to say that I do like this game, I think it's fun and I will continue to play it and (usually) enjoy it. The models and textures are very well done and add a lot of flavor, the voice lines are well done, and the campaign is really fun. It is genuinely probably one of my favorite games at the moment.

However, it is plagued with some serious issues that really should not be a problem this late into development. The AI seems to have slightly more "realistic" pathfinding than Men of War, the vehicles take roads and so on, but if you aren't constantly paying attention to your units and micromanaging them then they will more often than not get stuck on some random entity, which is something that did happen in MoW but not nearly as much as it seems to happen in this game. Half the time if I order my towed artillery to move somewhere they don't even move and I have to enter direct control and do it myself. The AI also does not fare well in combat, units often don't engage in combat even when ordered and when using the attack ground option with artillery I sometimes have to do it 5 or 6 times before they actually listen or even do it in the direct control mode because they just refuse. Infantry combat is mostly up to RNG, and at times even your experienced infantry can repeatedly miss their shots while a random Soviet partisan domes your squad leader in the head with a rusty mosin. On top of that, if infantry is engaged while moving they will often just keep sprinting into the enemies line of fire and all get gunned down. It doesn't help that in multiplayer, people are really sweaty (obligatory "skill issue") and it is borderline unplayable for anyone who is playing against someone who memorized every single hotkey meanwhile you just got home from work and want to relax and play a game.

There are a lot of issues with the AI and those are just some of them, but I feel the need to explain that with heavy scripting, the game is perfectly fun. For me, I play a lot of the single player missions or ♥♥♥♥ around in the editor and the issue is usually when I decide to play multiplayer, skirmish, or conquest that the game can get extremely frustrating (again, skill issue). Firstly, why is there no reverse option for vehicles? It is really annoying when I have to micromanage all of my infantry from getting killed by a single HE round and at the same time I have to slowly right click right behind my vehicles for them to reverse out of a dangerous situation. You would think this would have been in the game by now considering it totes itself as being ultra realistic. In skirmish, you start the mission off with either no or a handful of infantry support units depending on which doctrine you pick before you start the game, which can be infuriating especially when you're trying to assault numerically superior entrenched infantry on a hill supported by mortars, machine guns, and tanks while you have some guys with rifles and a truck with a machine gun strapped to the back and little to no infantry or anti-tank support to speak of, which AGAIN, isn't realistic at all. And once again, this wouldn't be so bad if it weren't so difficult to utilize some of the features of the game like smoke grenades or even something as simple as making your units engage the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemy. It was also a weird decision to make most of the heavy weapons in the game have the same ranges. For some reason, mortars have to be in range of AT weapons to bombard the position, light AT guns have only a slightly lower range than the heavier ones, heavy artillery has surprisingly short range, etc. At least in the OG Men of War it would scale even if the ranges were ridiculously short. The devs also didn't even bother to make the units in skirmish remotely accurate to the period that any of the missions take place in. Also, why did they decide to remove the swastika from Finnish vehicles? I understand Germany to an extent (not really, considering it's supposed to be a realistic game) but the hakaristi was completely separate from the Nazis and was first used in 1918 after a plane was given to them by Sweden, the leader of which used the swastika as a personal symbol. If you don't want to show that ♥♥♥♥, then don't make a game about world war 2, it's that simple.

Again, the design choices are odd and there are more that i'm just not remembering right now, but DESPITE ALL OF THAT, I could forgive it. Most of this stuff can be fixed with mods which is really what made the Men of War series so great. But I can't forgive the devs for REPEATEDLY releasing an unfinished product. I bought Ostfront in December of 2021 so most of the campaign missions had been fixed but I know that some of them were unplayable when the game was released and clearly no one had play tested them. And now, with the Talvisota DLC there is more unpolished slop. Spelling errors, bugs, unplayable areas, even on the Bagration map the assets for bridge on the right aren't even put together properly. I couldn't even finish the last mission in the Talvisota DLC because for some reason the Germans stopped spawning after the second wave. It also seems like they forgot to put the Finnish skirmish mission in and it took them an extra day to put it into the game. They charge people 18 dollars for a DLC that isn't even finished. Not to mention several people have noted that the devs are extremely rude if you critique their product, even if it's for things that really shouldn't even be broken in the first place. I think it's ridiculous that we are expected to sit here and put up with the lack of effort by dev teams to release a polished and playable game. If you're going to make somebody get a completely unrelated game just to play it, then release an overpriced DLC that adds a lackluster faction with reskinned units at least make it finished.

In conclusion, if you're a long time fan of Men of War, are willing to spend the money on both Call to Arms and Ostfront, and can deal with dumb AI or you are just going to have fun in the editor like I normally do, then yes the game is fun. But the single player missions, the skirmish, conquest, and the multiplayer all have some serious problems and at this stage the devs should really be focusing on the core game issues like AI and quality of life and not releasing an extortionately priced unpolished DLC.

Amazing real time tactics game, focusing on immersive and realistic mechanics, with full control down to the inventory of the individual soldier. Plenty of mods to enhance and expand the experience, just like it's heritage of CtA and MOWAS2.

Very deep historically accurate roster of units, with split time periods of WW2 in Early, Mid and Late War inventories for the factions in game. Currenly it features only the Eastern Front, with Germany, USSR and now Finland with the Talvisota add-on DLC. Everything from basic infantry with even outdated WW1 weapons all the way into the largest tanks and artillery cannons. Manual control of everything is a big feature, you can and you should take control of your tanks to accurately shoot weakspots in enemy armor. If you ever played something like War Thunder or World of Tanks in the past, you should already be familiar with this concept, of what caliber gun can penetrate what kind of tank. Infantry combat is also deep, with whole squads bringing in all different roles, such as machinegunner, machinegunner assistant (with extra ammo), Squad leader, snipers, engineers, AT infantry, or even flamethrowers. They are all individually useful for their roles. The German Pionier squad will become one of your best friends. Good positioning of stationary weapons such as infantry support guns, mortars, AT guns, AA guns, all are extremely important.

Only weak spots of this game stem from having to utilize the CtA engine as it's base. It is a good evolution from the old GEM engine of MOWAS2, with greatly improved visuals, view range and framerate, but it also has... Not very good unit AI and pathing. And by not very good I mean *really* bad. You'll get used to manually splitting your infantry and controlling them yourself to try and minimize the babysitting you have to do with them to keep them alive. It's better than CtA, where they're literally braindead, but it's still not as good and responsive as old MOWAS2.

This game is, for the most part, a very solid experience and provides something that I haven't seen from any other studio: a legitimate WWII battalion-level RTT. It has an impressive amount of vehicles, troop types, gun emplacements, artillery pieces, etc, allowing you to use a huge variety of tactics against your enemies, whether they be player or AI. It's basically the closest thing you're going to get to a WWII Total War game. Given these factors and the fun that I've had with the game so far, I have to give it a thumbs up, but I should clarify that it is a reluctant thumbs up.
The game has a litany of annoying and/or un-intuitive design choices, as well as a ton of bugs that seriously detract from its overall quality. First of all, the tutorial is atrocious, as it is so obviously designed by a dev who just assumes that the player will be able to magically guess how to carry out every action with their soldiers. They never give you any indication of which keys correspond with which actions and every weapon and vehicle seems to have its own wildly different set of key bindings. Additionally, there are no hotkeys at all for most orders, meaning that you will have to dig through layers of menus every time you simply want to give an order to a single soldier. This leaves the controls for the game feeling cumbersome and uncomfortable which is a huge deal in an RTT game where you are managing dozens or hundreds of soldiers across a battlefield that is rapidly evolving in real time.
Second, the AI is underwhelming and the game tries to compensate for that in a few less than adequate ways. AI units seem to have a hidden accuracy stat that makes them hit their target perfectly on the first shot every single time. I can't empirically prove it but my units just seem to have clearly worse accuracy. This means that if even a tiny sliver of one of your panzers is spotted by an enemy AT emplacement halfway across the map, you're getting hit and you're probably gonna lose a driver or gunner, rendering the thing practically useless. Of course, when MY units are firing at an enemy tank things all of a sudden seem to be very different. This, in addition to the fact that the AI can clearly see through the fog of war (a mechanic that only allows you to see enemies within the direct sight lines of your own troops), and WILL use that to its advantage to screw you over. I understand that the AI needs to have some crutches in order to make it more engaging to fight against but the devs have clearly chosen to take the easy route and just give it cheats instead of actually designing it to be truly intelligent.
Finally, the game suffers from a number of bugs that definitely should have been fixed by now. The cover system, one of the most fundamental features of how you manage your infantry, simply does not work. The option to place your men behind cover objects often just doesn't appear or it flickers, making it very difficult to get them exactly where you want. Sometimes they will go behind cover but then stand up straight even though they are under heavy fire. Again, its another thing that adds to the cumbersome nature of the game's controls, forcing you to think about things that you shouldn't have to, and making it harder to coordinate large battles with lots of units. On top of this, the pathfinding is completely broken and trucks/tanks will frequently move to a point, stop to re-adjust their facing, move to the next point, stop again, and so on. This means that it is nearly impossible to pull off a true Bewegungskrieg tactic which WWII is famed for, as tanks are terribly slow unless you are directly controlling them.
Ultimately, while these issues are bad, they do not outweigh the good that this game has to offer or the uniqueness of its gameplay. I just wish that the devs would not market this as a full release title and produce $20 DLC for it when it clearly should still be in early access until it has been more refined. Definitely only get this on sale, as the base $45 dollar asking price is absurd given the major problems the game still faces.

I've greatly enjoyed this game but noticed some issues the more I kept playing and figured I'd voice it since many reviews don't really get into the details.

- AI. The AI in this game is bad, not incredibly terrible but up there with pretty braindead stuff. You can camp their reinforcement area with tanks and essentially just say "GG" at that point. They rarely if ever attack when they are initially deployed and the only downside is that they are invunerable for roughly 10 seconds after coming in from off-map. At the same time, the AI has to receive some absolutely broken accuracy comparatively to your troops. My stationary AT team that has a reasonable amount of experience nearly always lose to an enemy brand new coming in from off map. Sometimes my troops won't fire at something within sight and the AI will. 

- Conquest (Dynamic) is a bad game type. I'm not saying it isn't fun, just really sucks and forces you to do down one tech path 99% of the time (tanks, literally always tanks, even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Finland tanks). The game really never provides why the opposing AI gets unlimited reinforcements (forcing you to never take your time and rushing the points...with tanks obviously). I'd always advise going for the 3 star difficulty because of the benefits of receiving more research and manpower at the end of those missions. These missions feel less strategic and more blitzkrieg all the time. You immediately win the mission after you captured all the capture points so no reason taking your time. Worst yet, they eliminated the ability to forfeit or surrender a fight, when you quit the match, you have to play it over. If you lose, you have to naturally lose because of the tickets which can take 30+ minutes because the game works off a capture point ticket mechanic. Defense missions absolutely blow and I hate them. Enjoy getting swarmed for 30 mins while you get your small group of troops and that's it. 

- Balance. The balance in this game is probably ♥♥♥♥♥♥ just because of the realism. Of course a tank is going to mow troops down easily. The issue arises when the tanks are only 3 times more expensive than a squad of infantry. Are you telling me that a tank is only worth 3x more than infantry? The efficiency you'll get out of the tank is ABSOLUTELY bonkers compared to what you'd get out of a infantry group. So much so, that it's nearly pointless to ever use troops. The game three killer things, stationary AT guns, mortars, and tanks. These three things negate literally everything else to the point where you'll be at a disadvantage for choosing anything else. 

- Direct Fire. This isn't a bad thing, it's just how it's implemented. At no point should you really be using this because if you are, your stuff is being either killed or destroyed because now your concentrating on one thing instead of your army as a whole. Now that really depends on if all your troops are currently fighting or not, it's best to Direct Control while not in combat and leave all your other troops behind. Things happen SO fast in this game that direct firing for just a moment could lead to all your other troops dying. The time to kill in this game is INSANELY fast, and you pair that up with the AI nearly pinpoint accuracy and it's not fun. The AI can do everything at once and react on the fly to everything (looking at you grenades as the AI can easily scatter but your troops are too dumb to do the same). NEVER turn on fog of war. The AI will constantly be at an advantage due to instantly reacting to any position being shown. This especially hurts with stationary AT guns and mortars. You'll just see your squads getting deleted from the fog of war while the AI rush you with it's unlimited infantry providing vision for those things. 

- Tanks. This is all you need and all you'll ever need, full stop. Makes everything else pointless (aside from stationary AT guns)

- Pathfinding and Cover System. It's a weirdly sometimes good with the cover system and other times it's absolutely ♥♥♥♥ and your troops NEVER take cover. You'll tell them to but it's more of a suggestion than a direct command. I'm fine with move fire but as long as they move to the area in which I told them to go, which they usually don't unless I tell them to double time it to that location (ignore combat, and use sprint). The cover system is inconsistent and would've really benefited with a command just like "Attack Move" but more of a "Move and Enter Cover". You're troops will never actively seek cover and the issue with this is the game is VERY micro intensive (it's fairly macro intensive as well but not as much as micro). Sometimes the pathfinding will take you down the dumbest ways and it's very reliable. It's better to do short distance movements than long distance.

- Tech Tree. It's bad. Like really bad. I'd say that all infantry should never be over 3 tech points. EVER. I'm fine with the progression but some of it doesn't make sense. When you unlock Engineers, you have to unlock the Flamethrower, AT mines, and AP mines separately but they are FREE? Developer. Just unlock everything for the player at once when it's available or just GROUP it all into one pack. If the next one is free, automatically unlock it. Once again, the only tree you should essentially ever go down is tanks. Everything else in my eyes isn't worth it when it comes to time to kill and survivability. 

Alright, so there are the cons and really that's what I like focusing on because this is exactly what you're going to be battling with this whole game. There are quite a few pros to this game and I overall really do think the game is worth it if you really enjoy a somewhat sim-like RTS. A couple of the pros are:

- Graphics. The game is really pretty (although grass and bushes usually get in my way when Direct Controlling) and it's really nice to take all in. I'm not going to say it's revolutionary but it definitely doesn't have points against it.

- Completely and utter control over everything. Want to swap crew members out of tanks for others? You can. Want to drop a weapon for another? You can. Want to loot other dead troops on the field. You can. Want to direct control all your troops to find the best defensive spots and cheese your way to victory. JUSTDOIT! It's really amazing the amount of control this game gives you. Need an officer to pared up with your machine gunner for accurate longer burst? You can do that.

- Realism. The TTK (time to kill) is really short in this game and for some it's really a pull. I do have issues with certain things in the game (like .50 cal hitting troops for 1/4 damage is really dumb but I can understand balance wise otherwise infantry would literally be 100% useless). Flamethrowers and Molotovs disable tanks if sprayed on the engine forcing the enemy to abandon the tank. Tanks are very oppressive and have to be dealt with, with cunning and precision. I find the game extremely entertaining just because of the fact that I need to think things out before committing. 

- MoW niche genre. If you like Men of War or Company of Heroes, this game is nearly a no-brainer in terms of picking it up. You really should. 

Even with all the cons I listed, it's definitely worth playing if you can get over the AI getting unlimited reinforcements and you get your small "Bad Company". If they were to fix and actually make the AI smart, it'd be way more pleasurable as they wouldn't have to make up the AI's deficiency with swarms of troops and vehicles. I don't like when limits are placed on me but not the AI, it takes me out of the world and makes me realize that the AI need a handicap in order to "win". It defeats the whole purpose of me conquering the map but still feel like I'm behind because the AI can call in as many tanks as they want along with a linear progression with their tech, meaning they are never behind

Easily one of the best RTT games I've played in a long time. It blows its predecessor, Men of War Assault Squad 2, out of the water despite it being, realistically, the same game. Why? This game is wonderfully optimized. Up to a certain point hardware means nothing for MOWAS2 as the GEM2 engine is limited to 32bit, having what should be overkill at the time, an RTX 3070 netted zero gains over my previous RX580. On top of this, mods made MOWAS2 unstable. All of this matters because Gates of Hell runs incredibly well on my current RX 6600 at Ultra, it's able to take advantage of more than 4GB of memory meaning no crashes and this has a significant graphical upgrade on top. 

Gameplay wise, it's more or less the same meat and potatoes you get from MOWAS2, with some caveats. Construction has been revamped, in particular the construction of defences by engineers and certain infantry units has been reworked for it to be a more accessible mechanic. Map design also seems to have changed, maps are far more "diverse" in terrain features, each one feels unique over the last, which unfortunately could not be said of the maps in MoWAS2 where they often felt somewhat generic, the only real differentiation being whether it was in North Africa or Russia. The biggest changes/additions in Gates of Hell are in the advanced direct control mode which is the most advertised (and in my view least important if you're in it for the RTT gameplay) mechanic. While it is cool in theory, I tend to think it is still somewhat poorly implemented as it is rather janky and the player often has more important things to worry about. I can understand it's inclusion to lengthen out playtime and for specially scripted missions but playing Skirmish and Conquest, I tended to skip over it to focus on micro. That's the other massive inclusion that blows its predecessor out of the water -- the inclusion of a dynamic campaign known as conquest. Very reminiscent of the old Blitzkrieg titles, which were somewhat similar mechanically and I would still recommend to dopamine addled zoomers as a way of kicking them out of Fortnite induced psychosis. In it you have limited resources and veteran troops, a tech tree and the option of what map and rewards you wish to unlock on a node-based strategic layer. It is rather simple, but that's the beauty of it as it is not intended to be a complex 4X strategy layer but rather what it says on the tin -- a *dynamic campaign generator*. Blitzkrieg had worked a similar way, minus the research, where selecting specific battles would unlock different veteran units (that could be carried over) for the player. Fundamentally the focus is on the tactics, the manipulation of your troops and their environment. A quick story: I had as my second battle of conquest, a defence mission as Germany. By the 70% mark I had virtually no ammo, lost most of my troops and the only significant firepower that remained and managed to carry me were my Kubelwagen with MG34 and MG34 MMG setup. The few infantrymen I had left had to be micro'd in order to scavenge for ammo from dead allies when they were under fire. Even my surviving tank commander had to pick up a rifle scavenged from a dead comrade to join the fight. While my troops had been worn down, so were the Soviets, who were sending decreasing numbers of conscripts into my grazing fire and had stopped sending tanks to be eaten up by my PzB 28s. I had managed to hold it, barely. I had to rely on elevation, line of sight, scavenging of ammo and well timed grenades to hold out towards the end. This is Gates of Hell at its finest. 

The few criticisms I do have are only really aimed at the lost content over its predecessor, though the depth of content more than makes up for it - there are far more units for the existing factions and they're far better implemented. As a window into the future, the newly added Talvisota DLC has the devs express intent to continue to broaden the number of nations and theatres. Second to this, I have noticed that they have, over the course of development, added plenty of free content drops for existing owners. The new DLC had also implemented a flurry of new units for base Gates of Hell owners that cover the early war, for Finland was at war with the USSR in late Nov 1939 and the other factions have to be balanced around this start date. Say what you will about the base Call to Arms with its oddly implemented DLC that had been rightly criticized, this more than makes up for it and I hope this monetization model works out for them. They have ensured that non-DLC owners (ie you don't own the Finnish expansion "Talvisota") can still play with DLC owners and on the same maps, thus not dividing their community. This is all very admirable and I hope to see more expansions in the future. If new nations are of interest, there is the valour mod on the workshop, by the same devs of valour for MoWAS2, that adds the "missing" factions and implements them into the conquest game mode.

Edit: after having played some of the singleplayer missions, they are incredibly well crafted in comparison with what shipped before. They're essentially large sandboxes, mission 2 of the Soviet Campaign reminds me of Halo CE in that while you have multiple objectives you have many different ways of approaching it. Wish to steal a tank? Sure. Satchel charges to blow up a barracks instead of poisoning them? Yup. It's truly impressive. Only problem is that the game can crash when playing these missions, I have not yet experienced crashes nearly as bad on the other modes. Could be a Proton thing as the dialogue is bugged as well but it could just be game bugs. 

Overall I am very impressed. I remember a friend showing me Gates of Hell shortly before it released and that I had dismissed it as a cut down Assault Squad 2, entirely skippable. Time has proven me wrong.

🔥 Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront – The Definitive Real-Time Tactics War Experience

🎖️ Overview
Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront (GoH: Ostfront) is a real-time tactics/strategy game developed by Barbedwire Studios and published by Digitalmindsoft. Released in 2021, it serves as both a spiritual and mechanical successor to the Men of War series, with an intense focus on historical accuracy, immersive tactical gameplay, and gritty realism. While technically a standalone expansion to Call to Arms, GoH distinguishes itself with a deeply atmospheric World War II setting and a commitment to simulating the chaos of frontline combat like few other games.
This is not a casual experience. GoH: Ostfront demands your attention, your tactics, and—most importantly—your respect for the lethality of warfare. It rewards intelligent planning, punishes laziness, and delivers some of the most thrilling combat sequences in modern RTS.

🎮 Gameplay: Tactical Depth and Brutal Realism
At its core, Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a real-time tactics game. You control individual squads or vehicles in battlefield scenarios that demand micro and macro decision-making. Unlike traditional RTS games, there's no base-building. Instead, the emphasis lies squarely on unit placement, line of sight, cover, flanking maneuvers, and resourceful use of limited troops and ammunition.

🔹 Key Features:
Direct Control Mode: As in the Men of War series, GoH allows you to directly take control of any soldier or vehicle—aiming, shooting, driving, and operating turrets manually. This creates a seamless blend of strategy and action.
Tactical Layering: Infantry can dig trenches, flank, use grenades tactically, and make use of terrain in surprisingly intelligent ways.
Line of Sight & Armor Penetration: Tanks and AT guns don’t just fire blindly. Armor values, angles, and shell types determine the outcome of engagements.
Destructible Environments: Cover and buildings can be obliterated by artillery or tank fire, dynamically changing the battlefield mid-battle.
Logistics & Ammunition Management: Vehicles run out of fuel, soldiers run out of ammo. You’ll need to manage resupply logistics or scavenge the battlefield.
The game shines in its representation of combined arms warfare. Infantry, armor, and artillery must work in unison. Sending tanks without recon leads to ambushes; pushing infantry without smoke support leads to slaughter. Every battle feels like a living, evolving organism.

🌍 Campaigns & Missions: Historical Authenticity Meets Variety
GoH: Ostfront offers two primary campaigns: the Soviet and German campaigns, both set on the Eastern Front during WWII. Missions are designed with historical battles in mind, though not always strictly 1:1 recreations.
Each mission can take over an hour to complete, and they’re far from repetitive. One mission might have you holding a crumbling trench line against waves of Soviets with minimal resources. The next might task you with orchestrating a full-on armored assault on a fortified village. There’s even some covert and night missions, adding spice to the usual frontal engagements.
Barbedwire Studios clearly put effort into historical authenticity. The weapons, uniforms, voice acting, and briefings are steeped in period accuracy.

🎨 Graphics & Sound: Atmosphere on the Frontlines
Graphically, Gates of Hell is not photorealistic—but it doesn’t need to be. What it delivers is immersion. The terrain is grimy and lived-in. Explosions send dirt and debris into the air. Smoke lingers after a barrage. Burned-out tanks dot the landscape. The visuals evoke a harsh, unforgiving battlefield.

Notable graphical highlights:
Gore and Destruction: Soldiers react to where they’re hit. Limbs can be lost. Debris flies. This isn’t sanitized war.
Weather & Time of Day: Rain, snow, fog, and night conditions affect visibility and atmosphere.
Animations: Infantry climb fences, dive for cover, drag wounded allies, or switch to pistols when out of ammo.
The sound design is a standout feature:
Gunfire cracks with terrifying realism.
Explosions thunder and echo.
The distinct sounds of each weapon add immersion.
Ambient soundscapes of distant artillery, shouting, and dying men fill the battlefield with dread.
The music, when it plays, is minimalistic and somber—often giving way to the brutal soundscape of combat.

🧠 AI & Realism: Ruthless and Responsive
The AI in GoH: Ostfront is smarter and more responsive than in most RTS games. Enemy soldiers will:
Take cover effectively.
Retreat when overwhelmed.
Use grenades to flush out campers.
Flank and suppress.
Use tanks intelligently and stay at range unless ordered otherwise.
Friendly AI can be a mixed bag, especially when not micromanaged, but their baseline behavior is competent. You can let them fight autonomously, but direct control always leads to better results.
The realism extends to:
Ballistics: Bullets and shells are physically simulated.
Armor modeling: Sloped armor and shell types affect penetration.
Medical system: Wounded soldiers can be revived or left to die if not reached in time.
Vehicles: Crews can be killed or bailed out. Damaged tanks can be repaired.

🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Multiplayer & Skirmish Mode: A Chaotic Playground
GoH supports both co-op and PvP multiplayer, and it’s here the game becomes gloriously unpredictable.
Co-op against AI in dynamic battles is a blast. You and friends can divide responsibilities—one controlling infantry, the other tanks, another artillery. PvP is brutally competitive, requiring quick reflexes and strong tactical instincts.
Skirmish mode allows custom battles with full control over unit composition, map, time of day, and difficulty. It’s a sandbox for experimenting or playing "what if" scenarios.
The modding community has also embraced GoH, further extending its replayability.

[h1] Gates of Hell: Ostfront - Gameplay review [/h1]

Let me just start off by saying that I've never made any major reviews on any game or franchise, this is mostly because I've never really been any good at writing them. But for once I'm going to give a semi detailed review for a game I actually enjoy. I won't be covering the technical sides of the game, only the main aspects of it such as the campaign.

[h1] The campaign: [/h1]

The campaign for GoH is a well structured series of missions taking place on the Ostfront during World War 2 (1941-1945) as Nazi Germany invades the Soviet Union. The game features a well scripted story line to keep you entertained through the very long missions with some stretching as far as 2 hours. With this said, the campaign is also one of the hardest I've experienced to date in any RTS game, and that's not a bad thing at all, GoH prides itself on it's realism compared to other RTS games currently available, with units being extremely fragile. This means you actually have to strategize a lot to maintain the course for the best possible outcome in the missions..

Each faction has a total of 6 missions available to them, with a total of 4 difficulties ranging from Easy, Normal, Hard to Hardcore.

[h1] Skirmishes: [/h1]

Skirmishes in GoH is one of the most entertaining parts of the game in my opinion. If you have played MOWAS2 before, you will definitely enjoy Skirmishes in GoH as it is essentially the exact same concept, you load up a map with a X number of bots or players (if you choose to play online) on a map of your choosing, with there currently being 29 playable maps varying from a winter setting, to a swamp setting. From what I can tell there is currently only one playable mission in skirmish which is Battle zones (Capture and hold positions) with more on their way. Skirmishes comes included when buying the DLC.

[h1] Conquests: [/h1]

Conquests is a unique aspect to this game, it's in a way a combination of Skirmishes and the campaign while offering unique features to the gamemode such as a tech tree that allows you to gradually build up your army by unlocking new units to "conquer" with as you progress through a series of missions. Some missions offer different rewards such as tech points that allows you to develop these new troops. Like the campaign a conquest offers the 4 difficulties previously mentioned to keep the game intense.

[h1] Gem editor: [/h1]

If you are familiar with the men of war series, you have at some point encountered the Gem editor. The Gem editor in GoH is the exact same as offered in the men of war series, but with updated looks and a few new features.


[h1] Review summary: [/h1]

If you are a fan of RobZ's MOWAS2 realism mod, you will most likely enjoy this game for what it is. The 45£ price tag can seem steep, which it is. But if you truly enjoy RTS games and want an RTS game with updated graphics and features, this is the game to get.

But please keep in mind, my review only covers the very basic of each aspect. If you wish to get a more detailed and in-depth explanation, I would suggest looking through more reviews and not basing your decision on just mine. Thank you for reading :)

As of this review, Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront is currently the runner up to the legendary Men of War Assault Squad 2. That being said, it also falls short on delivering some of what its predecessor greatly achieved. 

Fans of the series will quickly notice the same gameplay and controls that made Squad 2 great. Graphics, sound and main interface have also been worked on. Also has Steam Workshop modding support and multiplayer PvP. There's some general issues present with AI but I found it still playable nonetheless.

The big new gameplay feature you'll find this time around is the ability to play in third person perspective. Although we've already experienced "Direct Control" (allows for control of each unit manually) in Squad 2, this new enhancement provides a refreshing experience that Men of War really needed. 

The smaller squad based Commandos-like gameplay with Direct Control in Gates of Hell, is simply amazing. That being said, the lack of larger scaled missions is a total shame because they were the best part of playing a "Men of War: Assault Squad 2-styled" game


My biggest gripe with the game mainly has to do with content. There's just not enough of it. 
For the price, it only includes two factions (Russia and Germany) and is very limited in the amount of single player missions. 

Yeah it comes with a skirmish mode, modding support and PvP but that's just not why most people play Men of War. We play for the handcrafted, storytelling singleplayer missions which this game just doesn't have enough of. In comparison, Men of War: Assault Squad 2 provides substantially more content at full price and during sales, for a mere fraction of the cost!

If you've played MOWAS in any variety, the first part of this review should be redundant, but for people new to the engine, its important to know the basics of your getting into.

Essentially, the game is simulated on a man-by-man basis, with each individual unit possessing a name, class (kinda), and grid style inventory. Thus, every weapon, ammo type, grenade, helmet, fuel tank, etc is all tracked on a very in-depth individual level. When a unit dies, they leave their weapon and a corpse, which can be looted by any other man for any equipment they might have possesed (one of the unique draws of the game). In actual combat, each man can be moved as an individual, team, or squad depending on the amount of units you are managing. More on this later. You also have the ability to directly control any unit at any point, taking control of their movement and aim to devastating effect. GOH uniquely adds a third person mode, which counts for a million coolness points, but is often not super practical.

Along the same lines, cannons and vehicles also have individual crew members operating them. They are tracked identically to infantry, with inventories and classes and names. This affords a lot of depth that many games can't hope to have. In armored warfare, for example, a lethal penetration may kill half the crew, leaving two men to bail. Those two men could be used to supliment crew on another tank, or (more commonly) for suicidal satchel attacks and the like. Low caliber anti-tank munitions also might JUST kill your crew, allowing the tank to be captured and turned against you. Same goes for cannons, which can be decrewed and recrewed by you or your enemy. This, to me, is the major draw of this style of game, and GOH is the most modern example of it. So how does it hold up?

Pretty damn good, but I'll start by addressing a common hang-up.

My major issue with the MOW games has always been the dissonance between infantry emphasis and the reality of WW2. When it comes down to it, infantry are great at a ton of stuff. They are easy to conceal, hard to hit, and can wield extremely devestating (though often close range) weapons. You also have the afformentioned level of depth on the individual infantry unit, which is commonly lost in the large scale destructive combat of the eastern front. To put it blunty: infantry are meatbags that die to everything, but are overwhelmingly neccesary for everything. MOWAS2 got around this by making infantry frustratingly hard to kill, GOH does not. Infantry die to pretty much everything and one inattentive or stupid advance (or stupid stationary position) can easily see a section go night-night. This can be frustrating for some people, which I understand. Meticuluosly kitting out your Riflemen with captured Panzerfausts and MG34s just to see them wiped out by a single 105mm shell is infuriating, but that's World War II, and that's where this game ironically shines.

The game is called Gates of Hell because randomness rules all things. Sometimes your 88mm shell will bounce harmlessly (several times) off a T-34/85, only to have it annihilate the cannon in a single shot. Your flamethrower might ignite themselves or their allies on accident, or get their tank blown by a stray bullet. You own tanks run over your men, your own artillery might fall short, and your left wondering what you did wrong. Get that out of your head. ♥♥♥♥ happens, people die. Welcome to Hell.

If you don't like the idea that your best effort might fall victim to the maelstorm of modern warfare, then the game just aint gonna be for you. If you want your German über Guns to brew commie tanks all day like in Guderian's book, it ain't gonna be for you. If you want your Russian conscript horde to overrun several dug in autocannons with nothing but the power of the Rodina, uhhhh the game might be for you? Watch your spacing I guess, and don't expect a miracle. Either way, the game thrives on a simple brutal randomness that affects your enemy as much as it affects you. It is frustrating when it goes against you, and brilliantly uplifting when it goes for you, but you can't have your cake and eat it. 

If what I just described sounds exactly up your alley, and your willing to put aside a competetive need for victory for a appreciation of the realities of combat, then the game just might be for you. Just get used to the term "unlucky," never overestimate anything, never underestimate anything and go raise some hell. The gates await.

The silence lies thick across the snowy plains, the snowflakes dancing in the wind the only movement to be seen. I'm sitting in my foxhole, eyes fixated on the treeline about a hundred meters away. It's almost too silent. The air in front of me is thick with breath that crystallizes in the cold.

When I look to my right I see a Maxim team that have set up position behind some sandbags. They look about as scared as I'm feeling myself. To my left I can see another rifleman in a newly dug foxhole. I will not look back as my job is to keep looking at that treeline, but I feel reassured in knowing that behind me are more of my comrades enduring the silence together with me.

We have come here through a series of brutal struggles, where at first it seemed like we were advancing, but then found ourselves outgunned and outsmarted by the enemy. Low on supplies and ammunition we must hold this farmhouse so that we can receive more supplies and begin pushing again - but we are all so tired now.

Suddenly I think I see something in the woods. I raise my Mosin to peek through the scope, scanning the treeline. Nothing. Maybe my mind has begun playing tricks on me? The trees are moving in the wind, that must be what I saw. Then there it is again. This time I'm certain I saw something, but it disappeared. My mind has all but forgotten now that my hands are freezing. I look through the scope again, and this time I can clearly see silhouettes of men moving between the trees. They are here.

Somewhere behind me I can hear someone shouting, and then the sound of a Mosin firing. I cannot shoot as I don't have a clear line of sight. The Maxim to my right is also awaiting the right moment. The shadows in the wood are now firing back at us - I can hear the echoes of their rifles and the bullets ricocheting near me. Finally I manage to get one of the shadows in my scope, and fire two shots. The shadow drops.

I can now hear machine gun fire in the distance, and something heavier, repeating, as well but I cannot identify the sound - our comrades at objective two have also connected with the enemy it seems.  Behind me I can hear the turret of our T-34 tank move slowly, then stop. As I raise my Mosin to fire another shot, the tank unleashes its deadly package, and just below the treeline the ground erupts in an explosion of snow, dirt and blood. The tank fires again and then opens up with the machine gun, three short bursts.

After what felt like an eternity, but more objectively probably closer to a minute or two, the shooting dies down slowly. I can still hear the heavy repeating sound from objective two - what on earth is that? - but then I hear a  loud impact and I can suddenly see fire and smoke rise from behind the trees. The silence settles in again as we check our ammunition stores. Now we wait. Again.

I've always enjoyed games like these, as far back as "Soldiers: Heroes on WWII", "Faces of War" up to "Men of War" series so of course I gave this a try and here is my thoughts.

So lets get to the elephant in the room with this game, and that is the "AI" which I barely would consider an artificial intelligece.
I lost track on how often I have to micomanage my units and repeat orders to get them to do what I want. 
We shall not speak of the high number of vehicle losses I've had when the pathfinding of each vehicle interrupts the other, leading to vehicles either to stop, make a strange turn, starts to reverse towards the enemy, run over a smaller vehicle or equipment (mortar, mg etc...), or flat out collide with each other which leads to either the vehicles flip over or detonates (if it's a truck vs tank), this is due that ALL vehicles prioritize moving on roads and having them move in a column is impossible as no vehicle can be near each other on the move as they can't decide who has priority and if the lead get stuck or slow down the others mission is to pass as fast as possible.

I have also lost track on how often the pathfinding of vehicles have lead to the vehicle in question gets stuck in map features such as trees, rocks, debries or trenches, and that is OUTSIDE of spawning in these features sometimes when you call your equipment into the map!
We shall not even speak of the friendly fire situation, make sure that the enemy won't flank you cause ALL will aim and shoot no matter what is in the way.

Before we had the issue that vehicles prioritized infantry, despite enemy tanks where shooting at them but it have been seeing a minor fix where you can lock vehicles from changing ammo, meaning you only run AP ammo in your tanks. But for me the core problems with the "AI" is still present and fixes like this won't resolve it at all.

Another part is the capture point placing, as a defensive gamer in strategy I've come to LOVE some of the trench systems and defensive possibilities the maps can provide, but the capture points will be placed so you can't utilize these position, making them just eye candy for most of the maps, and some of these points makes no sense with the placements. 
In other games the capture points are placed in a way that makes it a logical point to take, here there have been instances of "there's a flag in the middle of the field"...

Campaign is a good introduction to the game but the ones I did is mostly defend missions, as stated a defensive gamer it was okay, it is however overwhelming when you have a line as big as the maps to manage and with the AI you can't leave you gaze on any sector which makes it stressfull given the level of micromanaging. 

Conquest on the other hand have been where I mostly play and it have been enjoyable, you start with basic things and research your way to better equipment, having to manage economy and research points in between battles and supplies (medical, ammo and fuel) in the field.
There is a learning curve but it doesn't take too long to get into the functions and one there it is a blast.
Though you must look into what you should research to have the upper hand over the enemy AI so you won't be overwhelmed by something you can't take out.

The workshop contains a plethora of mods that enhances the game with functions and some even a new game within, the top for me atm is "Hotmod 1968" and for me this is a huge plus.

Overall, it is a 50/50 split for me. I bought it because I like these types of games and I've ploughed through the AI and bugs that are haunting the game. 
It is sad that we are here as this game have so much potential and needs more tweaking, though the devs appears to focus on DLC's now instead which leads to the final verdics of "Not recommended" and are you considering this game get it at a sale, it is not worth its current pricetag in this state.

After the Liberation DLC:

Most of what I said before still stands sadly as I haven't seen any noticable changes. 
On these new maps for the Liberation DLC however, things have gone worse on the capture point placement. 
Some points on a few maps are placed almost directly next to where the enemy spawns and on other the far side of the map which makes it difficult to capture them when reinforcements almost spawn on top of you and to get there on time to be able to make defensive positions when on the defense. 
I've come to use a workshop mod that allows you to have more "prep time" when defending due to this. 
Sure there are new toys to play with and that is a plus but maps also makes a huge difference on wether you will enjoy the game or not and this DLC have few maps I actually like.

There is also a running isse with tanks not wanting to drive over trees, sure a forrest I understand, but a single tree that happens to be in the way. No lets drive around it and that have made some issues when tryin to be offensive and bring a shock and awe attack to the enemy. 
Many times I've forced to stop the advance because one or two vehicles must make a complicated maneuver around a single tree in their path, sometimes ending up reversing towards the enemy at that (remember, tanks are front towards enemy type of asset). 

So do I stand on a 50/50 split still? 
Given how little I've seen on the AI part I am more leaning on the more negative side now. 
I've found myself playing this game less and less as these issues still persists. 

Do I recommend the game even at a sale?
I honestly can't even do that now which saddens me, I wan't this game to get better but I feel based on the update news that there is only cosmetic changes coming and DLC rather then doing something about the issues with the AI, aside making the enemy AI more versatile/challenging to fight and that from what I've seen is leading it to just spamming more artillery instead.

Call to Arms: Gates of Hell - Ostfront is an exceptional WWII RTS that nails both the tactical depth and the gritty atmosphere of the Eastern Front (and the Western Front if you have the DLC!). The attention to detail is impressive, from realistic sound design to beautifully rendered battlefields.

The gameplay is a perfect mix of strategy and hands-on control. You can command individual units like infantry or tanks, and the decisions you make feel meaningful. The missions are challenging and rewarding,

Multiplayer is smooth and competitive, offering great replayability. Each faction has its own strengths and weaknesses, adding variety to how you approach battles.

If you're into tactical RTS games, this is a must-play. It delivers a great combination of realism, strategy, and fun.

One major downside is the AI, which can be pretty frustrating at times. Units often fail to follow orders properly, get stuck, or make questionable decisions, which can break the flow of the game and lead to unnecessary micromanagement. It’s definitely an area that could use improvement.

That said, the game is still a fantastic experience overall. Highly recommend it!

While not a full successor to something like Men of War: Assault Squad 2, Gates of Hell: Ostfront improves upon many mechanics from that game, even with less actual content. If you liked Men of War and you see this one sale, it's definitely worth getting as it's an amazing piece of work, and hopefully with more updates or installments, there'll be plenty more to come.

Played the closed alpha and beta version of the game and have played it since its early days.  Gates Of Hell has been around long enough and has added enough content to call it a full game on its own if not similar to the offering of the base game of ( MoW)Men Of War which is most likely what the community will compare this game to.  GOH has vast improvements over MoW in both unit control, visuals, audio, and most importantly performance (as MOW is limited to 32 bit engine).

The game does a good job of setting itself apart with more attention to detail than MoW with a greater focus on  historical accuracy and authenticity that take center stage in its campaign in recreating authentic battlefields and maps true to the airal photography.  Its balancing, and even the 1st person gun sights for cannons are also examples of this authenticity with gun sights being pulled from historical documentation and references. Balancing obviously utilizes units and gear not often seen in other games but plays well as pacing in its online and skirmish battles scale as your game goes on.

Unit control has been improved a great deal  such as path finding for vehicles being able to progress through tree lines,  click and drag for infantry cover, and easy to use hotkeys for infantry controls such has tapping "ctrl" to have inf units lay down while selected, its never been easier to control your squads.  Tanks will sometimes have issues deciding if they want to back up or attempt a crossing of fox holes or ditches, this could be down to map design or the unit avoiding getting stuck, its still better than MOWs. 

Music is better than MOW but still can feel a little out of place and doesn't hit nearly as well as Company Of Heroes 2 which also presents the eastern front, granted the pacing and scales of both games are different but still it'd be nice to have some better tracks.  Audio outside of its music is well done, ambient birds, wind, tree cracks, and bugs fill the scene as distant explosions and cracks go off.  Going back to the "attention to detail" the audio team or lead has done a good job of adding the sound of tank treads to even things like wooden bridge crossings having different audio than stone/cobble. Gun sounds are punchy and have more "clank" than "bang" for small arms and large booms for larger guns (as it should be), and voice lines for unit are authentic and driven by the faction you are playing.

 
Overall I think this game has more to offer up front and is an overall better product that I'm sure over time will only get better as they add in more maps, factions, and units. As its stands this game has a solid footing and is worth checking out.

Looks Good at First; But Full of Problems

At first, Gates of Hell looks like an excellent RTS experience, with impressive visuals and a wealth of content. But after spending more time with it, serious issues begin to surface — and the real disappointment is how little progress has been made despite years of development and strong community support.

Basic Unit Control Still Feels Broken
One of the core problems lies in the game's command system. Units often fail to follow even the simplest orders, making competitive matches incredibly frustrating. For a real-time tactics game, that’s simply unacceptable.

No Dedicated Servers — Seriously?
It’s hard to believe, but Gates of Hell still lacks dedicated servers. For a game with such potential and a growing player base over recent years, this is a major letdown. Even more baffling: there’s no ranked leaderboard. How is that still missing?

Developers Who Don't Seem to Listen
The development team appears more interested in flashy graphics, immersive sound design, and flooding the game with content than in addressing core gameplay issues. Long-time players — the ones who helped build the game’s community — often feel ignored or even disrespected.

[h1] Critical Game Review: Realism vs. Expectations [/h1]

For those who like to read a few reviews before purchasing a game, here's my perspective on this controversial title. Some might be surprised by my findings.

[h2] Looking for Realism? [/h2] 

If you're seeking true realism, I recommend the Combat Mission series. Unfortunately, you won't find it in this game. I've spent many hours with this "parody of realism" that I would rather have dedicated to other titles. If newer, less experienced players didn't have such an aversion to games with older graphics (like the CM series [url=Combat Mission series] https://store.steampowered.com/app/1502380/Combat_Mission_Black_Sea/ [/url] ), I would certainly have invested my time there.

[h2] Brief Summary [/h2] 

Realism: The game isn't as realistic as it might appear. Yes, the uniforms are processed in great detail, but that's just surface-level polish.
Technical Implementation: The absence of dedicated servers means that even the most powerful hardware won't guarantee a smooth experience. Connections often feel like playing from a distant planet.
Expert Background: The game isn't backed by renowned experts who could ensure authentic realism. While the American DLC received support from U.S. consultants, other nations didn't get such attention.
Price vs. Value: For over €70 (including all DLCs), you essentially get an improved version of the ROBZ 2.0 mod in 64-bit, with fewer nations. At least the game doesn't crash most of the time.

[h2] Final Note [/h2] 

It's interesting to compare the developers' promises with reality. They stated: "We want CtA - Gates of Hell to be as realistic as possible... The magic word is 'history'." They claimed to avoid artificially enhancing or weakening units. However, the reality is different - everything they supposedly wanted to avoid [b]they ended up doing it.... [/b]

In conclusion, I ask: Which Russian testers determine the "correct realism" in this game? Is it truly historical accuracy, or just another marketing ploy?

I've played lots of WW2 RTS/Strategy games, from the OG Close Combat series, up to MoW2: Assault Squad.

I was disappointed with Call to Arms-- like, really disappointed. The engine and some of the mechanics were improved a lot from MoW, but the gameplay was just too ridiculously "fast" -- that is, battles weren't anything more than spider webs of tracer fire and repeated explosions. Add to that the friendly AI (unit AI) being stupid af.

So, I had my fingers crossed when I got CtA: GoH: Ostfront. In short, this is *awesome*.

Okay, so it still has a LOT of the problems that MoW2:AS had, as far as units doing what they're supposed to, and pathing sometimes, and a lack of a playable pause (freeze, give orders, unfreeze)-- the best you can do is the lowest speed setting (1-5, 3 is default) but only on certain game modes. However, it is as detailed as the MoW games have ever been, but with a lot of optimizations (probably coming from the CtA added features).

This isn't a rollback, either-- it seems as though all of the German/Russian units from the MoW games are brought forward, with vehicles having detailed damage models, and numerous visual variations within one specific unit type (outside equipment attached, extra panels and gear, graffiti, numbers, etc.).

The play feels about the same as AS2, but smoother, deeper, and a little less frustrating most of the time. I've played through the German tutorial, and spent a lot of extra time on those maps to play with things and see how they work, and I've played through a few of the Russian SP missions. I'd say the missions, so far, are well-designed, though have some soft-lock problems, like I saved a tutorial missions after I had completed the objectives. When I came back later, I got the pre-roll video/VO for the mission, and it set up the first objective again, however, the rest of the map, including my units, were still in their prior state, so it was kind of odd. Also, if you complete a mission, and then start the next mission and quit, when you come back, if you do Continue Game, it will go to the last Autosave, which is usually in the map you already finished. There's little stuff like that.

This most reminds me of WW2 models I built as a kid-- not just the vehicles, but the soldiers, too-- like they've come to life.

Big downside: if you haven't played an MoW game before, there is a BIG learning curve. The tutorial doesn't explain many of the things on the interface that become important to know. I could see that making a frustrating experience for a first-time player.

Still, a ton of fun-- glitches, but the rest of it makes them forgivable.

Updating to add: some unit behavior is infuriating, and there are definite wayfinding issues with some of the SP missions (e.g., "Now how do I find this Oberfuhrer now that everyone is dead?" or "Which side of the map is the extraction point?" Still, I'm however many hours in and it's fun as hell-- even if aggravating. It does feel like an MoW game with a lot of polish.

Let me break it down for all those kids that keep crying about this game with negative reviews. First of all this game is not a basic strategy where you click and things happen. This game requires thinking(Which a lot of people nowadays dont have). Thats probably where negative reviews coming from. And also lack of understanding on how complicated this game is. This game is realistic battlefield simulator with pretty much all aspects of physics. Meaning you dont just click and wait. You need to use environment for your advantage. Same as you would in real life. Physical objects can be used to sneak, hide, be out of line of sight. Tank positioned on hills can prevent your turret to hitting an enemy. You can take 10 stupid shots and never damage an enemy tank. You can land 1 strategically placed shot and take out heaviest enemy tank. This is more like a chess. Yes units do their part but micromanaging is necessary. Each unit can do so much if used properly. Ive played plenty of games and this one is truly incredible in my opinion. Yes theres things that need to be fixed but it will never overweight the positive and fun side of it. A lot of time people complain about in game online PvP issues in terms of connection, lag. Here are some tips.
 - When you create a server and waiting for people to join its is best to start fresh. Meaning you need to restart the game before each game, which takes less than 30 seconds. Whether you join another server after playing a game or someone is joining you - Restart. Restart between ALL games/creating games/ will get rid of any lag as long as you PC and internet is stable. The more games you play the buggy your game gets. Restart gives it a fresh start. It feels like game stores files which after clearing makes it smooth. 
- When game is loaded its better to use right click on mini map to run through all the map(Takes 5 Seconds). This will load map and will not make you that laggy player. It pretty much synchronizes  possible outcomes. Also when timer is ticking during start up go through all units lists. And do that when game starts(Takes 3 seconds). 

If your computer is not good or connection please don't ruin it for everyone else. If you planning on playing for 5-10 min please dont even bother starting. This isnt a quick game. 


If you follow those steps and have people in your server that are stable in terms of PC and Connections you can have beyond explainable fun games. I never have bad experience unless someone quits. Which makes you re-host the game and its a time waste on other players. But in this community people get banned or kicked due to their prior selfish behavior. Because nobody wants to waste their time.

This is a bug filled, poorly optimized, and disappointing beta being put together by a rag tag group of developers. To keep this review short and to the point, here are some the major issues currently afflicting this game:

- AI is painfully bad even on heroic difficulty, enemy soldiers will run right up to you/past you without even firing their weapons
- AI utilizes tanks and equipment very poorly 
- Troops will become frozen and unable to move frequently when crewing vehicles and equipment
- The inventory system is bugged when used frequently and results in item duplication and bugged inventories
- Troop movement and unit pathing is a mess. Moving troops out of cover only moves one man of the squad while the rest don't move at all, and troop spread is now laughably too large for map sizes which causes movement difficulty
- You currently cant lose battles in Conquest (A core game mode) because the devs had to remove taking losses because their game was crashing too often
- Multiplayer is laggy, and desync ridden. The game's net code is horrible. 
- The fire at ground command is not functional with artillery, mortars, etc.
- Damage and penetration model sometimes makes little sense

This game is a buggy beta at best, and a complete disappointment from MOW:AS2. But this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ product really shouldn't come as a surprise, as the dev team is quite literally made up of "closet salesmen, gas fitters, mechanics, and retired pornstars". Don't waste your money on this game...

This is an update to my original review. More than a year has passed, and my original assessment of the single-player experience still holds true. However, I must warn potential buyers that the multiplayer aspect of the game is currently a mess, with unresolved issues such as crashes, out-of-sync matches, rubber-banding, and unresponsive controls due to poor netcode, performance, or lag.

Despite these issues,I still recommend the game for its single-player and co-op experiences. The single-player campaign, which features 10 missions, is reminiscent of old-school games like Faces of War or Men of War. The campaign is a micro-intensive game that requires patience, and it will not hold your hand to complete missions.

Additionally, Gates of Hell is an excellent addition to the original Men of War game from 2009, both in terms of single-player and multiplayer. It stands on its own without needing mods, unlike Assault Squad 2.

In terms of multiplayer, there are currently only two factions (Germany and Russia) and three game modes: single-player co-op, dynamic campaign co-op, and an equivalent to Battle Zone with objectives to capture. While two factions may not seem like much, the inclusion of doctrines and early and mid-war set-ups cater to different playstyles of players.

However, the multiplayer is still buggy, especially for those familiar with the multiplayer of Call to Arms. The developers seem to be working on bringing a stable and optimized experience, but only time will tell if they are successful.

Overall,I highly recommend this DLC, especially for those who already own Call to Arms. While it has its limitations in terms of AI and pathfinding, it offers a lot in terms of gameplay and editing options. It would be beneficial if there was a demo available for players to see if this DLC is for them, especially in comparison to other games like Steel Division or Company of Heroes, which are good in their own right but should not be compared to this one.

FYI: This game is pretty buggy. Although I have not encountered any game breaking bugs, you should expect to encounter some visual bugs and minor annoyances. From what I've read you can report bugs at the owner hub. This should really be made more clear though. The reason I'm giving this game a recommended is because when it works, (which it usually does) it's amazing.

     GAMEPLAY: When it's at it's best, this game feels like a movie. The new third person mode is great, although I mainly only use it for infantry. Conquest us honestly the best mode in the game, hands down. Although the number of in game factions has been reduced to two, these factions are in significantly more detail (I mean, had you heard of the ampulomet before you played this game?). Overall, a major step up.

     VISUALS AND SOUND: Overall, the visuals are a major step up. Explosions are no longer just a massive fireball, and the game is much less colourful On the other hand, I would like to see more cook-off effects for tanks as well as more particles when the environment is destroyed. Sound, however, is more of a mixed bag. The voice acting is a far cry from the generic "Za Rodinu!" of vanilla AS2 as well as them crispy low quality band of brothers voice lines RobZ Realism had. Combat noises, on the other hand, don't sound as good. The best way I could describe it is that it sounds afraid of hurting your feelings  bullet impacts feel like spitballs and tank combat feels wimpy as well. High caliber rounds pinging off thick sheets of metal shouldn't sound like crumpling aluminum. Explosion noises need some work as well. The current ones work for small explosions from frags and mortar shells, but bigger things like artillery need to be louder and have more noise of dirt scattering.

     CAMPAIGN: It's passable. There isn't really a story, instead you mainly just play through interesting battles of the war. Good if you've got an hour to waste.

     PRICE: People seem to be upset over this and I don't really see why. To illustrate my point, let's compare this to Assault Squad 2
GOH is 45 bucks. It would have been cheaper, but for legal reasons this game had to become dlc. AS2 Is 30 dollars. However GOH comes with AI bots in the base game, something AS2 charged you 10 dollars extra for. Because of this it's really 45 bucks for GOH vs. 40 bucks for AS2.
For five extra dollars you get a new campaign, conquest, and third person mode. In my opinion that's worth it.

     THE FUTURE:I'm Going to list of some things I'd like to see improved in the future

1. Grenades: Grenades could use a serious buff as they feel more like the snapping fireworks your parents gave you to throw on the ground for the 4th of July than frags. The devs said the reason they nerfed grenades is because people used to spam them in AS2. However, after going back and playing vanilla AS2 I think the issue was not  grenades being too powerful as it was guns not being powerful enough. I'd like to see grenades buffed to more realistic values

2. Commander Hatches: In game, some tanks, like the Tiger, have the ability to open/close the commander hatch. I would like to see this become a uniform thing for all tanks with hatches, improving their vision

3. AI: In some ways the AI has improved but in others it feels like it regressed. For one thing, AI will now buy snipers and flamethrowers, something I don't recall it doing in AS2 without mods. On the other hand, it has pathfinding issues sometimes choosing to take the stupidest paths and running over friendly units. If the AI was smarter this game would be a masterpiece.

4. BUGS: This one's kind of a given but hopefully in the future there'll be less bugs.

5. EDITOR: Due to legal reasons, the devs couldn't port over most of the old MOW assets. Because they had to start from scratch the editor feels kinda empty. I'd like to see them add more assets

6. MAPS: I'd like to see more MP maps, in particular urban ones.

7. MORE UNITS: I mean, duh.

8. MORE FACTIONS: I'm not sure about the direction the devs are gonna take with this one. Whether they are gonna add the classic MOW five, go down the Steel Division 2 route of adding minor nations like Finland and Hungary, or have more exotic dlc locations like the Spanish civil war. Regardless I'm excited.

I recently watched some Youtube videos on how to play this game, and was intrigued enough to try it again. While the included tutorial is completely worthless, there are now in depth guides on Youtube that I would recommend to anyone trying to learn this game.

It is fun, and the level of detail is astounding. The sound effects and visuals really do a great job of heightening the tension and urgency of play.

It does have a couple of problems. You do have to micromanage a bit to get the best performance out of your soldiers, and the enemy ai is not great. They've offset this by making sure you're outnumbered, which is a little strange from a historical perspective when playing the Russians.

There are not a lot of pre-scripted scenarios (I think its 6 per side) included, which brings the weaknesses of the campaign mode to the fore.  The campaign mode is cleverly done, whereas you unlock later war units over time with points earned during battle, making it feel as though the war is progressing while you play. *But* there is no option to just jump into a later war scenario and start running later war units like Tigers and Panthers around. Trying to recreate any engagement with heavy Russian tanks in the early part of the war is impossible in campaign mode, as it takes scads of points to unlock them. It's a bit disappointing.

All that said, the game is well worth the price of admission, and has a lot to offer (assuming you don't rely on the tutorial to learn how to play). I'm changing my review to positive, and am currently considering purchasing some of the DLC.

[b]Disclaimer: haven't played the singleplayer so this will just be about the multiplayer[/b], which I surmise a significant amount of potential players will only care about. I've also played a ♥♥♥♥ ton of Men of War: Assault Squad 2 so I'll compare the two directly since Gates is like its unofficial sequel. Which you'd think would be favorable to this game considering MOW:AS2 came out many years ago, but sadly it is not. 

I do believe the developers can make Gates of Hell a better game, but it's been a year from release and it is simply STILL not worth it to get the game in its current state if all you're looking to do is play multiplayer. The same problems that plagued MOW:AS2 are still present, namely the netcode (in fact in some respects it's gotten worse).

- They definitely either lie about the ping of public lobbies or have f*cked it up so much. You'll see most lobbies with pings of ~50 ms, but 1 second of actual gameplay will tell you instantly that this is not true. Some games even with "25 ms" feel like 1000 ms would in other games. And your obvious response if you're not familiar with MOW is probably "just join lobbies that have low ping!!!" but you should know that the community isn't large enough to be this picky about lobbies. Sometimes the only options for a game is the one that in actuality has 500 ms ping. 

- As a result of the poor netcode, the game constantly runs in this stupid ass fast-motion slow-motion time skip. Gameplay will lag and slow down for a few seconds, then speed up a ton as it's trying to catch up, then slow down again, then by the time it finishes speeding up again your units have already rushed into enemy fire and died before you can do anything about it. It seems like the developers were trying to figure out a way to make the gameplay smoother than in MOW:AS2 when there's high ping. In MOW:AS2, the game's FPS would just drop when there's high ping. That is IMO preferable because at least the lag was predictable and consistent. Now it's just unmanageable. 

Another example of shoddy implementation being the air-strike call-in that some factions have. You can call in a plane that will drop a bomb on where you selected. The only thing is, as the plane flies over the target, the bomb magically appears right below the plane, and falls in a perfectly straight vertical line down to the ground. No forward momentum, no nothing. It's like some freshman game development major with no understanding of physics implemented it. Great job, developers. It's really humorous to see other players say "tHis Is tHe m0sT ImMerS1ve wW2 coMbAt sImUlAtoR" when sh*t like this happens. 

- There is simply not enough content right now. A few more maps and [strike]2[/strike] 3 factions (yes I know each nation has different doctrines but they're really pretty similar)? I know they have plans to add more later, but in that case just wait, cause you're gonna end up doing that after you get bored in 3 days anyways. After release I got bored playing this after only a few hours cause the games were just the same over and over again (the new maps update renewed some more interest, we'll see how long that lasts) But if you're looking for variety, just get MOW:AS2. There's so many mods for singleplayer and multiplayer that you'll probably have thousands of hours worth of content just in that game alone. 

- Even after the update, a lot of the maps are not original content. Some of them are reworked vanilla maps from MOW:AS2, and a lot are old maps from MOW:AS2 mods like #valour and RobZ realism. So if you played those then a lot of maps aren't gonna feel fresh.

- [strike]There are fewer players than in MOW:AS2, which is honestly the sad part because of how small the MOW community is to begin with.[/strike] The player count has actually improved and at times it's more popular and easier to get into a game then MOW:AS2

All in all, even a year after release, I wouldn't get this game full price (maybe on sale) if you're a new MOW player, or even an old one. [b]If you're new to the MOW games I'd wait until MOW:II comes out and compare the two to see which is more worthwhile. If you're an old MOW player, just keep playing MOW:AS2 with Robz Realism.[/b] It does everything this does and better. More factions, more units, more maps, [strike] more players [/strike] about the same players, better performance (how???? just how???). Sure the one thing they fixed in this game from MOW:AS2 Robz is the crashing but vanilla MOW:AS2 doesn't even crash either. And the crashing in Robz isn't really a big deal either as long as your PC isn't an absolute potato.
