[h1] Somewhat flawed, but still good [/h1]

[u]Pros:[/u]

* Graphics look pretty good and fitting, despite simple style. If anything, palette's a bit too brownish.
* Sounds and music are nice. 
* Basebuilding/filler part is a nice breather between long-ish missions. Campfire stories give characters some much-needed personality, too.
* Missions are tight, yet challenging. Not overly long like with other games in this genre.
* I do like the setting and even story. Russian villagers, partisans and their struggle against nazis and collaborationists is a welcome fresh breeze in game industry.
* A possiblity to sometimes solve a problem with guns reduces fatigue and boredom such games usually cause.
* Not too many nasty mission objectives with timer or curveballs. Hate when games do this; you think you've won, and now defend against a tank or something. Few tricker missions exist, but it's not too bad. 
* Pacing feels about right

[u]Cons:[/u]

* Characters sound too much like politruks giving speech. While it's probably accurate due setting, still reads too much like a marxist propaganda novel. I'd rather see Morozov get drunk and into fight or something, for a change. I don't think anyone's proper and moral communist after having just cut throats of 30+ enemy soldiers.
* If you're doing English voiceover for a slav-setting game, don't employ [i]actual Englishmen[/i]. The  brit accent sounds totally out of place. 
* UI is absolute garbage, especially anything related to inventory management. Even simplest of things, like hover-tooltips or "replace inventory item with that's on the dead soldier" or auto-stacking ammo and tools doesn't exist. It's needlessly annoying and stupid.
Entire inventory system does what I hate most about games; [u]it wastes my time[/u]. It's not a challenge, not a puzzle, not important to the plot or setting, not anything interesting. Just a stupid, complex chore that this game doesn't need. Why do I have to spend tens of minutes managing broken gun parts and tobacco leaves in inventories? Why can't game just say "you picked up some useful stuff, laid it aside and took it back to camp after the mission". I don't need to actually carry all this trash around, is this a homeless simulator or what?
* Commandos-style games have usually a kill loop for every character. Throw cigarettes, wait, throw knife. Lay trap, play flute, wait. And so forth. 
But it doesn't seem to exist here [u]at all[/u] until you hire Morozov. You can't [b]throw[/b] bottles for some weird reason, and bottles disappear if enemy gets to them, you have to manually count and collect rocks, this is all so needlessly complicated and useless, why do this? Morozov is only character with (almost) reliable kill loop, so you'll be using him until the end of the game. In other words, characters could use more variety and actual design. At least Sanek can kill knocked-out guards. If that also didn't exist, I'd be quite bad.
* Most characters feel pointless. I tried, but couldn't find their quirks (a medic/sniper, a fast runner/acrobat, an... old man? etc) very fun (or useful). It was all Sanek and Morozov due their reliable, practical skills. 
* Gunplay feels badly implemented. I mean, there's gun skills and tons of guns, but using guns is so punishing  and random that it feels pointless. Almost like this game doesn't know what it wants to be. That said, stealth part is really good so I'm not sure if it's really a problem. I just don't use guns, unless game really forces me to (that dreaded village defense mission).

Feels like there's more problems than good, but the good outweighs the bad. This genre needs more games like this and Partisans 1941 can stand proudly next to classics and modern takes of the genre. Totally worth the money.

At first I drew attention to this game not because of the gameplay, but because it told the story about german invasion in an unusual way (unusual for modern movies, games and books in Russia and western world as well). The Nazis are shown as Nazis: thea are shooting women, children and prisoners, taking hostages, burning and plundering villages. They are not shown as reflective cultural "europeans" who are sometimes forced to do terrible things (as in modern Russian films). Collaborators are shown as scum and opportunists who take advantage of the occupation for personal gain. And Soviet partisans are shown as heroes who have no questions about their duty to fight for their motherland (again, not like in modern Russian films). Some of the heroes are directly communists or Komsomol-member, and this fact is not hushed up or shyly avoided (again, not like... ). Essentially they are fighting for Soviet power and for the legacy of the October Revolution (while in modern films the heroes fight at best for "Russia", but more often "for themselves" or "for the girl").
Such a straightforward look is inherent in old Soviet books and films about the war, in each letter of which there is more truth than in all modern rubbish.
Born in the Voronezh region, as a child, I listened to stories about the occupation, about how the Wehrmacht soldiers put children on their armored vehicles so that the partisans would not fire at it, and arranged mass executions for every successful partisan action. In these stories of my great-grandfathers, old soldiers and old partisans, there was also no reflection about why they fought: they fought for Soviet power against the Nazis, period.
Therefore, I bought this game without paying attention to the quality. To my surprise, the quality is quite decent. 

In terms of gameplay, this is a retro game "Commando look alike". Missions take place on fairly large maps with dozens of enemies, and as a rule, you need to kill most of them or all of them with a group of 3-4 partisans. As with all such games, most of the time you bypass the "cones of view", hide in the bushes and throw knives. Most maps can be passed stealthily (through the bushes with a knife) or loudly (with shooting and explosions). Some characters are more suitable for a stealthy style of play, and some for a more straightforward style. As usual in such games, the player gets used to one favorite technique: for me it was the main protagonist's throwing knife, which accounted for two thirds of frags.

The difference between this game and other "commandos" clones in two things. Firstly, this is the base management, but it is essentially purely cosmetic. The second is the loot, inventory and weapon system. Which makes the game more similar to the "Men of War" series: each partisan can take any weapon in his hands, ammo and grenades can run out and they must be counted. The combat system is again similar to "Men of War" and is based on covers. Clashes are usually fleeting and brutal, partisans die quickly enough under the crossfire or in open areas. Therefore, to win, you first have to crawl through the bushes with knives thoroughly in order to reduce the number of enemies.

I have not encountered a single bug during the game, perhaps because I played it six months after the release. Control, camera are familiar to fans of "commandos" clones. 
The only drawback of the game is that it is relatively short and released DLС does not fix the matter.

If you liked Commandos back in the day, or you like stealthy turn-based tactical games, then Partisans 1941 is enjoyable enough. And a little addictive. (It's not turn-based but these games still kinda play like ones in a way.) I never quite liked Shadow Tactics. That game never brought back fond gaming memories in the same way Partisans does. 

Much like in Commandos, you lead a small, isometric team against the Nazis, only this time it's partisans on the Eastern front rather than a ragtag crew of commandos on the Western front. Very much in-character too, if we put it that way. It's all WWII Eastern rethorics and ethos this time, a novel experience for a Western gamer.

Clearly a hommage to Commandos, Partisans 1941 include sneaking around enemy 'cones of vision' since taking on too many enemies in a firefight is a very bad idea, much as it was back then (I'm not only referring to Commandos). But then the devs also threw a mini resource management game and RPG elements on top. It doesn't add all that much to the game experience, but it's a little extra on top of a game idea that is over 20 years old by now. But still works just fine.

I read some complaints in other reviews here about the interface being clunky. It's not too bad really. Besides, it's NOTHING against how Commandos was. Commandos was sort of retro already back when it was released and, boy, was it clunky! But that never mattered. It was fun anyway. Here, due to significantly larger maps and more complexity, the game becomes more unpredictable. You end up quicksaving your way through basically every move you do, at least if you go the full stealth route for the achievements, but as opposed to Commandos you never really save yourself into a corner since there are three quicksave slots (plus you can do hard saves as well). You try something, screw up, reload, try something else, screw up, reload, try a third approach, phew, it worked, better save immediately! That's how it plays. Playing through a map takes a little time and that seems to be the intention.

The one thing Partisans lack compared to Commandos is that humorous charm that made the latter game so irresistible even during its most frustrating moments. It was like one of those old WWII movies back when wars were still portrayed like an adventure on the silver screen. But with Partisans it's like it can't quite make up its mind whether it's a dead serious game or not. It's sort of strung up in between Commandos, on the one hand, and on the other hand a movie like Come and See, portraying the real horrors of the Eastern front from the civilian perspective.

As someone who has played a few games of this genre (XCOM 2 👎, Phantom Doctrine 👍), I went into this expecting it to be turned based just like both of them, but this game doesn't play the same as those two mentioned above. Is that a good thing? I certainly think so.

There are no "turns" in this game like the normal top down, no overwatch, no room breach etc. it's all done in real time with the ability to slow down time and sync up your Partisans to do actions at the same time (given that both of them are in range). While that can be fun most of the time, because of the way spotting works on some of the higher leveled enemies, it can be super frustrating to try and get into a bush and be hidden, but still almost instantly get spotted because where you pathed or where you clicked "technically" isn't part of the bush hitbox.

The movement feels a little bit weird, sometimes (like stated above) I would click on a bush and still be standing outside of it until I turned my camera around and clicked the same spot. Sometimes you'll click something and the way your character walks to it they'll get stuck, and sometimes they'll start walking and then stop in the middle of getting there like you canceled the action all together.

Combat feels rewarding and difficult (I played on the middle "medium" setting), doing missions in stealth is fun because of how each character has their own unique ability, or getting into cover and syncing your Partisans to shoot at different targets and letting it go is satisfying to watch.

I wasn't a big fan of the inventory management in this game, in-camp or out, each time you move an item the game gets stuck for a few seconds like it's saving, and then it starts again and plays the sound a few seconds later making moving things in and out of your units to other units sometimes take awhile.

My biggest gripe however was how the way the interacting works with the environment, [spoiler]Zorin can use his throwing knife to instantly kill someone from range[/spoiler], but then you have to go and pick it back up to be able to use it again, which makes it super clunky in the fact that you can click the button and it won't give it back to you unless you move the camera around, and even still it will sometimes require you to move the camera to a sweet spot just to be able to pick up dead bodies, this caused me to be seen quite a bit because I couldn't pick up the bodies in time and would be spotted.
The best fix for this would be to make UI scale work on the orange buttons. I was so upset when I maxed out UI scale and it didn't fix my problems.

I did like the characters and how they each had their own corresponding abilities, however I didn't get a lot of use out of a few characters [spoiler]like Trofim and Sanek later on[/spoiler].

The story was okay, another world war 2 game but this time seen from the Russian side instead of the American side which was something different and nice.

All in all I would recommend this game to people who like these types of games and are willing to work with the bugs, however in its current state I would tell you to wait until it's on sale again.

I put this game down in frustration when it first came out because I was struggling to come to grips with its mechanics, which are more punishing than I am typically used to in games that emphasize stealth. But I picked it up again to give it another try, and it's grown on me much more now. 

I wasn't a huge fan of the missions where you instant lose when you get spotted, but the game does have a generous quicksave system. I initially didn't like this because it felt like I was being encouraged to do extreme save-scumming through every mission (since they tend to be quite involved and it would be a pain to restart), but I've now grown to appreciate it as a tool for you to set your own checkpoints. It only breaks the immersion if you use it every few seconds, and it is nice to have it there to encourage taking more risks and trying new things, because you can reload very quickly. So in the end it did end up enhancing my experience. 

I think also just playing better and learning to wrap my head around the mechanics has made me enjoy the challenge more. The game is not forgiving mechanically, but it is cool to pull off plans and maneuvers that require split-second timing and precision. The tactical pause feature is very nice that way. 

All in all, I've changed my negative review to positive after giving it another go, and I do recommend trying it out!

Good story, WWII historical game from the perspective of Soviet soldiers and citizen-soldiers fighting a guerilla war on their German-occupied home turf.  Interesting cast of characters, including a 14 year old boy armed with a slingshot, a hunting knife, and a grudge against the Nazis.  On most missions you can choose to go in guns blazing and grenades flying, but usually I preferred the stealth approach.

I found the gameplay to be kind of like XCom, but it real time.  There is a tactical feature that lets you just about pause the game (time still advances, but really slow) so you can issue your keyboard/mouse commands without getting blown to pieces while you're fumbling with the controls.

Graphics are as good as they need to be.  View is from above at an angle, but you can control the camera to spin any direction you want and there's an amount of zoom in-out to be used too.  Controls seemed a little wonky at first, but I got used to them.  Voice acting is there, it's all in German and Russian, but you get subtitles (mine were in English, I don't remember if there was an option for others).  The game crashed on me one time, but I didn't really get the feeling that it was buggy.  I saved frequently so it wasn't a big loss.

Maybe skip this one if you don't like stealth, or lack patience trying to figure out how to progress.  If you have the patience to solve these puzzles and play the stealth game I highly recommend.  It took me just under 35 hours to complete the story on "easy" level (which I found plenty challenging).

I mean, it does look like a cheap indie game and optimization is kind of horrible (I've experience some serious [b]FPS[/b] drops on the machine that can easily run the third [b]Witcher[/b] on max settings), but still, there's something about it that gives you an authentic feeling. Playing this game is like having fun with those plastic miniatures from [b]ZVEZDA[/b]. You know, that certain manufacturer of scale models and historical miniatures. Some sort of Russian [b]Airfix[/b]. [b]Partisans 1941[/b]? It does look like one of those great historical dioramas. Talking about historical part, though. That's the tricky part here. See, this game? It's far from being historically accurate. The funniest thing about it is the fact that it feels [i]exactly[/i] like Soviet schoolbook. That's [i]exactly[/i] how Soviet kids used to learn their history. Every single character here is superhero, saint and a poet. All at the same exact time. Fighting in the name of [b]Lenin[/b], [b]Stalin[/b] and other butch... I mean, God (wait, mentioning God was against the law in Soviet Russia, my mistake). Even the criminals here are saints. Because those are [i]Soviet[/i] criminals. And, as we all know, those [b]Red Army[/b] dudes were without sin or fear. [i]Not[/i]. Like I said, though, that's the tricky part about this game. And you know what? I actually liked all that. I mean, come on! Having a serious approach on all that “[i]for Mother Russia![/i]” stuff from [b]Red Alert[/b]? It's pretty fun. Heck, it's your unique chance to get into a Soviet kid's head right here. And since the game claims to be a fiction from its very first screen... Like I said, I kinda enjoyed that “very Soviet” approach.

Finally, like many other Russian games out there, this one comes with some really nice ideas. Technically, there's nothing groundbreaking here. Don't expect this game to show you anything you haven't seen before. And yet, [b]Alter Games[/b] (not to be confused with [b]ALTAR Games[/b], creators of [b]UFO[/b] trilogy) created a pretty interesting blend. What we have here is a mix between [b]Silent Heroes: Elite Troops of WWII[/b] ([b]Men of War[/b] series spin-off) and [b]Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines[/b] with some base building elements. Sounds great, right? I mean, seriously. Controlling a group of Soviet partisans during the [b]World War II[/b], getting the new members on the way, building the base, playing through non-linear missions full of stealth and action? It's gotta be great, right? [i]Right?![/i]

Well, unfortunately, it's time for me to put my [b]Grumpy Cat[/b] face on and say “[i]nope![/i]”. Because this game? It's anything [i]but[/i] great. First of all – it's terribly, [i]terribly[/i] made. “Fog of war” mechanics is so screwed up that very often you'll die just because enemies will appear from nowhere (the game will assume that enemies are still covered by fog of war, while it totally won't look like it to you). Stealth is mess and lacks the most basic indicators. You played [b]Desperados III[/b]? [b]Shadow Tactics[/b]? Yeah, well, this game is nothing like those. Ages old [b]KOREA: Forgotten Conflict[/b] was more advanced than this bull. Heck, even the very first [b]Commandos[/b] was more advanced than this. You want an example? Here's an example: in this game you can whistle to get enemies' attention. But there's no way to tell who'll hear you. Like... seriously, [b]Alter Games[/b]? [i]Seriously?[/i] And it's not only that. [b]Partisans 1941[/b] is also one of those games, where half of the time you'll get “game over” screen just for being seen or heard by the enemy. One mission even comes with a timer. Because everybody likes having stealth, instant deaths [i]and[/i] timer at the same exact time, right? In other words, the conditions here are pretty brutal (especially on high difficulties), but the tools you have are so dumb and limited that it feels absolutely... completely... terrible. Playing this game is like driving the Russian car. Long story short – you won't want that.

Naturally, quite a lot of bugs is included too. For example, it's pretty easy to get one of your characters stuck in some objects with no way to get out. Happened to me in pretty much every single mission here at least once. And I played the game almost a month after the initial release, after it already got some updates. And the worst thing? Sometimes you'll only notice that you're stuck [i]after[/i] you'll overwrite your save file. Seriously, once I've almost finished a pretty hard mission and then noticed that one of my guys got stuck in the bed and therefore I can't move him to the exit. * Sigh * What am I doing with my life... I must be a very bad person to deserve all that...

And you know what? It's not like the actual game makes it worth all the suffering. Just because... like everything else here, the core mechanics is surprisingly dumb and limited too. I mean, OK, we didn't get quality. But can we at least get quantity? Well, the answer is still no. Because it looks like in Russia, you can't have even that. Even though you will have some tactical freedom during the missions, there are only [b]15[/b] of them, the maps are very small, level design is really boring and uninspired, etc, etc, etc. No optional missions available, of course, and even the base building turned out to be a huge disappointment. Long story short – you just send your troops to get some loot (alternatively, you can collect it during the missions by yourself) and then you build some structures, in which you'll be able to make food (hunger is a thing here, but most of the time you won't even think about it) or upgrade weapons. The end.

So... yeah. Even though [b]Partisans 1941[/b] is far from being the worst game I've ever played (like, seriously, [i]far[/i] from it, since I've sure seen things in my life), it's still far from being good. This game is a sad story of some nice ideas meeting lack of skill and talent. As usual. Paying [b]$29.99[/b] for a game, in which you'll fight terrible [b]UI[/b], bugs and lack of any balance whatsoever is... Well, with enough vodka on you, you may as well go for it, but honestly, go buy yourself a balalaika instead. You'll have more fun that way. Dixi.

What a delightful piece of eurojank.
Ok, techincally, russ-jank. But the point remains. It's a flawed little gem in the vein of S.T.A.L.K.E.R or the first Witcher. If that seems like high praise, it is. 

It's a lot of fun once you start to wrap your head around the lack of polish. Simple inventory commands we think of as standard are hidden in sub-menus, sometimes the HUD is a law unto itself and guards get stuck on alert, partisans get stuck in skills and you'll catch yourself asking "bug or feature" over several unexplained design choices, but despite all of this, I really loved it.

 I'm getting towards the end of the campaign now and the story isn't complex, but it's engaging and serves to drive some interesting missions, the characters are solid and come with a good range of skills, however there are some that are infinitely more useful than others. "Whistle" for example is borderline game breaking and will let you happily lure guards, one by one, to their deaths all day. 

The stealth aspects are solid, if somewhat 'cheese-able' as mentioned before. I feel that the game could have used a little more polish in that aspect, for example, A stationed guard who sees you for a second will either ignore you or go straight to combat, there is no jump to the 'search' state  (as triggered by finding a body or an explosion etc.) for a partial detection. A guard will return on his loop to talk to a room full of guys who have all mysteriously vanished and won't notice. However at it's core, despite my nitpicks, it's a solid system and it works very well for the core gameplay. 

The gameplay loop relies on this solid foundation. Each area of the map is a fun little puzzle to be solved and the variety of skills available give you plenty of room to be creative. Here stealth and combat intertwine. You can choose to pick off the guards one at a time, ghosting them one by one as you misdirect and lure them from their buddies. You can set up a devastating ambush to lure them into a minefield. Take out a few key pieces of their defence and set up  a  characters special ability to clean house. Combat and stealth follow the same DNA, for open combat to be successful it must be planned and prepared. 

Several reviews point to the combat being a bit ♥♥♥♥, I disagree. While your partisans can't hit the broadside of a barn in the first mission or two, they gain proficiency quickly. Simply opening up into a pitched battle with a german platoon with your 3 guys doesn't work and it if it did, that would make 99% of the game redundant. Funnel that platoon through a chokepoint into your crossfire and drop a grenade on them or trap them where your skills can work. The maps are varied and interesting, sometimes very challenging, sometimes blown wide open by the inclusion of a certain skill in your roster. 

The graphics are functional and I had no performance issues on a mid range PC. The base building/management is easy enough and just serves as an way to top up resources, heal fighters and upgrade weapons. The resource management doesn't add anything, or take away from the game. 

I guess what I'm getting at is that to me, it's that pure eurojank vibe, like S.T.A.L.K.E.R you can have a lot of fun with the game, but you'll get out what you put in.  Don't expect a polished perfect game, but a fun little sandbox to kill fascists in.

Well made game, squad members have diverse abilities, numerous ways to resolve most of the combats - stealth vs special abilities vs gunfights. Subject matter is well presented - neither the Soviets nor the Nazis are caricatures. Touches on matters relating to atrocities committed against civilian population by Nazi and their collaborators.

Overall, I recommend this game to people who love the genre. It have some interesting pivots from the typical tropes that I like, however they aren't always well implemented. For those wanting to get a first taste in the genre I'd recommend the much more polished games like Desperado III or Shadow Tactics.

Pro's: 
*The non-stealth combat is actually fun and engaging. I honestly think there's a better game buried within focused on using their combat mechanics across larger and more expendable squads.
*Killing lots of Nazi's

Con's: 
*The story and character building is as basic as it comes.  
*Glitchy. It's frustrating when you have to completely change how you are fighting through a mission because enemies are stuck on doors or just flat out see through them.
*It's not always clear when attacking an enemy squad with combat will result in the entire base falling on you or just an isolated skirmish. Why does getting caught put the entire base on alert and effectively end the mission but shooting at them doesn't?
*The inventory and menu system needs a revamp badly. Highly frustrating at times, particularly in-between missions.

Neutrals: 
*The overarching "meta game" of collecting resources and materials is a great idea, but it's implemented in a way that makes it mostly pointless filler. Upgrading weapons is nice, but feels pointless when some late-game key missions require stealth.
*The skill system is a good idea, but ultimately not particularly impactful as there are key skills (weapon updates, abilities) and non-key skills like sprinting, backpack space, etc. And you really only level up enough to get the key skills.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
Partisan 1941 is a real time tactics where you control a group of partisans resisting against invading Nazi force. For what was seemingly a Commando clone, Partisan shuffled up the system to accommodate a more combat-oriented gameplay and light role playing system. The result is a fun, flexible system that encourages more adaptive playstyle than almost strictly stealth focused gameplay of Commando likes. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]
[*] Good sized level that can be tackled in multiple ways with different strategies.
[*] Variety of characters with different skill trees to fit into your plans and setups.
[*] Well done resource and inventory management adds layers to the tactical choice during gameplay.
[/list] 

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
[list]
[*] Inventory UI is clunky.
[*] Game Performance left a lot to be desired considering the level of fidelity it offers. 
[*] Base building element is shallow and doesn’t add anything meaningful to the overall experience
[/list] 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The main bulk of your time will be spent on missions. It’s where your partisans will stab, shoot, or blow up nazis. In this segment, you choose 3 Partisans of your choice, and thrown into the level. The freedom given in tackling the levels is quite satisfying. With one or two exceptions, players are given goals such as eliminating certain enemies or rescue missions or gathering intel. 

[b]Combat[/b]

Combat works similar to real time isometric RPG. if you choose partisan(s) and click on enemies, they will attack with their equipped weapons. Cover and positioning matters as these are the key to casualty-free combat. The real time element actually feels refreshing especially when you see your plan unfold. In turn based games like xcom, time basically stops until either player or AI take actions, resulting in unlimited moments to think about your next move. In Partisans, your survival in combat depends on how you react to the events happening on-screen. 

The addition of slow-mo also will help you, but the clock will still tick, so a fast response is still needed. One of my best example was using my SMG unit to drew fire while my shotgun wielder ambushed them. Another squad were closing in to ambush my SMG, so i threw a grenade on them with my 3rd character, got 2 of them while 1 ran and i killed them with a melee attack. 

It’s not a perfect system, as sometimes cheese just happens on its own. I’ve killed like a dozen units with a single grenade because the enemies were clumping on the screen and reacted poorly. They usually ran from grenades, but it might be a glitch that the crowd didn’t disperse and the explosion caught all of them at once. Overall when it’s working as intended, the combat is brilliant and fun. When it doesn’t it either can lead to funny, cheesy moments or just reload from your save before you engage. 

[b] Stealth [/b]

Discretion is another option when going through a level. Detection is based on 2 factors: vision and sound. Each enemy has a vision cone, and each action made by your character such as running, or shooting a gun produces sound. If you are either seen or heard, enemies will send one or more squads to investigate for a time. If you are detected during this time, combat will ensue and you will be on a disadvantage. 

Stealth-kill is directly related to melee skill. With high melee skill, you can take out higher-ranked enemies silently and quickly. If your character’s melee skills are low, you can kill regular soldiers easily. If you try to take on an officer, your partisan will make a lot of noise as the victim struggles that will ensue instant detection unless the surrounding area is clear of enemies.

Maximum melee skills are also only owned by certain characters. The decision of who you bring during missions will affect your style as each character has their own forte. Each character has 2 types of skills: unique and generic. Generic skills are shared between other characters like gun skill or carry capacity, but each also has their own unique ability. One character specializes in stealth and has the skill to lure enemies out and take them out silently. One specializes in machine guns for suppression or crowd control, et cetera. All these factors meld together into a flexible, fun gameplay. 

[b] Base Building and Morale[/b]

To be honest, it’s a part of the gameplay that can be easily omitted and wouldn’t change anything for better or worse. In between missions, you have to manage your partisan’s camp. Each day will consume food for each member of the resistance. There are daily tasks that you’ll assign to each member, each have different functions. Some will raise the soldier’s morale (which determine their effectiveness), some will get you resources or food. There are some “off-screen” missions that basically can give you extra XP or equipment. The problem is the system is really shallow. You will basically never run out of resources as long as you spread the tasks evenly. The only useful part about the base is, you can spend resources and assign characters to craft usable items like health packs or grenades.

[h1]Technical Issue and Performance[/h1]
[b][u]Specs: GTX 1080, Ryzen 3700x, 16 GB RAM, 1440p[/u][/b]
The game’s performance leaves a lot to be desired. In later, bigger levels the game runs at 40-50 FPS. The game visual isn’t technically demanding so it should have been better. It doesn’t really distract your gameplay experience since the game doesn’t depend much on quick reflexes. 

As for bugs, per v1.03 minor bugs still exist such as weird enemy behavior and overall lack of polish. My main complaint is how cumbersome the UI is, especially the inventory screen. Organizing your equipment feels like a chore because you have to click right for a drop-down menu to show weapon stats instead of a floating bubble that automatically appears when you hover over the items. 

[h1]Visuals and Graphics[/h1]
This game doesn’t have zillions of polygons nor fancy shaders and effects but strong art direction glued the pixels on the screen very well. For example the muted color palette reflects well on the game’s setting of early wintry russia. Aesthetics wise, I have no problem but functionally, some parts of the design can be confusing. With some characters, especially those who wear similar clothes and body type, it’s sometimes hard to distinguish them on the screen unless you click on them. 

[h1]Audio and Sound[/h1]
The sound is acceptable across all boards. Sound effects, voice acting, music does all it’s job enough. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Partisans 1941 shakes the formula of real time tactics games enough that it is quite worthy of your time. Some of the edges are rough, but if you are a fan of commandos and the like and looking for something similar yet different, i cannot recommend this enough.

This game is really very, very similar to Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun, up to the animation of stealth kills. Which is honestly great - because the former is one of the best stealth RTS games. But instead of shinobi clan, here you will lead a band of partizani fighting nazis.

Pros:
-Very interesting stealth actions
-Deep, realistic and lovable characters

Overall: 9/10, great tactical game, albeit a bit linear. But if you don't mind and just want hardcore stealth-oriented tactical game - buy this. Also, must buy if you liked Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun.

Partisans is a good game, but it isn't a flawless game. Controlling the actions of your partisans can be complicated. It is probably meant to be easy and/or controller friendly, but in reality it is annoying to use and sometimes flat out impossible. Also, vision cones don't always accurately show what the AI can see. The game generally does a good job explaining various mechanics, but it isn't always clear how various mechanics actually work for various types of enemies. Trial and error seems to be required and if things do go wrong, there is a plethora of options to go 'loud'. 

The missions are engaging and fun to play. Level design makes sense and, with the exception of some later ones, does not feel 'bloated' like desperados III. 

The story is garbage Russian revisionist history. Jewish people don't seem to exist. Partisans are portrayed as white knights in shining armour. Germans are portrayed as sadistic, evil brutes. The painful irony is that the protagonist would have been a victim of the Gulag system after the war since he starts the game as a POW. The Soviet brutality is not even mentioned in passing. The commissar who makes his appearance later on is portrayed as a grizzled fighter rather than the useless waste of space commissars usually were in historical reality. (Their sole job was to keep the fighting men ideologically 'pure' and loyal to Stalin. They were the ones ratting out people, for both real and imagined failings.) Apart from this, the story is apallingly bad as a story. The game doesn't need the story, though. 

Partisans has some rpg elements to it, as well. Your partisans level up along the way and you get to loot weapons, food and equipment during the missions. You have to build your base as well and manage food and morale. It is largely meaningless. It is easy to manage. It is a nice touch you need to loot everything you need, as it adds an authentic touch. Partisans wouldn't be normally in any kind of position to receive supplies. This aspect could be very interesting, but it needs more than a little bit of work. Especially the fact that killed soldiers drop random loot rather than the weapon they use is absolute nonsense. 

What makes this game great regardless of the above is the fact both stealth and guns truly work. If you want to ambush patrols with grenades and smg's: you can do so. If you want to sneak your way through, this works too, with some notable exceptions. The game is at its worst when large numbers of enemies are spawned and thrown at you in waves. (Easily dealt with through mines.) The combat relies heavily on cover. The AI is more than capable and should not be underestimated. As most commandos type games, nobody seems to care much if fellow soldiers disappear one by one. Officers do mind, though, and following searches can quickly escalate to nasty gun fights. 

Ultimately, as an avid commandos fan, I loved playing my way through the missions that despite the cringe worthy story nearly always feel meaningful. I just wish there were a few more missions to play through. Despite the fact I am a slow and careful player who combes through every nook and cranny, I finished the game in under 40 hours.

1. Bugs. A lot of them. 2. The number of people on missions. The logic of sending three people to the last, most difficult, tasks is incomprehensible. I was sure that four could be sent on the last assignment, but no! Well, come on, does it religion that won't allow you? Or is three is some special lucky number? I understand that this is explained by the need not to attract attention, but I am not asking a whole squad. At least four! Moreover, on some assignments we have four people - but not on the last! No, of course, in fact, the tasks are quite comfortable with three, but still ... In general, here I rather grumble and the voice of a swag lover speaks in me)
3. Level-up. Even Zorin himself cannot be leveled up to the end - not to say about other characters. And this despite the fact that almost all killings I committed secretly (the game generally directly pushes on a secret path, but this is its plus, which I will talk about later). And I also don't quite understand why the developers decided that. Is it for partisans don't turn into uber killing machines? They will not, even with full skills. Now is ointment, because, as comrade Isaev teaches us, it is the last words that remembered.
1. I never imagined that I would play my favorite Commandos in a genetically familiar environment. For this alone, the game can already put an unconditional A.
2. The characters of the heroes. They are really different, so the heroes differ not only in their abilities. The authors somehow managed to create real, living characters that you empathize with with a few lines of biography and voice acting, and together with Fetisov you shout "Eat the lead!" and together with Morozov you whistle falsely "Buy bagels, hot bagels") The commissar is absolutely wonderful, a man of iron will and iron hand. "I myself will not give up and I will not allow others" - that is how it should be.
3. Much has been written about this already, but it is a true reflection of reality. The Soviet people are not represented as bloodthirsty madmen who kill for the sake of murder, and at the same time are at war only because there is a "zagradotryad" (c) behind them. Moreover, for an attentive player, the game provides an opportunity to feel those conditions. If you have no food, what will you do? It is not good to take food away from local residents, who were already robbed by the Germans, but you are taking away, in essence, not in order to eat and be in comfort, but in order to continue the struggle. The commissar blew up the train and thus caused a punitive operation against local residents. Yes, he did it on purpose. But had he rather to sit in the headquarters and do nothing? It isn't him who started this war, it isn't him who harm civilians.
4. Excellent display of battle. First of all, guerrillas shouldn't get involved in combat at all. If the battle has begun, then the partisan was mistaken. Combat is the task of the regular units. The partisan's tasks is sabotage and stealthy murders; he will lose in a direct battle. Therefore, the game is pushing with all its might to covert passage, and rightly so. Skirmishes are well displayed. Leaned out - fired, didn't really aim - hid. Repeat until you hit or be hitted. One, or, if you are STRONGLY lucky, two hits on you - and you're gone.

[h1][b]Introduction[/b][/h1]
I was naturally interested in [b]Partisans 1941[/b], as real-time tactics games based on [b]World War 2[/b] are quite rare lately, especially when they offer a bit more unique view on skirmishes behind the enemy lines rather than on commanding the [b]Red Army[/b]. In the end, it surprised me how I was thrilled to start a new mission each time, but my enthusiasm went a bit down due to constant performance issues and occasional minor bugs. As if we could not get a decently done game in all aspects lately.
[h3][b]Story[/b][/h3]
[b]Operation Barbarossa[/b] is in its full swing. [b]Axis[/b] and their allies cut deep into the Soviet territory, on their quick way towards [b]Leningrad, Moscow[/b], and oil fields. However, the plot takes place behind the enemy lines, where commander [b]Zorin[/b] tries to form a partisan group. His goal is simple: sabotage Axis forces as much as possible, which would help his comrades on the battlefield. So, get your ushanka, papashka, and a bit of vodka because we will need them for some time.

While a simple plot like this is enough for such a game, I would expect that the characters on which the game focuses would have more depth and that their relationships would develop during the campaign. Unfortunately, all the characters just fulfill the basic character tropes without bringing anything new to the table. There is an over-enthusiastic kid, a commander who gets along with everyone, a woman in the role of a caring medic, and so on. I found myself rolling my eyes a few times as I successfully predicted the dialogues’ outcome based on the characters’ personalities.

Nevertheless, the plot still manages to provide a decent amount of motivation for finishing it, as Germans often take revenge on innocent civilians, so, as a good samaritan, I have to help these poor souls. An addition of which I am fond of is [b]Polizei[/b] forces, which consist of Russian turncoats, so you even have to fight your own kind. There are also a lot of collectables, presented by authentic newspaper, letters, and photos, from which you can learn a bit more about this conflict, which is something I appreciate a lot.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2279674796
[h3][b]Gameplay[/b][/h3]
Even though the plot is a mixed bag, the gameplay itself makes up for it. I finished the game’s campaign in about twenty-five hours, playing it rather stealthily with a few gunfights. If you are familiar with other games from this genre, such as [b]Commandos[/b], you will feel right at home. You have to plan your next steps carefully, or your beloved partisans will end up eating dirt. Enemies always outnumber you, so patience is the key to successful sabotage. Your main objectives are something you would expect: killing commanders, destroying Germans’ stuff, and so on. It is both hard and enjoyable to get to these targets.

You always choose up to three partisans before each mission, allowing you to equip them with various weapons, grenades, mines, medical items, and other accessories. However, each partisan has a bit different and unique skills, so you want to give certain weapons, like shotguns, to someone who is suited for it. As I preferred a stealthy approach, I chose a partisan who can whistle to attract enemies, while the other one kills them with throwing knives. Various skills like these allow you to combine them in action, making the game very satisfying to play.

Even though you can hide in bushes or behind obstacles, stealth is not always that easy. Sounds are as important as your visibility, and enemies can even hear the bodies which fall on the ground. The bodies also have to be hidden from their sights. Later on, there are often dogs that can sniff you out, and I had quite a lot of troubles with them. Also, Nazi officers control the numbers of their soldiers and can start an investigation even if only one is missing. The last thing that I found interesting about stealth is that not every partisan is capable of performing quick melee stealth kills. While a trained soldier does not have a problem with slicing enemies’ throats, a boy or female medic struggle with it. That does not make them useless, as they are useful in different situations.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2279673867
However, open combat might be inevitable at some point, and being careful during gunfights is even more important, as it might turn into a slaughterhouse within a few seconds. The AI tends to take cover a lot, tries to flank you, or use grenades to lure you out from cover. They also love to call for additional reinforcements, which is overwhelming for your tiny but brave group. Using firearms does not always lead to a massacre, as you can set up ambushes by spacing out your partisans and placing a few mines. And witnessing the successful outcome is just delightful to watch.

Missions are not the game’s only content, as you have to manage a camp between them. You have to gather food and upgrade materials there, which is important for your crew’s survival and upgrading your equipment and the camp. There are also several tasks, which partisans do automatically. It reminds me of [b]This War of Mine[/b], although it is simpler, and the game’s main focus is still the missions, yet it is a great addition. Overall, I loved all the Partisans 1941’s gameplay aspects. Each mission is a bit harder, providing new challenges to overcome. It does not give you anything for free, but it is also fair.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2279673205
[h3][b]Audiovisuals & Performance[/b][/h3]
What [b]Partisans 1941[/b] excels in is the atmosphere of the gritty Soviet lands, as it looks quite realistic with a bit of cartoony style in characters’ appearance. Despite being set in one region, it still manages to provide the environmental variety, from muddy villages and swamps to train stations and fortresses. It is not only the visuals, as all the sounds and soundtrack just absorbed me into this game.

To make your experience even more immersive, I recommend switching to Russian voice acting, which you should do anyway because the English one is terrible. Germans are not affected by that, as they always speak in their native language. Even though I hate Nazis with passion, I find censoring svastika as a bit hypocritical decision, especially as the game shows other questionable symbols and hints on Nazi war crimes all the time.

Unfortunately, the worst aspect of this game is its optimization. I tested the game with an [b]i5 8300H, GTX 1060 6GB, and 16GB RAM[/b], running at high settings, at [b]20-50 frames per second[/b], at [b]1920x1080[/b] resolution. With such a framerate, it is sometimes a bit unpleasant to play, and four missions did not even go above 20 frames at all! I also encountered a few minor bugs, such as not being to loot items until finding the right camera angle. Admittedly, the developers work on fixes with passion, and several bugs got fixed during my playthrough.

[h1][b]Conclusion[/b][/h1]
[b]Partisans 1941[/b] excels in its gameplay and atmosphere, which I enjoyed so much that I can overlook horrendous optimization. While I am giving it a positive rating, you should reconsider whether to wait with your purchase. Nevertheless, fans of the real-time tactics genre should definitely give it a try sooner or later.

This game was a very pleasant surprise. It's the best new release that I've played in quite some time. The look, feel and sound all do a great job of transporting you into the setting of the game (world war 2's eastern front resistance). The storyline is quite basic, but I grew fond of the different characters and I think the game does a very nice job of giving some representation to the often overlooked eastern front. And even with a relatively straight forward narrative, I was drawn to continue playing often, because the actual gameplay was so rewarding. 

The missions are a nice mix of various tactics, heavily focusing on stealth. However, even though stealth is the primary focus of the game, I was really impressed by the wide range of viable tactics that one could take to approach any given situation. All of the characters have interesting and unique abilities which can be combined for even more diverse strategies to accomplish objectives, and playing with all the various characters is fun and engaging (except maybe Trofim....sorry Trofim).

The one caveat I will give is that the game is currently still undergoing some developmental polish, so there are some bugs that range from inconsequential to potentially gamebreaking. In my opinion, the game is good enough to still recommend in its current state, despite the rough edges. The developers are actively engaged in the forums and are constantly taking and responding to feedback, which is also encouraging. 

The only other criticism (which is actually more of a compliment) is that I wish there was more. That's not to say the game is too short; I think it was actually a pretty decent amount of missions (I finished the game in about a month playing it semi-regularly) I just enjoyed playing it so much that I wanted to keep playing. Hopefully the developers will continue the series in future installments.

This game has many technical issues:
- way too long load times, even from an M.2 SSD (and you'll be reloading a lot)
- quicksave doesn't always save the game, even though it says it does
- after load the gamestate isn't always the same as it was when you saved it, eg. loot disappears, closed doors are open or vice versa etc.
- steam achivements don't always trigger
- vision cones don't work right
- AI enemies change their routine when you get near them, even though they aren't "officially" aware of your  presence
- the list goes on, there's just too much to list.

With all that being said... it is a fun game, if you can get past the problems. The gameplay gets the tactical stealth formula right, every kill is satisfying, and the combat strikes a good balance between chaotic and tactical. The atmosphere is really nice, it does a good job of painting the eastern front of WW2 (or more like behind the front,) which is often sadly underrepresented in games. The characters are likeable if one-dimensional, and the story is predictable but still draws you in. The dialog is cheesy, with a professional but not great Enlish VO, but it all adds up to a consistent experience, that maybe mimics a Soviet propaganda movie, with the devilish Nazi villains and the overidealized heroic partisans.

Conclusion: if you like Commandos-like games, interested in the eastern theater of WW2, AND they fix the bugs (I played on V1.01,) then it's worth a buy.

I had high hopes for Partisans 1941 but was unfortunately disappointed by the playstyle encouraged by the game's mechanics. To put it simply the game requires a lot of trial and error, a lot of "save scumming" to progress through the levels. This makes the game quite slow to play as players will find that they'll have to repeatedly load previous saves due to information not conveyed effectively by the game.

Another problem with Partisans is that the controls themselves are not really that ideal. It isn't always super clear which character you have selected and on numerous occasions I've accidentally moved a character that I thought I didn't have selected and had my cover blown. It's almost as if the game pushes you to use the number keys to select your units instead of with the mouse. There's also the fact that anytime one of your units are spotted the enemy instantly knows the positions of the rest of your units even when seperated.

Furthermore I'm disappointed by the lack of small-scale limited missions. There's no opportunity to set up small, isolated ambushes, raids etc. Every mission is a large setpiece with a unique objective. While this is good as it means variety it also means that each level plays out the same, stealth kill every enemy before going loud for the last three opponents.

I can't recommend this game until they fix the awful loading times (installed on M.2 SSD) and the finicky and imprecise controls. The number of times I have had to reload because one of my partisans walked into a bloodbath because the game decided I wanted to click on the item a good ~half-inch away from the cursor marker is infuriating. The optimization is also so-so; with a 5700XT and 3600 I often float around ~50fps on larger maps with lots of enemies.

Partisans 1941 has been every bit as good as I had hoped.  The campaign has established main characters with some level of character development as opposed to generic characters with permadeath like you'll find in other RTS games.  The inventory management and base-building systems are a welcome addition and they add lots of time to the playthrough.  These systems are crucial to progression so the player is rewarded for the time they spend strategizing.

There are a few bugs here and that is to be expected in an indie title like this but there is a save-scum option on all but the highest difficulty so the bugs aren't much to write home about so far.  Another complaint is the load times on larger maps.  In a save-scum-style game in which you load often, waiting 20+ seconds per load gets very frustrating.  These times do seem to be proportionate to the map size so it's not an issue on smaller missions.

Partisans is for sure worth the money.  If you enjoy games like Shadow Tactics, Desperados, or Mutant: Year Zero, this will be right up your alley.

This prevents quick takedowns and relocating of the body.. and regularly is a reason for being spotted. If only the characters were trained in keeping hold of their victims.... (or at least through the use of a skill point).

[b]Static cover[/b] 
Cover only allows for 2 or 4 sides to be used depending on how big the cover is. If an enemy is diagonally placed relatively to your cover, you will have no cover at all from any of the sides. 

[b]Bad pathfinding [/b].
Your characters will get stuck behind the smallest of obstacles and sometimes even take a detour instead of a straight line. This can result in moving into enemy vision (instead of the saver straight line) where they will blitzkrieg your ass in a heartbeat.

[b] Unwanted interactions [/b]. 
Left mouse button triggers movement, (theoretically) opens door, interacts with hiding places, takes cover, loots supplies, picks up enemies, loots enemies, picks up thrown weapons, interacts with gun emplacements, interacts with objectives, interacts with light/alarm switches and attacks enemies. This goes wrong more than once.. and always at the wrong time. I would like to see key + mouse click combinations to seperate these actions.

[b] Unwanted interactions part 2. Stealth [/b]. 
While doing a mission full stealth, it doesn't help if your characters randomly decides to attack an enemy rambo style. There's also one character that can go incognito and walk around. But if you've clicked too close to an item (wall or crate), he will suddenly take cover and open fire. If you've clicked on a bush with a body in it, he will grab his big ass shotgun and of course trigger the enemy to go instant blitzkrieg. 

[b] Confusing character shortkeys [/b]. 
You can select your characters through keys 1 - 9 as you would expect.. BUT, characters are placed in order that the game wants. This would be fine, if not for the fact that each mission you can have other characters and they are always placed on the first few keys. You will have to remember what character is placed on which number by the system each time you start a new mission. Sometimes these placements are even changed after loading a quick save. It would've been better to allow users to assign their characters to certain keys, or simply have a dedicated key per character (which should be possible as long as there are max 10).

[b] Kamikaze nazis [/b]. 
You found great cover and flanking positions? Too bad. These nazis got nothing to lose. They will swarm your position without taking cover themselves, or even throw a grenade at their own feet if they can take you down with them.

[b] Unclear hiding places [/b]. 
You can use foliage for cover. But with the angle of the camera it's not always clear what's considered hideable foliage or foliage simply functioning as a wall. If you do find foliage where you can hide, it's not always clear where it ends. The character is marked as hidden or not through a barely noticable striped overlay.. so maybe it would help if the bushes themselves could have some sort of highlight on mouse over or when a character is in it.

At first it seems that the creators really want to be the new Mimimi Games, but this impression quickly dissipates, because they immediately offer many interesting things that create the obvious face of their game. To be honest, this game is much more real Commandos than the recent «Commandos 2 - HD Remaster», truly the spiritual successor to this great game. Real-time tactics, telling about the frightening time of the beginning of the Great Patriotic War, when Nazi troops of Germany treacherously attacked the Soviet Union. The player will have to take control of a detachment of partisans, gradually growing into a full-fledged military force, beating the enemy with inexorable methods. What is especially pleasant - we not only participate in direct partisan operations, but we ourselves equip life at our base, plan to supply the detachment with food, materials, create new buildings that help to more effectively survive difficult everyday life. All this skillfully alternates, so there is no time to get bored, and the gameplay becomes much more unusual.

The game is skillfully distinguished by one feature that you do not immediately feel, but after understanding it, you begin to experience emotions in a completely different way. The game world is completely insecure. You cannot endlessly hide in the bushes, knocking out enemies one by one, even if the enemies will not find you there easily, but German Shepherds can easily sniff out your trail, exposing your shelter. You cannot headlong into open combat, enemies with much more powerful weapons will blow you away in no time, so you start thinking like a partisan - to plan ambushes, engage in open firefights, only by correctly placing your fighters in good cover, use laying mines on patrol roads or approaching routes of possible reinforcements, think over all your moves in advance. The feeling of constant anxiety will become your main companion, fleetingly letting go only during gatherings in a partisan camp. And it all becomes a huge win for the game.

What pleases even more is the humanity with which the writers reacted to their characters and story. The heroes are very convex, their emotions are natural and understandable to the player, they are not just cardboard dummies, but real characters. Fetisov and Mellenberg turned out to be a little stereotyped, but not to say that they were especially critical. Russian dubbing of characters is generally great, I advise you to play with him and subtitles, I have not heard such an excellent performance for a long time, a deep bow to each of them for their excellent work. I sincerely empathized with each character, and at some point I wanted the developers to use their rights more often and force them to play for different characters, and not just for your favorite three of heroes. On assignments, you can find various interesting interactions, and I would like it to be even more. Much more, as well as additional quests. After all, when the locals share with you the location of the caches with weapons, the routes of the occupiers, while still telling their story, this is just an invaluable feeling of the completeness of the world. The player can also find a lot of real archival materials telling about the exploits of the partisans of those years, and also get acquainted with the famous guide to guerrilla warfare.

The difficulty is extremely high, the enemies are smart and do not allow you to relax. The gameplay at the maximum difficulty level generally requires a brutal expenditure of forces. Yes, the game still needs to be polished, especially the famous Doors, which are almost more insidious here than the SS men, living their absolutely special door life. I met a critical bug only once - in Prison, when the game stubbornly failed my mission when Morozov hit a certain point in a location near the prison cells, and this place had to be defeated in very clumsy ways, moving towards the goal almost by a millimeter. And after polishing, the game should finally shine the way it deserves. My personal big thanks to everyone who made this game, you did not shame the memory of the winners in that war. There should be more of these games, I am absolutely delighted.

It's a fun game in the same style of Commandos or Desperados (or Shadow Tactics), albeit with simpler mechanics:
* There is no concept of height, no towers, no high ground with better visibility
* Enemies don't go looking for their suddenly missing comrades, they just keep patrolling their paths, even if you lure dogs away from three-party patrols and kill them, the patrols will just go about their business as if they never had a dog
* Your partisans aren't as specialized as your characters in the other mentioned games are. Most skills are interchangeable with just a few being character-specific. Eventually I found myself using the same three partisans over and over as one can lure people out by whistling and one can then kill them quickly by throwing knives. All the other partisans and their skills are basically redundant.

It also has A LOT of bugs. All of which I could work around:
* Sometimes the camera gets locked in one place of the map. This happened to me during the prison mission when one partisan was still outside the compound. The camera would lock on them after another partisan triggered the cutscene inside and couldn't be moved. Only solution is to reload a savegame and move the partisan inside before triggering the cutscene.
* Enemies will sometimes stop dead in their tracks and stop patrolling. Saving and reloading can fix this.
* In some missions, you cannot lure people out of rooms as they won't find the door. They will just run into the wall next to the door and then return to their business. 
* Enemies can often see you through closed doors.
* Sometimes enemies will randomly start searching for you with no apparent reason. This is especially frustrating when there are achievements that require you not to trigger alarms.
* Several achievements seem to be broken. For example, I finished the game and thereby destroyed the train gun, yet didn't get the achievement. Same for multiple "finish mission without being found" and "don't trigger an alarm" achievements. I carefully watched not to do those things, yet never got the achievement. Also didn't get the one about completing the whole group nor the "kill three people with one landmine", despite doing that several times.
* Often the roofs of buildings don't disappear when they should, making planning with people inside rooms difficult
* Skill radiuses don't respect elevated territory or work inside rooms. Especially when luring people out of rooms, you need to see the radius of the whistle skill. It will show on the outside but not on the inside. 

Some things are a bit odd in terms of gameplay for a game in this genre:
* Some missions require you to fend off waves of enemies. You don't know this in advance and hence cannot plan ahead (by choosing and equipping the right partisans for example). These situations just randomly happen and you're in luck if you brought enough mines along to deal with this quickly. Otherwise these situations are a total pain to deal with.
* Between the missions there is some X-Com style base building and chore-running that you need to feed your partisans. This doesn't really add to the gameplay and quickly becomes tedious. Just as chores are. 
* For a game that considers saving and reloading part of its gameplay, loading takes a heck of a long time. 
* You cannot replay individual missions after finishing the game. If you don't create a single save per missions (which I didn't for most of the game as it wouldn't let me before the first hotfix), you cannot go back to them after the campaign is done.
* It it sometimes extremely hard, if not impossible, to interact with something in the world. If you pile multiple corpes over another, interacting with one in particular becomes insanely finicky. Same for boxes and cabinets. Also it is close to impossible to plant mines or tripwires among corpses as the corpses apparently have higher interaction precedence. 

I still recommend the game to both lovers of the genre and newcomers. It's really fun to play, challenging but not unfair and tells a nice story that I enjoyed following. Most the bugs and quirks will surely be fixed soon and I can totally see myself come back to the game in a few months to play it again and see how it developed.

Partisans 1941 is a mix of the old Commandos games and the Russian-made real time strategy/tactics series Men of War, with a dash of the XCOM style metalayer in there too. As the title suggests, you control a band of Soviet partisans during the Nazi invasion of the USSR in 1941, and the game consists of a series of missions (semi-scripted and hand-crafted, not procedurally generated and random – worth clarifying I think) with the opportunity to manage your partisan hideout between them, and send your guerrillas off on tasks that will resolve off-screen, such as supply raids or ambushes.

Proper missions consist of a mix of stealth and combat, often switching from one to the other – you can sneak around to set up the perfect ambush, then Go Loud with grenades and gunfire before returning to sneaking around – as long as your brief firefight didn’t result in any alarms being set off or reinforcements called in. This means you want to target things like German radiomen, or maybe set up traps near alarm systems that enemies might run to activate, while also trying to get it all over and done with as quickly as possible and with as little meaningful return fire as you can manage. Your partisans are capable, but they’re always heavily outnumbered and even on the lowest difficulty (which the devs recommend you pick for a first playthrough) they’re vulnerable to gunfire if not in cover.

This all combines to make for a very satisfying gameplay loop – reminiscent of XCOM 2’s ambush phase out of combat, or even the feeling that you get from clearing a room quickly in an action game like Hotline Miami. The stealth itself is robust enough (although it can get a bit fiddly indoors – more on that later) and you have some fun abilities to get you through the few enforced stealth segments in the game. For the most part, missions are generous in letting you raise the alarm and still continue, but a handful of missions are either entirely or partly dependent on a failstate if you alert the enemy. These missions are also the more linear ones – most of the others present you with a location and let you pick how to approach it, but the forced-stealth missions are more reminiscent of the ‘one optimal path from end to end’ design seen in games like Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. This isn’t necessarily a negative.

The partisans themselves are also fixed characters, unlike most other similar games where they’d be randomly generated to some extent and based around archetypes or classes. Each character can use every weapon and item but they have their own skill tree that boosts their effectiveness with, say, rifles or shotguns or pistols, as well as some unique abilities for each one. Red Army captain Zorin can throw knives, for instance, and ex-sergeant Fetisov can fire long bursts from SMGs that kill everyone in a cone in front of him. As another example, Sanek the 14-year-old who’s definitely lining up some heavy-duty PTSD for later in life can exploit his youth and saunter around in the open without attracting attention because the Germans just think he’s a kid. This variety is cool and gives each partisan their own particular niche, but since they can make use of every normal weapon and item anyway the game gives you a lot of flexibility in how you approach situations.

The characters themselves don’t have particularly deep characterisation or development as the story progresses, but it gives a nice sweep of the different kinds of people who would potentially get involved in a partisan unit – soldiers, aggrieved locals, ex-criminals, and so on. It’s also nice to see the representation of women in the unit, since female partisans were not at all uncommon historically. The story is also fairly straightforward and doesn’t really have a particular arc, but it does a good job of presenting different scenarios for each mission – rescuing a hunter in the woods, ambushing a supply convoy, saving townsfolk from SS deathsquads, staging a prison break, etc.

The plot is also pleasingly willing to confront the brutality of the Nazi invasion of the USSR – reprisals by the Germans against civilians are a constant theme, and the threat of torture and murder and casual cruelty from collaborators is always looming. The atmosphere is compelling and convincingly realistic, even though your unit of defined partisans has an unbelievably good success rate – I suppose if the developers wanted to convey the high rate of deaths among WW2 partisans then they’d have had to come up with another couple hundred characters to rotate in and out of your unit, which is a bit of a tall order, I guess. Even so, the portrayal of the Eastern Front is head and shoulders above that of the whitewashing of games like Company of Heroes 2. I also appreciated being able to switch the spoken audio to Russian while keeping the subtitles in English – I don’t speak Russian but I do enjoy that kind of linguistic immersion, and I liked that the Nazis still spoke in German throughout too.

The user interface is generally good but could use some tightening up. The way cover positions are calculated and displayed is a bit fiddly, especially indoors (it’s impossible to take cover around open doorways, for instance), and doors themselves are a pain in the backside to deal with at the moment as they’re prone to swinging open and shut repeatedly when you activate them, although I understand the developers are looking to fix that. While the inventory management is mostly fine you’ll definitely get bogged down in swapping the appropriate ammunition between people who need it (and it took me quite some time to be able to distinguish the different types of rifle and pistol ammo based on the icon rather than having to meticulously hover the cursor over them each time). It made me miss the feature in Men of War where looting bodies or containers with a group selected would ‘smartly’ assign ammo to everyone who had the relevant weapons in their inventory. It can also be annoying that view cones – showing where exactly enemies are looking at any time – are the same overlay colour on the ground as markers for using abilities, which can make it tricky to set up ability usage while also keeping an eye on who can see what.

The last thing I have to say about Partisans is that when it ended, I really wanted more. The story, as mentioned, doesn’t really have much of a climax, and while I guessed that the final mission was in fact the finale based on its title, it doesn’t feel like an appropriately large event to close a narrative campaign. I held out some hope that it would in fact just be an End Of Act 1 situation, especially as the last shot in the game before credits is of your partisan camp now snow-covered and wintry – I was really hoping for a winter segment to the campaign, particularly with the mentions in-game of ‘fishing before the lake freezes’ and so on. This is both a compliment and a criticism, I guess – it felt like the game was a bit too short, but also I was having so much fun with it that I wanted to keep going. I hope the developers are able to make more of this game, either in the form of DLC or an expansion or sequel.

[u]Leveling[/u]
This current system is great if you can pick 3-4 favorites that you will use through out the game. But if you would like to keep things interesting by changing up your squad composition each mission it is not really worth it because of level differences between all your partisans.

It would be much better if all XP gained would be added to all your partisans equally. That way they would all be the same level and it would not feel like putting your self in a disadvantage just for trying to enjoy the game by playing all the possible characters. If not as a update to the default way this game plays, it would be nice to see it added at least as a playthrough modifier that you could turn on at the start of a new playthrough and could not disable it later on.

[u]Deciding who you will bring for each mission[/u]
For most missions you get to pick who gets to come, but there are few where the game forces 1 or even all three (very rare). I would change this up for all the later missions where the player can only pick 1 partisans so that they can always pick two at least. If we fail to pick a combination that works, we can always restart the mission, that should be up to us. Maybe the game could just say "you should probably bring X and Z for this mission", but leave the choice to the player, because taking this choice away from the player when he had it previously is just no fun.


[u]Only being able to bring 3 partisans for each mission[/u]
A lot of times I was thinking how cool it would be if I could bring all my Partisans to a mission, especially past the first half of the game when you already have quite a large group. I understand that with how leveling works in the game now it would not be really balanced, because you would soon have a small army of really strong (high level) partisans. Just as with my suggestion for the different leveling system, I think being able to bring as many partisans as we have would make for another really cool playtrhough modifier which we could only enable at the start of a playthrough and not disable it later on. The way I would go about balancing it would be to lower all XP gains...


[u]Difficulty[/u]
I played on normal difficulty, but would have really loved to played on hard. The only reason I did not pick hard was because in this  game on hard there is no saving the game! I would add the "no saving" as a playthrough modifier that can only be enabled at the start of playthrough and not disabled later on. This way players who actually have the time can still play like that, and the players who do not have the time can also experience the hard difficulty mode.


[u]Mission design[/u]
Out of the 15 missions the game has, I really enjoyed 13 of them, the other two, not so much and they both shared one same mission objective - defend against waves of enemies. I was playing on normal difficulty and these two game segments were impossible to overcome using the same tactics I was using everywhere else. The only way I was able to beat this was to restart the mission, bring all the explosives I had stashed, and abuse the system in the game where you know roughly where the next wave will come and I would just put a mine there or throw a grenade there just as the enemies were spawning. This was the least fun I had in the whole game because I knew I am exploiting the system and was just save scumming to make sure my mines are in the right place.... I would change these two missions so there is only maximum of three waves.

Formula of the game: Shadow Tactics + WW2 setting + Russian "Great Patriotic War" propagandistic narrative + "quality" of Russian gamedev.

This game was clearly aimed at Russian audience first and foremost, it has soul and atmosphere, and those are something that got the most love from the devs. Russian voice actors did a fantastic job, so did the artists and the composer. If I were revieving this in Russian, I'd probably have given it a thumbs up after all.

And yet, if one refrains from aforementioned subjectivity and evaluates this game for what it is, things are much less pleasant.

1) Very buggy and unpolished, with bugs ranging from mild annoying to major feature-breaking ones.
2) Nonexistent balance, with some characters having lots of OP abilities at once, and others being absolutely useless.
3) Totally dumb AI which makes laying huge minefields on every level your main tactic - make some noise and whole level will happily run into these, in a nice tighly packed groups of 5+ enemies, no less!
4) Stealth is broken at worse and frustrating at best, meaning the most non-annoying way to play is to kill everyone on the level - meaning no replayability.
5) Game is pretty short and mechanics like base management are only there to artificially extend the playtime.
6) The story is pretty generic, no love given towards character development or similar. Instead, there's a lot of "patriotic" black-white propaganda, like the game going out of its way to make you hate polizei (your own people) more than Nazis and to actually force you to kill all of them, either giving you xp for that or outright making that your level objective. Polizei are exclusively presented as looters, thieves and murderers, which is ahistorical and makes no sense. 

Long story short, while the game copied gameplay and features of games like Shadow Tactics diligently, it is much less polished&balanced, and you are not likely to enjoy it unless you're a Russian player with a thing for the atmosphere and the narrative.
